operator_plays.name: Distressed Asset Recovery
operator_plays.mechanism: Locate mispriced, orphaned, or administratively stranded assets—tax-sale overages, unclaimed state funds, dormant judgments, government surplus lots, or distressed micro-businesses—and capture a contingent recovery fee or acquisition spread.
inputs: Tax-sale excess proceeds ledgers
Unclaimed property & judgment dockets
Surplus auction manifests
workflow: Audit statutory fee caps, claim windows, and chain-of-title encumbrances
Execute skip-tracing or asset inspection to confirm net realizable value
Lock in contingent recovery agreements or below-intrinsic buyouts
metrics: Gross spread / contingent fee per case
Claim approval rate
Days from filing to disbursement

platform_risks.failure_mode: Statutory fee-cap compression or administrative hold
platform_risks.trigger: Jurisdiction updates finder fee limits, waiting periods, or filing documentation rules
platform_risks.impact: Reduced net fee margin or extended cash conversion cycle
platform_risks.detection_metric: County/state rejection notice rate and days-to-payout variance
platform_risks.fallback: Diversify across multi-state dockets and use attorney-backed filing partnerships where required

operator_plays.name: Dormant Chrome Extension & Shopify App Roll-Up / Monetization Flip
operator_plays.mechanism: Scan the Chrome Web Store, WordPress Plugin Directory, and Shopify App Store for high-install (10,000–250,000 active users), 4.5+-star free utilities neglected by solo developers, acquire them at 1–2x potential annual cashflow, and introduce clean freemium Pro tiers or opt-in contextual partner offers.
inputs: Chrome Web Store / Shopify / WP plugin scraper filtering by active installs, rating, & last-updated date (>12 months)
Asset Purchase Agreement (APA) & Chrome Web Store developer-account transfer checklist
Freemium Stripe checkout SDK + non-intrusive opt-in partner recommendation module
workflow: Identify utility extensions and micro-apps with strong organic weekly installs and zero monetization whose solo creator has not pushed an update in 12–24 months
Acquire the codebase, store listing, and domain for $3,000–$35,000 with an escrowed transfer through the official developer console
Ship a Manifest V3 maintenance update first to build user trust, then grandfather existing free features while adding a $7–$19/mo Pro power-user tier or explicit opt-in partner deals
metrics: Acquisition payback period (target 2–5 months)
Free-to-Pro conversion rate (1.5–4%) + monthly ARPU per 1,000 WAU
Post-acquisition review rating stability (>=4.4 stars) and uninstall rate (<3%)

platform_risks.failure_mode: Chrome Web Store malware/policy takedown or mass 1-star user revolt after acquisition
platform_risks.trigger: Injecting silent background adware/tracking scripts post-acquisition or locking previously free core features behind a sudden paywall
platform_risks.impact: Permanent Chrome Web Store removal and total write-off of acquisition capital
platform_risks.detection_metric: Zero CWS permission-scope expansion without user opt-in and daily 1-star review velocity monitor
platform_risks.fallback: Never inject hidden tracking or background ad scripts; keep existing permissions narrow, grandfather all legacy free features, and monetize strictly via additive Pro workflows

operator_plays.name: Chapter 11 Bankruptcy Schedule E/F Trade-Claim & Convenience-Class Rollups
operator_plays.mechanism: Purchase documented small trade claims below risk-adjusted expected plan distributions, accounting for objections, assignment procedures, and plan rules that may prohibit claim splitting or aggregation benefits.
inputs: Bankruptcy schedules E/F and claims register
Invoices, payment history, and assignment documents
Proposed plan classification and distribution waterfall
workflow: 1. Reconcile scheduled trade creditors with filed claims and supporting invoices
2. Model recoveries under plan amendments, objections, setoffs, and convenience-class eligibility
3. Buy eligible claims through documented assignments and complete required transfer notices
4. Monitor objections and confirmation, then reconcile distributions to each acquired claim
metrics: Purchase discount to risk-adjusted recovery
Allowed claim value versus purchased face value
Realized return and days to distribution

platform_risks.trigger: Disputed invoices, setoff rights, or plan restrictions on purchased or split claims
platform_risks.impact: Reduced distribution or complete capital loss
platform_risks.detection_metric: Objection rate and eligible allowed value per portfolio
platform_risks.fallback: Stop affected purchases, enforce documented seller recourse where available, and price only supported general-unsecured recoveries

operator_plays.name: Aged Shelf-Corp Reinstatement, Primary Tradeline & 0%-APR Corporate Credit Stacking
operator_plays.mechanism: Compare reinstated entities and genuine business credit facilities for working-capital financing; entity age is not operating history, and promotional APR economics require accurate underwriting and repayment capacity.
inputs: Entity filings, beneficial ownership, and liability searches
Verified operating financials and genuine supplier tradelines
Lender eligibility, promotional APR, fee, and guarantee terms
workflow: 1. Audit the entity's ownership, tax liabilities, and reinstatement requirements
2. Disclose acquisition and actual operating history; establish only genuine paid supplier accounts
3. Compare lender-approved applications with full debt disclosure and consolidated exposure limits
4. Fund documented business expenses and repay before promotional expiry using cash-flow reserves
metrics: Effective borrowing cost including fees
Debt service coverage under post-promotion APR
Utilization and days to promotional expiry

platform_risks.trigger: Misstated operating history, undisclosed debt, or expired promotional terms
platform_risks.impact: Account closure, accelerated repayment, and guarantee exposure
platform_risks.detection_metric: Underwriting discrepancies and stressed repayment coverage
platform_risks.fallback: Halt applications, correct disclosures, and use a transparent term facility or reduce financed spending

operator_plays.name: FERC / ISO Substation Interconnection Queue & Powered-Land Option Flipping
operator_plays.mechanism: Overlay public interconnection queues with land-use and substation data to option potentially useful sites, treating queue position and nearby infrastructure as signals rather than guaranteed deliverable power.
inputs: ISO and utility interconnection queues and study results
Parcel zoning, transmission corridors, and substation maps
Utility service estimates and developer site requirements
workflow: 1. Match queue activity and infrastructure constraints to suitable parcels
2. Verify site control requirements, zoning, environmental limits, and utility capacity assumptions
3. Negotiate assignable diligence-contingent options within capped carrying-cost budgets
4. Assign approved options to qualified developers with explicit disclosure of unresolved power and study conditions
metrics: Option cost per qualified developable acre
Utility-validated capacity versus marketed capacity
Net assignment proceeds after study and option costs

platform_risks.failure_mode: Queue withdrawal or prohibitive network upgrade cost
platform_risks.trigger: Restudy, milestone failure, or capacity estimate unsupported by utility commitments
platform_risks.impact: Option expiry and unrecoverable diligence spending
platform_risks.detection_metric: Study cost revisions and unresolved interconnection milestones
platform_risks.fallback: Let contingent options lapse or reposition land for independently viable uses without claiming secured power

operator_plays.name: Automated Form 8850 WOTC (Work Opportunity Tax Credit) & Section 41 R&D Contingency Engine
operator_plays.mechanism: Automate employer-authorized WOTC screening and separately substantiate Section 41 research credits, earning outcome-linked service fees only where permitted; program authorization, qualifying activities, wage coordination, and professional fee restrictions govern each claim.
inputs: Consented hiring records, Form 8850 responses, and payroll hours
Research project evidence and qualified expense ledgers
State workforce certification procedures and tax-year credit and fee rules
workflow: 1. Confirm WOTC authorization for each hire date and complete required prescreening by the job-offer date
2. Submit Form 8850 and required supporting forms within the applicable 28-day deadline and track state certification and qualifying hours
3. Separately document Section 41 qualifying research and expenses, reconciling wage overlap and applicable deduction adjustments with a tax professional
4. Obtain employer and preparer approval before filing, retain audit support, and collect permitted fees without guaranteeing credits
metrics: Timely WOTC certification submission rate
Substantiated credits realized by the employer
Net permitted service fees after review and filing costs

platform_risks.failure_mode: Credit denial or impermissible contingent-fee arrangement
platform_risks.trigger: Expired program authority, late certification, unsupported research expenses, or restricted practitioner compensation
platform_risks.impact: Reduced credits, amended returns, penalties, and fee repayment exposure
platform_risks.detection_metric: Deadline exceptions, certification denials, and unsupported expense share
platform_risks.fallback: Exclude unsupported claims and use compliant fixed-fee payroll and research-documentation services under independent tax review

operator_plays.name: Commercial Solar Tax-Equity Flip & Bonus-Depreciation Strip Syndication
operator_plays.mechanism: Arrange commercial solar partnership-flip investments that allocate supported tax benefits and cash flows to genuine equity owners; depreciation cannot be sold as a standalone credit, and allocations require economic substance, tax compliance, and securities-law review.
inputs: Solar project costs, ownership records, and operating contracts
Investor tax capacity and dated depreciation eligibility analysis
Counsel-reviewed partnership waterfall and securities offering documents
workflow: 1. Underwrite project cash flows, eligible basis, construction and service dates, and current credit and depreciation availability
2. Verify investor suitability, tax capacity, at-risk and passive-loss limits, and applicable securities and intermediary requirements
3. Structure counsel-approved partnership allocations and flip terms with genuine equity risk, basis adjustments, and recapture protections
4. Close through authorized intermediaries and monitor operations, tax reporting, and flip conditions before distributing permitted fees
metrics: Qualified tax-equity capital closed
Realized investor distributions versus underwritten waterfall
Net permitted placement fees after legal and diligence costs

platform_risks.failure_mode: Tax allocations disallowed or unlicensed securities placement
platform_risks.trigger: Unsupported depreciation stripping, inadequate economic substance, ineligible project timing, or unauthorized transaction-based compensation
platform_risks.impact: Tax assessments, recapture, investor losses, and fee disgorgement exposure
platform_risks.detection_metric: Unresolved tax opinion conditions and securities compliance exceptions
platform_risks.fallback: Suspend solicitation and closing, use appropriately licensed intermediaries, and restructure only as independently reviewed genuine equity ownership

chapters.question_prompt: What is entrepreneurship through acquisition, and why would someone buy a business instead of starting one?
chapters.title: Entrepreneurship Through Acquisition: The Case for Buying Instead of Starting
chapters.subtitle: ETA defined by professors, brokers, and attorneys; search funds vs. buying outright; startup failure risk vs. acquired cash flow; who ETA fits; and university ETA programs from HBS, Booth, MIT-adjacent, INSEAD, UW, and Texas A&M
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners from HBS, Booth, INSEAD, the brokerage desk and the M&A bar converge on one thesis: buy a cash-flowing small business rather than build one. Startups fail at roughly one in five in year one and half by year five, while the SBA default rate sits at 2%, and small firms trade at a half to a third of private equity multiples. The street mechanics are specific: source through brokers, trade-show lists and direct outreach; screen at about 4x cash flow; close on an LOI, 60 days of diligence and a QoE; and fund with SBA 7(a) debt up to $5M, a seller note and $100-150K of working capital. Disagreements center on brokers, who are fertile ground to one buyer and picked over to another; deal-size floors; entry multiples of 4x versus 6.3x; and whether to take investor money.

key_metrics.context: Stanford data cited at the William & Mary ETA session as the average return across the ETA ecosystem.

key_metrics.label: Small-Firm Multiple Discount
key_metrics.value: $1M EBITDA sells for about $4M; $10M EBITDA sells for $100M at 10x
key_metrics.context: Ruback and Yudkoff on small-firm multiples running roughly half to a third of private equity multiples, their 'magic is in the multiples' thesis.

sections.title: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every operator on this roster opens from the same premise: a startup has to invent a product and a market at once, while an acquisition buys demand that already pays. Doug, a four-time CEO with 26 M&A deals and $390M of equity deployed, puts the startup baseline at about 10% dead in year one and about 50% dead within five years, and argues the buyer inherits licenses, processes and, above all, customers [nOnsMlkLh10 @ 00:05:05]. Dallas M&A attorney Kevin Henderson runs a harsher set: one in five startups fails in year one, half by year five, cash flow is the number one killer, and front-loaded build costs run to hundreds of thousands or even millions [YXFpxJrIjD0 @ 00:01:23]. Against that, Henderson sets the SBA's current 2% default rate and states a preference for a 2% chance at failure over a 20% chance 'any day.' The INSEAD faculty framing is the same logic: the founder must create both product and market, whereas the ETA buyer purchases proven demand [i7FBr84AUfY @ 00:01:17]. Dominik Höhener, six months into a first search, compresses it to one image: buying a fruit-bearing tree rather than planting a seed [ybzODlrITiw @ 00:01:43]. The consensus is not that acquisition is easy; it is that the risk is visible, priced and manageable.

The second point of agreement is supply. Joel Ankney's William & Mary session labels it the Silver Tsunami: $7-10T of small-business value transferring or shutting down over 10-15 years, with a claimed 1,500 businesses closing or changing hands daily, a figure the speaker openly doubts [cl31TiHq92Y @ 00:02:30]. Brian O'Connor of NextGen Growth Partners counts more than 200,000 US companies between $5M and $50M in revenue, roughly half run by owners near retirement, with little organized capital chasing them [60ZOJolZwOo @ 00:08:48]. Business broker Kristina Wynne sees the street-level version of the same wave: owners selling for health, family and age, and most of their children not wanting the business, which is why Wynne frames ETA as buying an existing team, systems, clients and brand [uwpDjf5v_jM @ 00:01:36]. The Prince George's Chamber panel layers in demographics: about 75M baby boomers retiring and passing on wealth against 82-83M Gen Z, plus late Gen Xers nearing 50, the age when 'a lot of your entrepreneurial millionaires started' [QtvW_tq7sAQ @ 00:03:10]. Wynne's own desk shows the flow in practice: new listings arrive 'pretty much every week,' from a $37,000 juice bar to a cannabis transport license. The shared operator takeaway: this inventory will either transfer to a new owner or shut down.

The baseline prerequisite the practitioners agree on is an operator's temperament, not a pedigree. Matt of the Fundamental Investing Institute stresses the 'entrepreneurship' half of ETA: these are operating entities that need leadership and owner oversight, not passive investments, and the buyer is not buying a stock [ei0nfdOmHL4 @ 00:01:45]. Royce Yudkoff and Rick Ruback, who grew the HBS course from 17 students to almost 4,000, say no MBA is needed: learn proof of cash from bank statements in Excel, since most current owners lack an MBA and, by their own admission, most HBS students can't do proof of cash either [c1OtHjDpymM @ 01:07:17]. INSEAD's profile of the winning searcher is industry-agnostic, self-confident but humble enough to earn the trust of investors, sellers, employees and customers, respectful of the existing culture, resilient and passionate about operations [i7FBr84AUfY @ 00:04:57]. Ruback, who works with about 200 MBAs a year, reframes risk: it exists in big businesses too, but the small-business owner gets visibility into it and gets to manage it [oJcm3Bn-lXE @ 00:11:39]. The shared baseline is blunt. You are buying the CEO seat of a cash-flowing company with customers, workers, suppliers and a working model already in place, and you must actually want to run it.

sections.title: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Deal flow is a volume game run through specific channels. Doug's sourcing map starts with roughly 6,000 business brokers, then lawyers and accountants, small investment banks and the deals PE funds reject, friends and family, and direct lists worked by phone, mail or email [nOnsMlkLh10 @ 00:13:46]. The first screen checks location, size, profit, B2B versus B2C and fit; the second checks price at about 4x cash flow, seller dependence and seller financing; and a buyer should expect to review dozens or hundreds of companies. Jesse Sapphire of ABG Print mailed an Oriana Capital brochure to about 250 brokers; one replied a year and a half later, the deal fell apart twice, and the full search ran two years [MpeYmBDptXs @ 00:31:52]. Brian O'Connor's NGP treats broker listings as picked over and builds target lists from trade-show exhibitor rosters instead [60ZOJolZwOo @ 00:49:02]. The UW panel names the data stack, Grata, ZoomInfo and Sourcescrub, and warns that high-volume cold email is now hard to send, while traditional searcher Nikita Sunilkumar still pairs cold email and calls with brokers to build a proprietary pipeline [c0fXb_wXv7A @ 00:40:39]. Doug's governing rule over all of it: manage deal flow efficiently, 'because the only thing you really don't have is time.'

Once a target clears screening, the paper sequence barely varies. Doug runs a non-binding IOI, then an LOI with exclusivity, then the purchase agreement, staffed by a small-deal lawyer, a QoE accountant, an insurance broker, an asset appraiser and a benefits broker [nOnsMlkLh10 @ 00:21:08]. Joel Ankney has closed about 150 deals on LOIs because lenders and brokers want them; exclusivity is binding, delisting is requested but negotiable, every NDA gets reviewed, and the speaker once struck a clause that would have made the buyer pay the broker's commission [cl31TiHq92Y @ 00:14:17]. Ankney's diligence clock is about 60 days, with a 30-day offer countered at 45, financial work first and legal second, an equity purchase where federal contracts would not survive an asset sale, a founder-signed non-compete rather than one signed only by the seller's LLC, and lawyer fees of 0.5-1.5% of price, about $15K on a $1-3M deal. Doug's diligence floor is 36 months of bank statements plus a quality-of-earnings report at about $20K [nOnsMlkLh10 @ 01:03:45]. On add-backs, the Prince George's panel walks a landscape design firm whose books carried three Europe trips; two were added back, roughly $30,000 of earnings recovered for valuation [QtvW_tq7sAQ @ 00:29:58]. The panel's closing rule: be willing to walk away.

The financing math is where the multiple turns into wealth. Kevin Henderson's worked example: $250K of profit bought at the 4x median for $1M, 90% SBA-financed as a $900K loan with $100K down, $11K a month for 10 years, or $132K a year, leaving about $120K in year one, with a 10% improvement adding $25K [YXFpxJrIjD0 @ 00:05:27]. Doug lays out SBA terms as a 75% guarantee, $5M maximum, 10 years, about a 10% rate, no covenants and up to 95% financing; on a $4M price that means roughly $600K of annual payments against about $400K of residual cash flow, with debt required at 50-75% of any deal [nOnsMlkLh10 @ 00:34:38]. Jesse Sapphire's $10M template is $6M bank, $2M equity and $2M seller note, with seller debt sitting second-lien, on standby or interest-only, at a fixed rate, and treated by banks 'almost as equity' [MpeYmBDptXs @ 00:41:52]. For the funded model, Brian O'Connor prices $2M of EBITDA at 5x for a $10M enterprise value, 50% debt and $5M equity, with the searcher holding 25% of common vesting one-third at close, one-third over four years and one-third on IRR [60ZOJolZwOo @ 00:34:25]. Doug's capital rule frames the whole stack: debt wants one times its money, equity wants three.

callout.title: Negotiation, Networking and Deal-Protection Moves From Active Searchers
callout.body: These are the small, specific moves practitioners use to win deals, preserve goodwill and avoid paying for terms that do not belong in small transactions.
items: Open low and concede gracefully: searcher Antonio's rule is to open at 2.5x, and Ruback advises giving a quarter or half turn to preserve goodwill, because 'if the deal is good at 3, it's still good' [HBS Rock Center for Entrepreneurship — oJcm3Bn-lXE @ 00:57:40].

Work a geography belly to belly: Ruback says 'belly to belly sales' beats national email campaigns, and a Houston searcher's rule was never having lunch alone [HBS Rock Center for Entrepreneurship — oJcm3Bn-lXE @ 00:46:43].
Spend marketing dollars where they land: Jesse Sapphire's top-ROI move at ABG Print was $800-1,000 of Chick-fil-A dropped off with business cards [The Wall Street Skinny — MpeYmBDptXs @ 01:11:45].

Refuse mid-market terms on small deals: Joel Ankney pays no deposit on deals under $5-6M, calls a deposit request 'a red flag,' and rejects breakage fees as 'mid-market creep' from $20-50M deals [Joel Ankney — cl31TiHq92Y @ 00:35:06].

sop_steps.title: Fix the Search Box and Funding Model
sop_steps.action: Decide location, time commitment and industry, then choose self-funded or investor-funded search.
sop_steps.detail: Doug frames the search on location, time commitment and industry, and calls the funding choice, self-funded or investor-funded, the most important decision of the search [Technically News — nOnsMlkLh10 @ 00:09:50].

sop_steps.title: Build Deal Flow and Run Two Screens
sop_steps.action: Source through brokers, professionals and direct lists, then screen twice before spending diligence money.
sop_steps.detail: First screen covers location, size, profit, B2B/B2C and fit, followed by a teaser or CIM under NDA; the second screen tests price at about 4x cash flow, seller dependence and seller financing, across dozens or hundreds of companies [Technically News — nOnsMlkLh10 @ 00:16:03].

sop_steps.title: Sign the LOI and Run Sequenced Diligence
sop_steps.action: Lock exclusivity with an LOI, then run about 60 days of diligence, financial first and legal second.
sop_steps.detail: Joel Ankney plans about 60 days in a 30-90 day range, counters a 30-day offer with 45, and uses an equity purchase when federal contracts cannot transfer in an asset sale [Joel Ankney — cl31TiHq92Y @ 00:15:14].

sop_steps.title: Stack the Capital, Protect the People, Close
sop_steps.action: Layer SBA debt, seller note and working capital, and make key-employee retention a closing contingency.
sop_steps.detail: Ankney makes key-employee and subcontractor retention a closing contingency [Joel Ankney — cl31TiHq92Y @ 00:39:49], and Doug's post-close rule is no personnel changes in the first six months [Technically News — nOnsMlkLh10 @ 00:58:40].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The opening fight is price. Doug, the 26-deal operator on Technically News, runs a second screen at roughly 4x cash flow and calls $1–3M EBITDA the sweet spot, branding anything under $500K too risky and anything over $3M too competitive [nOnsMlkLh10 @ 00:30:10]. Brian O'Connor of NextGen Growth Partners quotes the Stanford entry multiple at 6.3x yet reports seeing 4–5x in practice, where a 5x purchase throws off a 20% unlevered free cash flow yield [60ZOJolZwOo @ 00:16:07]. On the HBS Rock Center panel, two-year searcher Antonio opens every bid at 2.5x and asked how Jeff closed at 3x. Rick Ruback's answer was blunt: "If the deal is good at 3, it's still good," so conceding a quarter or half turn to keep seller goodwill is acceptable, though "maybe not at 6 or 5" [oJcm3Bn-lXE @ 00:57:54]. Size floors split even harder. Ruback and Royce Yudkoff on Acquiring Minds say ETA is moving down-market to $200–400K of cash flow, which forces corporate employers to improve their offer just to compete [c1OtHjDpymM @ 01:11:19]. Doug's playbook would reject most of those targets outright, while the Yudkoff camp argues the multiple discount at the small end is precisely where the magic lives.

Capital structure splits the field. Jesse Sapphire of ABG Print, speaking on The Wall Street Skinny, chose self-funding to own 100% of a "cockroach" printer profitable since 1992, arguing the search fund's 25% carry above a hurdle only pays on high-growth plays and pushes searchers into bigger deals, though "smaller isn't always safer" [MpeYmBDptXs @ 00:25:16]. Jeff Duckworth took no outside money so no board could force a sale, bought six months before COVID, and dodged "ridiculous" board questions [oJcm3Bn-lXE @ 00:51:28]. Newton Campos counters that self-funders raise only after finding a company, which is "harder," while traditional searchers line up roughly $500K of search capital first and $5–20M of acquisition capital later [LOtte4Lq1OY @ 00:07:31]. Sourcing splits the same way. Doug calls the roughly 6,000 business brokers fertile ground [nOnsMlkLh10 @ 00:13:46], while O'Connor warns brokered deals carry winner's-curse risk and broker listings are picked over, so NGP mines trade-show exhibitor lists and goes direct to owners instead. Sapphire landed the deal through a broker anyway, after mailing a brochure to about 250 of them and hearing back from one, 1.5 years later. Geography adds a third axis: Jeff's one-hour Boston radius deterred investors, yet Ruback insists belly-to-belly selling beats national email blasts.

Even the return math and the risk story are contested. Joel Ankney cites Stanford's 34% average ETA ROI against roughly 9–10% for the stock market [cl31TiHq92Y @ 00:06:23], while INSEAD puts search fund IRR at 25–35% and warns returns have gone bimodal, with experienced value-adding investors outperforming and most others underperforming [i7FBr84AUfY @ 00:08:32]. Personal guarantees divide operators too: Doug flags that SBA debt carries an unlimited personal guarantee, $3.8M in a $4M example, and Sapphire calls the guarantee required of anyone owning over 20% "dead on arrival" for search funds, yet Trilogy Search Partners investor Aaron Perrine says the 10-year guaranteed note is "probably not that risky if you do it right" [c0fXb_wXv7A @ 00:35:10]. On pedigree, Campos reports about 85% of searchers hold a top MBA, while Ruback and Yudkoff say no MBA is needed if you can run proof of cash from bank statements in Excel, adding that most HBS students can't do it either [c1OtHjDpymM @ 01:08:00]. Turnarounds split hardest. Campos says a turnaround "is a completely different business," not a search fund at all, yet Sapphire's lived reality was a 95% pandemic revenue collapse, and Ruback dismisses demanding a COVID-proof target as guarding against an alien invasion.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: Deals rarely die on price. Jesse Sapphire lists the real killers: diligence and financing contingencies in the LOI, a key person like "Deborah" quitting, and a target whose top five clients all routed through one referrer, which is why every searcher deal "has hair" [MpeYmBDptXs @ 00:43:23]. Sapphire's own search ran 2 years, and the deal fell apart twice before closing. Jeff Duckworth's 3x purchase came from a fourth-time seller who expensed inventory under nominal accrual accounting with no inventory system, so the P&L had to be backcast and several banks refused to underwrite [oJcm3Bn-lXE @ 00:55:53]. Doug on Technically News sets the forensic floor: read 36 months of bank statements, budget about $20K for a quality-of-earnings report, and treat two sets of books as a red flag [nOnsMlkLh10 @ 01:08:24]. Joel Ankney, after roughly 150 LOI-based closings, catches traps buried in paperwork: an NDA clause that would have made the buyer pay the broker's commission, deposits demanded on deals under $5–6M, breakage fees creeping down from $20–50M mid-market deals, and non-competes signed only by the seller's LLC instead of the founder personally [cl31TiHq92Y @ 00:35:06]. Timelines punish the impatient too: the chamber panel saw one six-week close in about 10 years, with nine months to over a year the norm.

The post-close traps are operational. Sapphire started June 17, 2019, then watched revenue fall 95% and headcount drop from 24 to 4, fully drew a $250K working capital line, took two rounds of PPP, and shifted financial services from 90% to 40% of revenue; 2024 finally beat 2019 [MpeYmBDptXs @ 00:53:49]. Nikita Sunilkumar closed Crown Health in early 2020 and within 10 days lost access to senior buildings, forcing the practice virtual, then spent 2021 hiring providers in a market that was hard "to say the least" [c0fXb_wXv7A @ 00:15:13]. Overconfidence wrecks the people side: Doug makes no personnel changes in the first six months and warns that growth is a suck of cash when you carry debt [nOnsMlkLh10 @ 00:58:40], while Dallas M&A attorney Kevin Henderson warns that day-one changes threaten employee retention, so don't be a "bull in a china shop" [YXFpxJrIjD0 @ 00:07:40]. Sapphire's rule is harsher: you paid for it, so if it breaks it is on you, which means being careful before deciding you know better. The bank failures cut both ways: ABG lost Signature Bank, SVB and Credit Suisse as clients, which Sapphire uses as proof that W2 risk is understated.

The personal toll and capital losses are real. INSEAD reports that about 20% of search funds end in partial loss and 10% in total loss [i7FBr84AUfY @ 00:07:55], and Aaron Perrine reminds searchers that investors' search capital is simply gone if the searcher fails [c0fXb_wXv7A @ 00:30:21]. On the HBS Rock Center panel, Doug traded corporate life for the factory floor, QuickBooks, poor benefits, a lost network and a prestige drop that is hard to explain at cocktail parties; former CTO Kiran went from a $150M budget to $150,000 and gave family an 18-month deadline, and Jeff Duckworth described "free-form anxiety" during the search [oJcm3Bn-lXE @ 00:15:42]. Ruback's antidote is to count contacts each day, not failures, and Ruback and Yudkoff stage a "Stephen King week" of failed searches, using the Great Recession and COVID as a pressurizer stress test while steering students away from capex and inventory-heavy targets [c1OtHjDpymM @ 00:46:09]. Debt economics leave little slack: Henderson's $1M example carries an $11K monthly SBA payment on a $900K loan, and Sapphire borrows at 11.5% because small business lacks good access to capital markets. Doug on Technically News adds that restaurants don't trade at 4x.

callout.title: Pre-Close and Post-Close Kill Switches
callout.body: Four tripwires practitioners hit firsthand. Clear every one before wiring money or touching the org chart.
items: Kill or reprice any target showing two sets of books, and do not close without 36 months of bank statements reconciled [Technically News — nOnsMlkLh10 @ 01:08:24].
Map revenue by referral source; a top-five client list routed through one referrer is a deal-killer, not a footnote [The Wall Street Skinny — MpeYmBDptXs @ 00:44:27].
Strike buyer-pays-commission NDA clauses, refuse deposits and breakage fees on small deals, and get the founder to personally sign the non-compete [Joel Ankney — cl31TiHq92Y @ 00:20:09].
Freeze personnel changes for six months post-close, make incremental changes, and only go drastic if things hit the fan [Technically News — nOnsMlkLh10 @ 00:58:06].

chapters.pull_quote: "Keep in mind price is the only thing that you really can control because you can always walk from a deal." — attributed to Technically News (nOnsMlkLh10 @ 00:30:45).
action_checklist: Lock location, time commitment and industry, then decide self-funded versus investor-funded before sourcing a single deal [Technically News — nOnsMlkLh10 @ 00:11:16].

Build proprietary flow from trade-show exhibitor lists and direct owner outreach instead of relying on picked-over broker listings [The University of Chicago Booth School of Business — 60ZOJolZwOo @ 00:49:02].
Count contacts every day, not failures, and never have lunch alone during a geographic search [HBS Rock Center for Entrepreneurship — oJcm3Bn-lXE @ 00:46:08].
Open bids in the 2.5x–4x cash flow range and stay willing to walk, since price is the only lever you control [Technically News — nOnsMlkLh10 @ 00:30:45].
Stack SBA 7(a) financing up to 90% with a 5% seller note and line up $100–150K of working capital [Joel Ankney — cl31TiHq92Y @ 00:30:48].

chapters.question_prompt: How do first-time acquirers use the Buy Then Build playbook to choose, buy, and grow an existing company without rookie mistakes?
chapters.title: Buy Then Build: The First-Time Acquirer's Playbook
chapters.subtitle: Walker Deibel's acquisition-entrepreneurship framework, the four paths of acquisition, acquiring vs. innovating, buying retiring boomers' businesses with little cash down, rookie buyer mistakes, Hormozi's warning on holdcos and hired operators, and the step-by-step buy-side process
chapters.executive_summary: Walker Deibel, Alex Hormozi, Neil Rice and Jonathan Jay all treat buying an existing, cash-flowing company as the play. Deibel pegs acquisition-entrepreneur success at 98% against roughly 10% for startups. SBA acquisition loans default under 1.7%, while 75% of VC-backed startups go to zero. Boomers retiring at 11,000 a day, with about $10T in business value changing hands, supply the deals. The mechanics are specific: target $1-5M revenue, pay 2.5-4.5x earnings, and finance up to 90% with SBA debt capped at $5M plus a personal guarantee. Run diligence legal first, then financial, then operational, and change processes in months 3-7. Deibel sends buyers to brokers to save two years; Jay sends beginners off-market. Rice leans on seller financing; Deibel has never used it. Hormozi and Deibel attack no-money-down; Jay sells training on it.

key_metrics.label: Acquisition Entrepreneur Success Rate
key_metrics.value: 98% (vs. about 10% for startups and 25% for VC-backed companies)
key_metrics.context: Deibel lines up success rates for startups, VC-backed companies and acquisition entrepreneurs side by side to argue buying beats starting.

key_metrics.label: SBA Acquisition Financing Ceiling
key_metrics.value: Up to $5M for up to 90% of purchase price, personal guarantee required
key_metrics.context: Deibel describes the 2016 SBA change that lets first-time buyers close with about 10% down and no hard-asset collateral.

key_metrics.label: Searchers Who Never Close
key_metrics.value: 90% of people who start looking for a business never buy one
key_metrics.context: Deibel blames missing target statements and missing urgency, noting a focused buyer could own a company within 6 months.

key_metrics.label: Small Business Valuation Multiple
key_metrics.value: 2.5-4.5x earnings (vs. 19-28x for public companies)
key_metrics.context: Deibel contrasts Main Street pricing with public-market multiples to show the arbitrage available to small-company buyers.

sections.title: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: The practitioners agree on the opening math: building from zero is the low-odds bet, and buying a cash-flowing company is the high-odds one. Walker Deibel calls startups "punishment for people that don't understand statistics." Deibel pairs the 75% of VC-backed startups that go to zero against SBA acquisition loans defaulting under 1.7%. Buying an existing company is, in Deibel's words, the "money ball for entrepreneurship," because the buyer inherits product-market fit, customers, infrastructure and positive cash flow [LlIJ71_IXbs @ 00:06:38]. On Jake & Gino, Deibel lines the success rates up side by side: startups about 10%, VC-backed 25%, acquisition entrepreneurs 98%. Only 4% of companies ever cross $1M in revenue, and fewer than 0.5% cross $5M [xpFa8hcRy_k @ 00:04:53]. The Buy Then Build summary on Master Afle adds the venture-side insult: startups raise an average of $41M and still fail 75% of the time [LzJITHl_i2k @ 00:10:09]. Deibel's conviction comes from scar tissue rather than theory. Before buying anything, Deibel worked as a stockbroker through the tech bust. Then an MBA-era startup died when its licensed IP was "yanked," a single point of failure the founders could not engineer around [u2bZWIf9b5k @ 00:07:49]. Every acquisition speaker draws the same lesson. The scarce asset is a business that has already survived its first years with real customers, not a better idea or a bigger raise.

The second point of agreement is supply. Deibel cites boomers owning 12 million businesses, 43% of the total. Eleven thousand of them retire every day, and roughly $10T in business value is set to change hands. That wave lands at the same moment SBA goodwill loans up to $5M opened up with small down payments, the third of three converging trends Deibel names alongside the tech wave [LlIJ71_IXbs @ 00:13:02]. Alex Hormozi reads the same wave from the buyer side. Acquisition is "in vogue" because so many owners are retiring, which creates a supply spike that course-sellers who never made their money buying businesses are now hyping [zVSWRRAfFO8 @ 00:00:11]. Business attorney Neil Rice reports helping "over a thousand people" and works this exact seller pool. Rice targets owners at or near retirement whose businesses pay them $150K-$300K a year and could "double or triple" with fresh attention [pTSIi3Y4_TA @ 00:00:36]. Where to aim inside that supply is settled too. Deibel tells first-timers to buy $1-5M revenue companies rather than sub-$1M shops, because a business doing $600K cannot pay its owner. The instruction is direct: "Buy one that already has achieved that" [SXwOv9QUWws @ 00:18:29]. The overlap is the point. Supply is peaking while acquisition debt has loosened, and the speakers treat that combination as the reason to move now.

The third consensus is that ownership is an operating job, not a coupon. Deibel tells Jake & Gino that risk sits in the entrepreneur rather than the asset, "because the same business under two different people is either going to perform or flounder." Buyers should therefore pick "skill set over passion" and accept that nothing about owning a company is passive [xpFa8hcRy_k @ 00:20:43]. Hormozi puts it more bluntly. A first-timer can close a business earning $500K-$1M a year with no money down and still lack the skills to run it. Hormozi compares that to managing to "BS my way through the negotiations" and then having to "build a skyscraper" [zVSWRRAfFO8 @ 00:01:21]. On what to buy, Deibel ranks tailwinds first and margins second, calling margin "the number one most important thing." One member bought a sandwich business at 1% net margin and was out of business within 90 days. Labor intensity, capital intensity and cyclicality each stack more danger on top [AKE-710SdA4 @ 00:27:47]. The structural rule comes from Deibel's own holdco. Deibel bought six or seven companies across verticals at 80-100% ownership with maximum debt, and the uncorrelated risks turned correlated. The advice to every new acquirer since is "buy one focus on one" [iYE-lc1tFUI @ 00:07:56].

sections.title: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The financing engine behind nearly every Deibel deal is the 2016 SBA change: up to $5M covering up to 90% of the purchase price, backed by a personal guarantee. That is why Deibel says "I've never done seller financing once in my life" and compresses the playbook to "Find a good business, pay a fair price, get SBA debt, and get the seller out of there" [iYE-lc1tFUI @ 00:41:01]. The worked example on DigitalTriggers starts with a $1M-revenue company producing $150K SDE. Priced at 3x, it costs $450K. Add $100K for inventory, working capital and closing costs, and the deal is $550K all-in. A 90% SBA-backed loan leaves a $55K buyer check. Ten-year principal and interest runs about $75K a year, roughly 45% of earnings, and the owner keeps the other $75K [u2bZWIf9b5k @ 00:36:45]. The book's "Nancy" model scales it up. The purchase is $691,200 at 3.2x SDE, plus $200K working capital and $50K fees. Nancy puts $94,120 down and borrows $847,080 at 6% over 10 years. That leaves about $9,400 a month of debt service against $18K a month of SDE, for over 100% cash-on-cash [LzJITHl_i2k @ 00:23:29]. The guarantee is unavoidable. In 14 years Deibel has found no lender without one, because a bank needs one of three things: cash, collateral or a PG [WP5MdYhV05A @ 00:30:25]. The SBA itself acts as the collateral that gets the bank comfortable.

Search runs as a funnel, not a hunt. The Buy Then Build summary sizes the search by SDE rather than revenue and defines industry broadly as product, distributor or service. It sets geography as the first limiter and compresses the result into a one-line target statement such as "$300-400K SDE, Chicago." It calls "the $250,000 to $700,000 SDE range" "the most affordable and stable sweet spot for firsttime buyers" [LzJITHl_i2k @ 00:48:23]. Deibel pushes that statement into the broker channel, which is wider than most buyers assume. There are about 5,000 US brokerage firms, findable through Google, IBBA, M&A Source and the Alliance of M&A Advisors, and they work with sellers anywhere from one month to 18-plus months before a deal transacts [u2bZWIf9b5k @ 00:26:19]. Going straight to brokers is "lopping off two years of time," because "that's where the sellers are going" [xpFa8hcRy_k @ 00:32:31]. In practice the target statement does the screening before any CIM is opened, and every broker conversation starts from the same filter instead of a fresh browse. Once the right deal appears, the LOI is treated as binding in spirit: "if you're not going to buy the business like don't put in a letter of intent it's really an engagement to get married." Brokerages also keep a CRM of buyers whose LOIs never closed, so a walked LOI follows the buyer into every future conversation with that shop [WP5MdYhV05A @ 00:44:00].

The first year runs on its own script. Deibel's own post-close mistake was closing with no plan, and the three-way miscommunication between seller, general manager and owner "destroyed value." The fix is to put a person's name next to every line of the P&L. In the week after closing, set meetings with the top 20 paying customers, and make suppliers wait four weeks [WP5MdYhV05A @ 00:16:59]. Salary discipline is the second rule. A business carrying acquisition debt is "overweight," so Deibel's instruction is "keep your salaries low don't just go in and you know take a CEO salary on day one." Build cash and safety first [aoPPGxWI8dY @ 00:01:31]. Change timing is the third. Deibel rejects the day-one overhaul, the "Elon Musk... Twitter" approach that belongs only in turnarounds. Deibel also rejects the popular "change nothing for a year" rule and steers buyers to the employee goodwill window around months three and four. On the first acquisition, Deibel waited too long and calls it "the mistake I made" [aoPPGxWI8dY @ 00:02:48]. The Buy Then Build summary sequences the first 90 days: assess in month one, build a 13-week cash flow in month two, then execute. It also warns buyers to expect an "11th hour freakout" before the keys change hands [LzJITHl_i2k @ 01:35:43].

callout.title: Edges the Buy Then Build Operators Actually Use
callout.body: Deibel's view is that off-market deals only start showing up once people know you are in the game, so these are the moves buyers use to out-work the fair weather buyers sitting on broker lists [Walker Deibel — SXwOv9QUWws @ 00:46:41].
items: Run the "Sabri curve": review every listing as an academic exercise, even ones you will never buy. Deibel says the reps let them get under LOI within 24 hours two or three times [DigitalTriggers — u2bZWIf9b5k @ 00:30:33].

Pull the time cards yourself. Lucas Phillips bought a quality of earnings report, but the time cards would have shown nobody worked 40 hours a week [Making Billions with Ryan Miller — iYE-lc1tFUI @ 00:31:15].
Strike working capital pegs from Main Street asset deals. Deibel calls them a middle-market import that will "lose your deal" with a small-business seller [Walker Deibel — SXwOv9QUWws @ 00:45:09].
Open a HELOC and line up key-man insurance before closing, while you still look strong on paper to the bank [Master Afle — LzJITHl_i2k @ 01:05:02].

sop_steps.title: Lock the Target Statement
sop_steps.action: Write a one-line buy box by SDE band, industry type and geography before opening a single listing.
sop_steps.detail: Size by SDE, not revenue. Define industry as product, distributor or service, set geography as the first limiter, and write it out, e.g. "$300-400K SDE, Chicago" [Master Afle — LzJITHl_i2k @ 00:50:49]. Put a 6-month deadline on the search, because the no-deadline drift is called "a fatal trap" [Master Afle — LzJITHl_i2k @ 00:54:46].

sop_steps.title: Work the Broker Channel One-to-Many
sop_steps.action: Send the target statement to brokers in bulk and review deal volume until one fits.
sop_steps.detail: Deibel uses brokers "one-to-many" for deal flow [Walker Deibel — t_yGWsgaZ_s @ 00:08:28]. Buyers who close review 60, 70 or 80 deals [Jake & Gino — xpFa8hcRy_k @ 00:34:57]. Show up to broker meetings with a personal balance sheet and resume [Master Afle — LzJITHl_i2k @ 00:57:43].

sop_steps.title: Stack the Capital
sop_steps.action: Structure a cash infusion, a small seller note and an SBA loan through a preferred lender.
sop_steps.detail: Deibel's self-funded structure is a cash infusion, a small seller note and an SBA loan, usually keeping 80-81% ownership at minimum [Walker Deibel — t_yGWsgaZ_s @ 00:07:17]. Use preferred-lender (PLP) banks to avoid 6-8 week delays [Master Afle — LzJITHl_i2k @ 01:02:25]. Pre-qualify early, because Canadian companies, soft growth, too few tax returns and commingled financials all block SBA approval [DigitalTriggers — u2bZWIf9b5k @ 00:47:29].

sop_steps.title: Diligence, Close and Take the Keys
sop_steps.action: Run diligence in legal-financial-operational order, close, then meet the top customers immediately.
sop_steps.detail: Ask only go/no-go questions before the LOI. Afterward, run legal for about a week, then financial, then operational, using Centurica on online deals and CPAs for quality of earnings [DigitalTriggers — u2bZWIf9b5k @ 00:51:13]. The week after closing, set meetings with the top 20 paying customers and make suppliers wait four weeks [Let's Buy a Business — WP5MdYhV05A @ 00:18:02].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: Deal sourcing is the sharpest split. Walker Deibel tells first-time buyers to go straight to brokers because that is where the sellers are going, a move that typically lops off two years of search time [xpFa8hcRy_k @ 00:32:31]. Deibel adds that off-market deals are near-zero odds for outsiders, that broker CIMs are poor, and that the edge comes from out-working the 'fair weather buyers' until people know you are in the game and off-market deals start arriving [SXwOv9QUWws @ 00:46:41]. Jonathan Jay runs the opposite playbook: avoid brokers and listing sites entirely, because beginners should not negotiate against professional sellers, and go off-market directly to owners, never by cold call or mass email [zrmjVDmvL1w @ 00:03:09]. Alex Hormozi sits on a third track, building proprietary flow through content and leverage; that machine produces roughly 3,000 inbound deals a month, about two LOIs a month, and nearly every deal comes from that owned flow [zVSWRRAfFO8 @ 00:03:06]. The volume math diverges just as hard. Jay says look at a minimum of six businesses so you can compare and get a better deal, Deibel says buyers who close review 60 to 80 deals, and Hormozi screens thousands to sign two. Pick the funnel that matches your reach, then run its numbers without blending them.

Financing splits the camp into two religions. Neil Rice, a business attorney who has helped over a thousand people, builds boomer deals around seller financing: on a $400K to $600K business the buyer puts in relatively minimal cash and pays the balance over years, structured so significant cash flow stays with the new owner [pTSIi3Y4_TA @ 00:01:47]. Walker Deibel says flatly, 'I've never done seller financing once in my life,' and points to the 2016 SBA change that funds up to $5M at up to 90% of price against a personal guarantee, which makes 100% seller-financing pitches outdated [iYE-lc1tFUI @ 00:42:03]. Even inside the SBA lane there is friction. The Master Afle summary of Deibel's book calls carrying a 10% to 20% seller note over two to five years highly advantageous, while Deibel notes SBA deals allow no earn-out and force a roughly 10% seller note to amortize over 10 years, which makes seller notes extremely unattractive to sellers [WP5MdYhV05A @ 00:26:47]. On zero-down, Alex Hormozi concedes a business earning $500K to $1M a year can be bought with nothing down, but warns it is not free, because seller or creative financing is still a liability [zVSWRRAfFO8 @ 00:01:47]. Deibel goes further and labels the earn-in path totally inefficient in time and labor.

The seller's role after closing is the third fault line. Rice wants the seller kept on a limited, specific consulting arrangement for six to twelve months to hold relationships and customers [pTSIi3Y4_TA @ 00:02:39], and Mark J Kohler frames a seller note as a 'relationship handcuff' across a first-100-days farewell tour, with the seller setting boundaries and getting paid for the help [eZBAyOccEhY @ 00:16:00]. Deibel's formula is the opposite: 'Find a good business, pay a fair price, get SBA debt, and get the seller out of there,' after downloading the seller's brain [SXwOv9QUWws @ 00:43:53]. Change timing splits too. Deibel rejects both the day-one overhaul outside of turnarounds and the popular change-nothing-for-a-year rule, targeting the employee goodwill window around months three to four [aoPPGxWI8dY @ 00:02:48], inside a broader months-three-to-seven window for process change. Growth strategy is the final contrast. Jonathan Jay sells buy-and-build as combining small companies and selling the larger whole, while Deibel calls a multi-vertical holding company the worst decision, preaches buy one and focus on one, and reserves roll-ups for a single vertical where multiple expansion actually kicks in.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: Walker Deibel's most expensive lesson is the horizontal holding company. After running the family book printer for seven years, Deibel bought six or seven companies across unrelated verticals at 80% to 100% ownership with maximum debt, and the stacked risk turned uncorrelated businesses into correlated problems; Deibel calls it the 'worst decision' and says eight companies in one vertical would have earned multiple expansion instead [iYE-lc1tFUI @ 00:06:05]. Too many verticals is what ultimately made Deibel stop acquiring [6KZrugmBkcs @ 00:34:19]. The margin trap is just as fast. Deibel calls margin 'the number one most important thing' and reports a member who bought a sandwich business at 1% net margin and was out of business within 90 days, with labor intensity, capital intensity and cyclicality stacking more danger on top [AKE-710SdA4 @ 00:27:47]. People risk hits experienced operators too: at one company, 'at one point 60% of my entire workforce walked out on me' [AKE-710SdA4 @ 00:33:19]. The fix is a one-vertical playbook: buy one, focus on one, then add companies in the same space to capture the arbitrage, while remembering that too many buyers in a sector kills it, exactly as the FBA aggregators showed.

Diligence misses are where buyers bleed quietly. Lucas Phillips paid for a quality of earnings report, yet the time cards would have shown that nobody in the business worked 40 hours a week [iYE-lc1tFUI @ 00:31:15]. A buyer named Joe nearly closed on earnings inflated by prepaid six- and twelve-month contracts, and Deibel runs diligence in strict order, legal first for about a week, then financial, then operational [u2bZWIf9b5k @ 00:53:33]. Trust failures are terminal: a friend bought a broom company from a seller the friend did not trust and nearly went bankrupt, and Deibel's rule is to get out of there [6KZrugmBkcs @ 00:42:18]. The paperwork phase kills deals too. The Master Afle summary of Deibel's book names lawyers as the number one source of deals that fail to close and prescribes a not-to-exceed legal budget, while Mark J Kohler warns that confirmatory diligence runs one to nine months, invites seller deal fatigue, and that a half-page deal led straight to a lawsuit [eZBAyOccEhY @ 00:13:22]. Kohler's line is 'trust but verify everything,' and Deibel adds that deals die one, two, three times before they close.

Post-close discipline separates survivors. Deibel's first acquisition closed with no plan, and the three-way miscommunication between seller, general manager and owner 'destroyed value'; the fix is a person's name next to every P&L line and meetings with the top 20 paying customers the week after closing [WP5MdYhV05A @ 00:16:24]. Deibel also admits waiting too long to make changes on that first deal, and warns against taking a CEO salary on day one because a debt-loaded business is 'overweight' [aoPPGxWI8dY @ 00:00:29]. Expect everyone to hit you up for a raise once you own it. Run the economics before signing: on $1M revenue with $150K SDE bought at 3x plus $100K of inventory, working capital and closing costs, a 90% SBA loan means about $55K cash in and about $75K of annual principal and interest, leaving the owner $75K [u2bZWIf9b5k @ 00:36:45]. Deibel puts the haggle in perspective: fighting over 3.2x versus 3.5x is about 90 days of earnings on a 10-year loan, and buyers belong in $1M to $5M revenue rather than sub-$1M shops [iYE-lc1tFUI @ 00:38:14]. Search itself is the biggest kill zone, since nine in ten searchers never buy anything.

callout.title: Four Kill Switches Before You Sign
callout.body: Every one of these gates comes from a deal that blew up or nearly blew up for a named operator. If a target fails any gate, walk or restructure before the LOI turns into an engagement to get married.
items: Margin gate: if net margin is razor thin and the business is labor-intensive, capital-intensive or cyclical, kill it; a 1% margin sandwich shop folded in 90 days [Darius Mirshahzadeh — AKE-710SdA4 @ 00:27:47].

Labor-reality gate: pull the time cards and phantom labor costs even after buying a quality of earnings report, because nobody at one target worked 40 hours [Making Billions with Ryan Miller — iYE-lc1tFUI @ 00:31:15].
Concentration gate: confirm no single client exceeds 10% of sales, or shift risk back to the seller with an earnout or seller note [Master Afle — LzJITHl_i2k @ 01:14:56].
Day-one plan gate: write a person's name next to every P&L line and book the top 20 paying customers before closing, and keep your own salary low [Let's Buy a Business — WP5MdYhV05A @ 00:16:59].

chapters.question_prompt: How do traditional search funds and self-funded searchers raise capital, run a search, and get a deal to close?
chapters.title: Search Funds and Self-Funded Search: Running the Search
chapters.subtitle: Traditional vs. self-funded search models, investor-backed searcher economics, the Harvard professors' buyer playbook, convincing owners to sell, favored searcher industries, search-fund financial projections, Booth's search and deal-structuring sessions, legal guidance for small-business buyers, the 8-stage M&A process, and an ETA reality check on SBA lending and deal killers
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners running and backing searches agree the job is a high-volume relationship grind: Pete Seligman's funnel ran 200 companies to 50 IMs to 20 conversations to 5 offers to 1 purchase, and Coley Andrews describes thousands of outreaches for one deal. Targets are healthy, cash-generative, recurring-revenue businesses priced around 4-6x cash flow, financed with roughly half bank debt plus seller notes and equity. Traditional funds raise about $400-700K of search capital for a two-year runway and hand the searcher 20-30% equity in thirds; self-funded searchers keep 60-73% but carry the runway themselves. The sharpest split is Robert Graham versus Greg Geronimus on whether traditional capital is a win-win or 'more expensive than a payday loan,' while Peter and Garrett reject mass broker spam in favor of authentic follow-ups every couple of weeks.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every operator who has actually closed describes the search as a volume business that only converts through relationships. Pete Seligman and a partner each pitched the other five business ideas every Sunday night, then worked a funnel of roughly 200 companies down to 50 IMs read, 20 owners spoken to, five offers and one purchase: 'we probably spoke to 20, put in five offers, and bought one' [_exEOi-Wxuk @ 00:15:42]. Peter and Garrett, who closed an HVAC business after 13 months, put it bluntly: 'it's simple but it's a numbers game,' with Garrett grinding 15-20 broker calls a day [Hh83Lc7sWf4 @ 00:22:15]. Coley Andrews of Pacific Lake Partners scales the same math upward: thousands of outreaches, hundreds of conversations and tens of meetings to buy one company, with about 90% of each day spent absorbing rejection [_rMBWgqtfUI @ 00:05:47]. Brian O'Connor of NextGen Growth Partners lands in the same place after building trade-show target lists: 'at the end of the day, I think it is a numbers game in this path' [ccaGmVeLcto @ 00:36:46]. The volume only matters because the close itself is relational; Peter called it 'not a finance game' but a trust game, with the seller still dropping in about three times a week after the contract ended.

The buy box is remarkably consistent across funded and self-funded operators: healthy, cash-generative, boring businesses that nobody needs to rescue. Tim Ludwig wants industry growth at least at GDP, recurring or 'actuarially recurring' revenue, gross margins of 50% or higher, and growth already underway, because 'it's hard enough as it is why not why try and make it any harder than you have to' [AWJaRrNXru8 @ 00:01:24]. Coley Andrews frames the same rule as risk control for inexperienced CEOs: buy companies that are 'unlikely to be broken' and sold by owners in their 60s or 70s with no successor child [_rMBWgqtfUI @ 00:01:17]. Brian O'Connor's preferred list reads like a checklist: recurring revenue, mission-critical product, low share of wallet, B2B over B2C, asset-light, and negative working capital [ccaGmVeLcto @ 00:42:07]. Pete Seligman screened for no customer or product concentration, stable earnings and good cash conversion, and specifically wanted blue-chip customers issuing purchase orders directly rather than sitting 'five layers down' a supply chain [_exEOi-Wxuk @ 00:17:28]. Peter and Garrett's HVAC search ran almost the identical filter: recurring revenue, low customer concentration, stable margin, stable EBITDA and a non-cyclical industry.

The baseline prerequisite is runway. Greg Geronimus describes traditional search capital as money that covers salary and operating costs for two years before a second raise funds the deal, and Robert Graham states flatly that self-funded search does not fit anyone who cannot fund two years of searching [0lg8Gh_uAPU @ 00:54:24]. Peter Harris prices that runway at a typical $400-700K raise with a median of $500-550K, of which $100-200K is searcher salary and the remaining $300K-plus goes to interns, legal, travel, bankers and diligence [i_Ownd9smbk @ 00:02:13]. Lenders demand the same staying power at the closing table: Jared Johnson, billed as the top SBA lender in the country, looks for liquidity well beyond the 10% down payment, experience mapped against the target, other income, and personal saving habits [pqmsev-3MPY @ 00:11:43]. The last shared conviction is how a searcher actually wins. Steve Divitikos, who closed in Toronto after just under two years, won over father-and-son founders who had developed 'a high distaste for private Equity' by presenting as 'a succession plan that's looking for the right business to succeed,' with a portfolio of one, a promise to keep the company name, and 99.9% of personal net worth riding on the deal [GYvpRW21sSY @ 00:00:59]. Price and structure only had to be good enough; the qualitative factors closed it.

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Sourcing runs on two engines: brokers and proprietary lists. Peter and Garrett split the labor, with Garrett making 15-20 broker calls a day while Peter systematized a deal tracker that took six to seven months to refine [Hh83Lc7sWf4 @ 00:22:01]. Their broker list snowballed from about 10 to 500, and instead of blasting thousands of brokers they followed up with every broker every couple of weeks in emails that 'sounded authentic'; 40-50 brokers ended up knowing them by name, which matters because brokers filter buyers too [Hh83Lc7sWf4 @ 00:23:59]. The proprietary engine is cheap labor plus lists. Peter Harris describes intern armies at $10-15 an hour 'smiling and dialing,' or a sector thesis such as personal care or an HVAC roll-up [i_Ownd9smbk @ 00:03:55]. Brian O'Connor works trade-show exhibitor lists of about 1,000 companies, uses interns for research, and narrows to 200-400 targets after scoring roughly three industry spaces on a weighted attribute scorecard covering growth, fragmentation, cyclicality, a TAM of about $1B per niche, and low operational complexity [ccaGmVeLcto @ 00:36:46]. Once deal flow is running, the cadence compounds: Peter's team read about five SIMs a week early, saw the first LOI die after about three months, and after six months always had one or two deals under contract.

The pricing and capital-stack math is standardized. Built to Sell's Harvard guest values targets at 'somewhere around four times' cash flow, maybe five for larger firms, so a $10M company carries roughly $2-2.5M of cash flow. On that $10M deal, the bank lends about 50%, or about $5M repaid over roughly seven years, usually without a personal guarantee at that size; a seller note of $1-2.5M sits subordinated and pays over about four years with interest; and investors supply about $3M of equity [004ptgWQ2TE @ 00:06:38]. Brian O'Connor benchmarks purchase prices at 4-6x TTM EBITDA with $5-10M of acquisition equity [ccaGmVeLcto @ 00:45:37]. In the SBA lane, Jared Johnson requires 10% down on the total project, meaning price plus working capital, closing and diligence costs; a seller can carry half of that on full standby, typically no payments for 10 years, but the buyer still needs at least 5% [pqmsev-3MPY @ 00:06:14]. Adam of ProjectionHub models the coverage test: lenders want a DSCR of at least 1.25, and the template's example, built from a $5M SBA 7(a) loan, a $500K seller note and $5M of search-fund equity with $500K earmarked for working capital, reaches a $10M purchase price and shows 4.64 in year one [uXEbfHnDSes @ 00:01:53].

After the LOI, the clock and the paperwork take over. The Harvard guest on Built to Sell signs the LOI before financing is lined up, budgets 2-4 weeks of business diligence, 1-3 weeks to collect bank proposals and about six weeks for the bank's own process, and stresses that the no-shop clause, usually 90 days, is 'in fact the only binding part of the agreement' [004ptgWQ2TE @ 00:16:54]. Laura D. Franchesco of Dean Street Law adds that confidentiality and deposits bind too, so an LOI is 'not entirely non-binding' [ScOjsEfBwZQ @ 00:22:50]. Josh Dennis and Brian O'Connor close in 60-90 days, 'typically 75 days on average,' 30-45 when rushed and 120-plus when it drags, and they negotiate buffer into exclusivity, such as a 60-day close under 90-day exclusivity [kKwXdeUVNOw @ 00:45:15]. They issue the data-request list the moment the LOI is signed, run good cop/bad cop, insist on 'the power of the pen' by drafting the purchase agreement, and do business diligence in-house before hiring a QoE firm to keep dead-deal costs near zero. Robert Graham and Jordan Carter put real prices on that work: typical QoE runs $10-25K and legal $25-30K, 85% of surveyed self-funded acquirers spent under $30K on QoE, 68% spent under $50K on legal, and 75% ate under $25K in dead-deal costs [KT5T3j2jVQ4 @ 00:51:02].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split in search is who owns the equity. In the live Acquiring Minds debate, Greg Geronimus laid out the traditional deal: the searcher earns 25 percent in thirds, with one third at close, one vesting over about four years, and one tied to performance hurdles [0lg8Gh_uAPU @ 00:10:12]. Robert Graham attacked that last tranche, arguing a searcher has to return 25 to 35 percent IRR to earn it, a hurdle 'over four times higher' than what LPs expect from a private equity firm, and adding that they have never been able to deposit a percentage of common equity in the bank [0lg8Gh_uAPU @ 00:17:15]. Robert's counter-numbers: Sig searchers average 73 percent ownership of businesses with $2.6M average EBITDA, while traditional searchers hold 10 percent or less at close of a median $1.8M EBITDA business [0lg8Gh_uAPU @ 00:12:55]. The wider self-funded survey shows 86 percent keeping more than 60 percent of the common equity [KT5T3j2jVQ4 @ 00:24:04]. The Harvard view lands in the same place: funded searchers carry up to 30 percent, more likely 20, while unfunded searchers may hold 60 to 70 percent [004ptgWQ2TE @ 00:11:26]. Greg's rebuttal is scale, with 46 percent of traditional deals above $12M TEV against a $3M to $8M self-funded range [0lg8Gh_uAPU @ 00:08:43].

Sourcing splits into volume machines versus relationship plays. Pete Seligman tried wining and dining brokers and found it failed because brokers were not proactive [_exEOi-Wxuk @ 00:14:26], while noting that some current searchers source 2,000 businesses a month and make hundreds of calls a week [_exEOi-Wxuk @ 00:15:24]. Peter Harris describes the hired-volume version: intern armies at $10 to $15 an hour 'smiling and dialing,' or a sector thesis such as personal care or an HVAC roll-up [i_Ownd9smbk @ 00:03:55]. Brian O'Connor at Booth runs the thesis version, working trade-show exhibitor lists of about 1,000 companies down to 200 to 400 targets and calling it 'a numbers game in this path' [ccaGmVeLcto @ 00:36:46]. Peter and Garrett, who closed an HVAC deal after 13 months, explicitly reject spamming thousands of brokers. Their list snowballed from 10 to 500, and every broker got a follow-up every couple of weeks in emails written to sound authentic [Hh83Lc7sWf4 @ 00:23:27], while Garrett made 15 to 20 broker calls a day and Peter systematized the tracker [Hh83Lc7sWf4 @ 00:22:01]. The payoff was 40 to 50 brokers who came to know them, and those brokers filter buyers too [Hh83Lc7sWf4 @ 00:25:20]. The real fork is not volume versus no volume; it is automated blast versus personal cadence.

Practitioners also split on what a buyer must bring before day one. Coley Andrews of Pacific Lake Partners says flatly, 'We believe in backing smarts and hustle, not experience' [_rMBWgqtfUI @ 00:00:54], and offsets the gap by buying healthy businesses that are unlikely to be broken [_rMBWgqtfUI @ 00:01:17]. Jared Johnson, billed as the top SBA lender in the country, wants the opposite profile: someone who has worked in consulting, PE, IB, or up through a company, managed people, saved money, and targets an adjacent industry [pqmsev-3MPY @ 00:05:02]. The Harvard buyer profile sits between them, with 7 to 15 years of management experience that is usually outside the target industry [004ptgWQ2TE @ 00:01:33]. The two debaters even agree on who each model excludes. Greg Geronimus concedes traditional search does not fit narrow-geography searchers or anyone weighing a startup [0lg8Gh_uAPU @ 00:51:39], after earlier conceding a narrow Milwaukee search will not work in the traditional model [0lg8Gh_uAPU @ 00:30:14]. Robert Graham concedes self-funded search does not fit anyone who cannot fund two years of searching [0lg8Gh_uAPU @ 00:54:24]. Coley's investor math frames the trade from the other side: $30K to $50K per searcher buys two years of runway, and even with some chance of losing that small amount, '75 out of a 100 is still pretty good' [_rMBWgqtfUI @ 00:05:15].

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The first economics check is attrition. One of the Sig study presenters, drawing on time at a PE firm, said an executed LOI there carried 'north of a 75 percent chance' of closing, and 'that's just not the case here' [KT5T3j2jVQ4 @ 00:40:09]. The self-funded survey shows the average acquirer submitted 6.9 LOIs to get 2.4 executed [KT5T3j2jVQ4 @ 00:45:01]. Pete Seligman's own funnel ran about 200 companies, 50 IMs read, 20 conversations, five offers, and one purchase [_exEOi-Wxuk @ 00:15:42]. Peter and Garrett's first LOI landed at about three months and died a week later; only after roughly six months did they hold one or two deals under contract at all times [Hh83Lc7sWf4 @ 00:20:17], and the partners tell searchers to expect to 'fail about 200 times' [Hh83Lc7sWf4 @ 00:27:36]. Jared Johnson watches searchers drift toward 'junk' deals eight or nine months in and refuses to finance them with a blunt 'I forbid you' [Hh83Lc7sWf4 @ 00:28:05]. Brian O'Connor names the two behavioral traps around that curve: sitting on your hands early in the search [ccaGmVeLcto @ 00:28:59] and tunnel vision once a deal is under LOI [ccaGmVeLcto @ 00:30:36]. Brian's reason: 'time when you're doing this, you'll find is your most scarce resource' [ccaGmVeLcto @ 00:25:54].

The second check is whether the numbers and the seller are real. Jared Johnson says the biggest deal-killer is usually that 'the cash flow doesn't work,' followed by red flags such as broker numbers that exceed tax returns or the QoE, low buyer cash, remote operators who show up 'once a month for a week,' and one or two customers dominating revenue [pqmsev-3MPY @ 00:09:02]. Jared's own first deal shows the cost of a prior owner's behavior: the bankrupt manufacturer had pre-collected customer payments, so the buying group put in $700,000 just to finish products for customers who had already paid [pqmsev-3MPY @ 00:25:33]. Robert Graham's first Pillar deal was the exception to a 78 percent positive seller-relationship rate, ending in an IRS fines letter, police involvement, and a lawsuit [KT5T3j2jVQ4 @ 01:04:14]. Tim Ludwig's rule: a gut red flag about the seller usually means problems elsewhere in the organization too [AWJaRrNXru8 @ 00:03:03]. Laura D. Franchesco adds the legal traps: an LOI is 'not entirely non-binding,' because exclusivity, confidentiality, and deposits bind [ScOjsEfBwZQ @ 00:22:50], and a waste-management acquisition must be a stock purchase with license transfer checked [ScOjsEfBwZQ @ 00:22:34]. Jared's adviser fix is to hire an acquisition specialist whose career this is, not a family-law or real-estate attorney [pqmsev-3MPY @ 00:19:28].

The third check is the first year after close, where practitioners report self-inflicted wounds. Pete Seligman ran an icebreaker at a strategy day that caused the owner to walk out, concluding 'application is everything' [_exEOi-Wxuk @ 00:29:30]. Pete's travel business lost to online wholesalers and exited around 2019 without a loss, summed up as 'can't fight a market' [_exEOi-Wxuk @ 00:42:22]. The Harvard list of failure modes covers external shocks, fixing broken businesses, mistiming cyclical bottoms, due diligence mistakes, and growth plays that amount to 'bolting a startup' onto the company [004ptgWQ2TE @ 00:48:45]; the counter is to avoid big, hard-to-reverse decisions in year one [004ptgWQ2TE @ 00:50:29]. Coley Andrews compresses the transition plan into 'do nothing,' holding off on a sales force, new segments, or senior hires until 12 to 18 months in [_rMBWgqtfUI @ 00:04:07]. Peak Frameworks puts the downside in aggregate: 31 percent of searchers never acquire and 29 percent of acquirers sustain a loss, which the speaker combines into roughly a 50 percent failure rate, alongside single-company idiosyncratic risk [0KhOZrLBMVQ @ 00:03:12]. The same speaker flags the timing collision with family plans in a searcher's late 20s or early 30s [0KhOZrLBMVQ @ 00:04:52].

callout.title: Four Kill-or-Proceed Checks Before You Sign
callout.body: Every check below comes from a deal that blew up, nearly blew up, or got repriced on these operators. Clear all four before the LOI or walk.
items: Run cash flow after deducting your own salary and kill the deal if coverage falls below the 1.25 DSCR lenders expect [Before You Buy or Sell a Business Podcast — pqmsev-3MPY @ 00:13:14] [ProjectionHub — uXEbfHnDSes @ 00:01:53].

Ask the seller why they are selling, again and again, and walk on any gut red flag about honesty [Before You Buy or Sell a Business Podcast — pqmsev-3MPY @ 00:18:48] [POWERS Pod — AWJaRrNXru8 @ 00:03:03].

Treat LOI exclusivity, confidentiality and deposits as binding, and negotiate exclusivity longer than the planned close [Dean Street Law — ScOjsEfBwZQ @ 00:22:50] [The University of Chicago Booth School of Business — kKwXdeUVNOw @ 00:45:15].

action_checklist: Before committing, talk to successful buyers first and then a trusted lender [Before You Buy or Sell a Business Podcast — pqmsev-3MPY @ 00:23:20].

Pick about three spaces using a weighted scorecard: growing, fragmented, non-cyclical, roughly $1B TAM, low operational complexity [The University of Chicago Booth School of Business — ccaGmVeLcto @ 00:15:59].
Build a broker list and follow up with every broker every couple of weeks in emails that sound authentic [Before You Buy or Sell a Business Podcast — Hh83Lc7sWf4 @ 00:23:59].

chapters.question_prompt: Where do buyers find businesses to acquire, both off-market and on online marketplaces, and what outreach tools do they use?
chapters.title: Deal Sourcing: Off-Market Origination and Online Marketplaces
chapters.subtitle: Codie Sanchez's hidden-business playbook, finding boomer businesses with no competition, step-by-step sourcing, off-market HVAC and search-fund origination case studies (5–10 seller meetings a month, sourcing without cold calling), a roll-up origination system built in 4 weeks, studying closed deals before calling brokers, buying and selling on Acquire.com, and cold-calling, CRM, and outbound stacks (HubSpot, Apollo, Clay, Smartlead, Pipedrive, Close)
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners agree the best small businesses aren't publicly listed: roughly 10,000 boomers retire daily, the average owner is 67, and the 7 Ds drive exits, so operators win by being the first call. Off-market mechanics range from Sales Navigator lists worked by an assistant to Avi's Apify-to-Instantly pipeline that produced 23 qualified HVAC opportunities and 3 deals in diligence in under three weeks on 500 emails a day. On-market, Kenny Finance cut 1,500 BizBuySell listings to 72, Codie Sanchez targets 50-100 reviewed deals, 30-50 NDAs and LOIs on about 20%, and Acquire.com accepts about 46% of submissions behind escrow and ID checks. Disagreements center on marketplace fees, quoted as a 4% success fee versus 8%, 7% and 6% tiers, on HubSpot versus Pipedrive or Close, and on done-for-you versus done-with-you origination.
