sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every practitioner sourcing small companies starts from the same supply shock. Mind Of Monte puts it at roughly 10,000 boomers retiring every day, up to 40% of them business owners, often with no second generation willing to take the keys, and calls it a once-in-a-lifetime window [MVmF4HlTHGM @ 00:00:00]. Codie Sanchez pegs the average owner at 67 and sorts seller motivation through the 7 Ds: departure, divorce, disease, disagreement, distress, death through probate and plain dullness, noting distress is where assets trade for pennies on the dollar [3mtS8rOAqoM @ 00:04:08]. Kenny Finance compresses the thesis into one line, the best businesses are not for sale, so the operator's whole job is to be the first call when a great company finally comes to market [7znMZDlxFBU @ 00:13:23]. Marco Palmero adds the structural reason listings alone fail: on-market deal flow gets capped the moment a thesis or geography narrows, which is exactly the box searchers and roll-up buyers live in [x4qfCP1pVmE @ 00:01:30]. The shared conclusion across all four is blunt. Listed inventory is the floor, not the ceiling, and proprietary origination aimed at aging owners is where buyer competition thins out, which is the core promise of the no-competition boomer play.

The second point of agreement is that owners choose the buyer before they choose the price. Mind Of Monte tells operators to build a deal structure that lets the seller keep their lifestyle after the handoff [MVmF4HlTHGM @ 00:01:46]. Codie Sanchez sharpens the avatar: the ideal seller is retiring, wants more than the bank will lend, wants an annuity, runs a boring business and already knows you, while the bad avatar is young, fast-growing, complex and juggling many offers [3mtS8rOAqoM @ 00:11:37]. Marco Palmero coaches searchers to lean on what private equity cannot claim, that they are buying one business and stewarding the legacy, the employees and the 20-40 year project the owner built [x4qfCP1pVmE @ 00:05:58]. Avi's HVAC campaign weaponizes the same instinct with the subject line 'This one's not from PE' and an opening jab at the private equity intern with a spreadsheet, positioning the sender as an operator-buyer [cS2OjyHbq8U @ 00:11:32]. Across the four, the message is identical. The consensus is that legacy, employees and a structure built around the seller's life open doors, and that anything that reads as corporate or spreadsheet-driven gets filtered out by the owner before a first call ever happens.

Nobody tells operators to ignore listings; the consensus is to work them hard as one lane among several. Kenny Finance runs three sourcing channels side by side, public listings, business brokers and cold outreach, and walks through each one as its own repeatable workflow [7znMZDlxFBU @ 00:02:02]. Codie Sanchez warns that every on-market listing pulls in 100-plus inquiries, so the buyer's first message has to follow the rule 'Be good. Be brief. Be gone.' or it drowns in the pile [3mtS8rOAqoM @ 00:27:13]. On the online marketplace side, Andrew Gazdecki of Acquire.com is categorical that nobody should ever do an acquisition without escrow, because it protects the buyer from scams and bad actors [nu3zh5FOFME @ 00:19:48]. jackhaigh confirms the platform gate from the user seat: buyers must verify their account before they can make an offer at all, a step the reviewer treats as obvious for any buyer on the platform [_m1Q0kLTooU @ 00:03:43]. The baseline prerequisites therefore repeat across every speaker who touches a marketplace or a broker. Verify identity early, keep the opening pitch short, move faster than the crowd of competing inquiries, and route every dollar through third-party escrow rather than a direct transfer when the counterparty is a stranger.

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The off-market machine starts with list building. Avi's HVAC team scraped Google Maps through Apify plus a Google SERP proxy to pull 9,000-11,000 contacts across HVAC and MEP operators, checked SIC codes, found emails with Find Email and Email Finder, cleaned them through MillionVerifier and piped everything via n8n, now driven by Claude Code with n8n, into Instantly for sending [cS2OjyHbq8U @ 00:07:10]. Mind Of Monte runs a lighter version: filter target criteria inside Sales Navigator, build the list, then hand it to an assistant or idle staff who reach out one owner at a time [MVmF4HlTHGM @ 00:03:13]. Kenny Finance shows the manual variant, searching phrases like top family-owned managed service provider California, sizing the target with ChatGPT, having ChatGPT draft the outreach email, and following up every one to two weeks across hundreds of targets [7znMZDlxFBU @ 00:18:16]. Marco Palmero insists the channel mix stays wide, testing email, LinkedIn, voicemail drops, letters and text, then keeping only what works for the specific thesis [x4qfCP1pVmE @ 00:04:49]. The mechanics scale from one assistant with a Sales Navigator seat to a fully automated scrape-verify-send pipeline, but every version runs on a defined list, persistent follow-up and more than one touchpoint.

Listings get worked as a filter exercise, not a browsing habit. Kenny Finance set BizBuySell filters to Texas, roughly a $2M price and about $500K cash flow, cutting 1,500 listings down to 72, then struck fitness, smoke shops, restaurants, law firms and healthcare before using the contact form to request an NDA [7znMZDlxFBU @ 00:03:54]. Codie Sanchez prescribes daily alerts and a disciplined habit of reviewing about 100 deals, built on a pitch that offers to sign the NDA and run two to four weeks of diligence [3mtS8rOAqoM @ 00:28:04]. On Acquire.com specifically, Andrew Gazdecki has buyers set a budget, revenue, profit and tech-stack criteria, save filtered lists such as more than $500,000 profit, and filter by revenue multiple, minimum profit, location and growth rate, with an LOI builder, asset purchase agreement builder and free Escrow.com closing built in [qjwlutaiugE @ 00:00:30]. Gazdecki's LOI advice leans on structure, packaging seller financing, a conditional holdback or a three-to-six-month transition period into the offer before drafting the APA and closing through escrow [nu3zh5FOFME @ 00:18:54]. The common pattern is tight filters first, NDA second, and an LOI that protects the buyer through deal structure rather than through headline price alone.

The numbers behind the outreach machine are specific. Avi spreads sending risk across lookalike domains, never the main domain, scaling from about 100 to 149 mailboxes pushing 500 emails a day in total, capping Microsoft inboxes at 5 a day and Google or SMTP at 20, warming up for two to three weeks and holding 91% inbox placement [cS2OjyHbq8U @ 00:16:56]. ToolColumn prices a HubSpot, Apollo, Clay and Smartlead stack for two-to-eight-person teams at $950-$3,200 a month as a directional planning figure, and stresses that suppression, reply ownership and rollback rules between HubSpot and Smartlead must be written down [W6A4gRp6eow @ 00:01:51]. Lean Stack argues the CRM line item hides the real cost: HubSpot Professional runs over $1,200 a month for 15 users plus $1,500-$3,000 of mandatory onboarding, and should only be chosen with heavy inbound and a dedicated RevOps hire [CoNZbm4aVto @ 00:02:06]. Kyle Norton's Owner.com data, built on Snowflake, scrapers and a confidence score, shows why list quality is the multiplier, with prospect accuracy lifted from 40% to 85%, BDRs roughly twice as efficient and decision-maker connect rates climbing from 3% to 14-16% [KAz03HJ5nHg @ 00:12:09]. Clean data, distributed sending and a cheap CRM the team actually updates carry the unit economics.

callout.title: Insider Pro-Tips From the Sourcing Desk
callout.body: Small operational edges the practitioners use to get answered first, land in the inbox and keep data clean.
items: Never send cold acquisition email from the main domain; run about 3 to 5 mailboxes per lookalike domain and keep Microsoft inboxes low-volume because Microsoft flags domains that send a lot [Avi — cS2OjyHbq8U @ 00:17:26].

Skip browsing broker websites because the listings duplicate BizBuySell; email the broker directly and aim to be the first call when a great company comes to market [Kenny Finance — 7znMZDlxFBU @ 00:08:53].
On marketplaces, complete ID verification and connect LinkedIn, which lifts seller response rates by more than 50% [Codie Sanchez — 3mtS8rOAqoM @ 00:44:52].
Fix prospect data before hiring more than 1-2 BDRs; once accuracy climbed to 85%, each Owner.com BDR produced over $60K closed-won ARR per month [SaaStr AI — KAz03HJ5nHg @ 00:12:09].

sop_steps.title: Lock the deal box and thesis
sop_steps.action: Write the buy box before pulling a single list.
sop_steps.detail: Target under $10M revenue, blue-collar fragmented industries and at least a 15% margin, passing on proprietary, patent-pending or biotech plays [Codie Sanchez — 3mtS8rOAqoM @ 00:14:22]; get clarity on the thesis first, including risk profile and preferred deal structure [Marco Palmero — x4qfCP1pVmE @ 00:02:21].

sop_steps.title: Build a layered, verified target list
sop_steps.action: Scrape, enrich and verify owners against the thesis.
sop_steps.detail: Pull contacts with the Apify Google Maps scraper and SERP proxy, check SIC codes, find emails and verify through MillionVerifier [Avi — cS2OjyHbq8U @ 00:07:10]; layer multiple databases instead of one provider to reach 80-90% accuracy [Marco Palmero — x4qfCP1pVmE @ 00:18:10].

sop_steps.title: Launch operator-buyer outreach across channels
sop_steps.action: Send researched, non-corporate copy through more than one channel.
sop_steps.detail: Use a subject like 'This one's not from PE', reference about 15 minutes of research per owner and ask directly for a chat [Avi — cS2OjyHbq8U @ 00:11:32]; run calls, LinkedIn and email together to sustain 5-10 qualified seller meetings per month [Marco Palmero — iPMw4FjbyRQ @ 00:02:32].

sop_steps.title: Route positive replies inside the hour
sop_steps.action: Stream positive replies to a shared channel and answer fast.
sop_steps.detail: Push positive replies into Slack from an Airtable CRM and respond within 5 minutes to 1 hour [Avi — cS2OjyHbq8U @ 00:20:42]; move qualified owners to NDA with a 2-4 week diligence pitch because time kills all deals [Codie Sanchez — 3mtS8rOAqoM @ 00:28:04].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The broker question splits the room. Codie Sanchez tells buyers flatly 'do not use a broker for the buy side,' pricing buy-side representation at roughly $10K per month plus 3–7% and adding 'I do not recommend them at all' [3mtS8rOAqoM @ 00:38:15]. Kenny Finance works the opposite edge of the same channel: sell-side brokers are a primary pipe, found by Googling 'business broker Michigan,' and the move is to skip browsing their listings because they duplicate BizBuySell, email the broker directly, and become 'the first call when a great company comes to market' [7znMZDlxFBU @ 00:13:23]. Mind Of Monte treats brokers as a screening service, because cold first contact will not surface economics, pay structures, stakeholders or profitability, while brokers sort that out 'ahead of time' [MVmF4HlTHGM @ 00:02:58]. Marco Palmero pushes back on broker-first sequencing entirely: searchers who start with brokers and only fall back on proprietary origination late lose the compounding effect, since owners sit on 2–6 month exit horizons and proprietary results take 3–6 months to arrive [x4qfCP1pVmE @ 00:12:58]. The operator synthesis: never pay a buy-side retainer, treat sell-side brokers as a relationship to be first in line with, and launch proprietary outreach on day one rather than as a fallback.

Online marketplace economics arrive in conflicting numbers. jackhaigh quotes Acquire.com seller closing fees on a sliding scale of 8% under $250K, 7% from $250K to $1M and 6% above $1M, calls them 'a bit high,' and promises a sale in 1–2 months [_m1Q0kLTooU @ 00:04:30]. Anna Stepura, who listed a startup on Acquire.com, Flippa and Tiny Acquisitions, reports no listing subscription and a flat 4% success fee, contrasts that with investment bankers charging 5–12% plus occasional upfront fees, and pegs the realistic timeline at 4–6 months [oplaAtHYPlU @ 00:00:53]. Andrew Gazdecki, speaking as Acquire.com CEO, matches the 4% at close and prices the buyer side at $390 per year for startups under $250K revenue or $780 per year for all startups plus tools [qjwlutaiugE @ 00:05:10]. Fit is contested too: jackhaigh rates the platform weak for blogs, local businesses and tiny sites, while Codie Sanchez works the on-market channel for blue-collar targets and warns that every listing draws 100+ inquiries, so the pitch must be 'Be good. Be brief. Be gone.' [3mtS8rOAqoM @ 00:27:13]. Confirm the fee in writing at signing rather than trusting any reviewer's table, budget the longer 4–6 month clock, and route SaaS targets to Acquire.com while hunting local blue-collar deals elsewhere.

The origination stack itself is a fault line. Lean Stack's cost audit says HubSpot only makes sense with heavy inbound and a dedicated RevOps hire, or VC funding, sending agencies and ops-heavy shops to Pipedrive plus Make and 80-calls-a-day sales floors to Close [CoNZbm4aVto @ 00:04:34]. ToolColumn builds the opposite way, making HubSpot owner of contact, company, lifecycle, deal, owner and suppression records while Apollo sources lists, Clay enriches selectively and Smartlead only sends [W6A4gRp6eow @ 00:00:23]. Avi skips both camps: the HVAC campaign that produced 23 qualified opportunities ran on an Airtable CRM rather than Salesforce or HubSpot [cS2OjyHbq8U @ 00:19:48]. The build question splits as well. Marco Palmero sells two models: done-for-you, where the firm runs the system and delivers opportunities, and done-with-you, where the buyer owns assets that 'pay you dividends' over time; the Bed and Biscuit roll-up took the second route and was running in-house within 4 weeks [6qKxeAkc2YY @ 00:03:54]. Small buy-side teams without a RevOps owner should start lean, because ToolColumn's own rule is to skip the full stack when Apollo alone is enough and add Clay only once enrichment depth becomes a repeatable constraint. Lean Stack's tiebreaker is blunt: pick the stack the team actually updates.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: Bad prospect data is the most expensive trap reported. Kyle Norton, CRO at Owner.com, found BDRs wasting about 40% of their time while prospect data sat at 40% accuracy; rebuilding the pipeline with Snowflake, scrapers, a confidence score and People Data Labs mobile numbers pushed accuracy to 85% and decision-maker connect rates from 3% to 14–16%, and the rule that came out of it is to hire no more than 1–2 BDRs before the data is fixed [KAz03HJ5nHg @ 00:12:09]. Norton also paid for discipline: rejecting about 40% of prospects dropped closed-won for two months, and Jason on the board said none of it showed in revenue [KAz03HJ5nHg @ 00:08:16]. Marco Palmero warns against relying on a single data provider, arguing that 'you can achieve 80, 85, 90% accuracy by integrating multiple resources together' [x4qfCP1pVmE @ 00:18:10]. Kenny Finance shows how AI research drifts: a target managed service provider called ICS was stated as founded in 1981, ChatGPT later answered 1987, and its revenue came back as a loose $9–24M estimate [7znMZDlxFBU @ 00:13:41]. The check is simple: verify every AI-enriched field against a second source before it drives outreach volume or valuation math, because Norton's read is that about 80% of companies have a pipeline problem, not a rep problem.

Sending infrastructure fails quietly. Avi never sends from the main domain, spreads roughly 100 mailboxes (later scaled to 149) across lookalike domains at about 3 to 5 per domain, runs 500 emails a day across the system, and holds Microsoft mailboxes to 5 a day versus 20 for Google and SMTP because 'Microsoft emails are very sensitive' to domains that send a lot, with 2–3 weeks of warmup buying 91% inbox placement [cS2OjyHbq8U @ 00:18:14]. ToolColumn traces stack breakage to collision rather than weak tools, since 'every tool thinks it owns the same record,' and runs QA for duplicate domains, poor fit, bad owners, suppression misses, credit burn and rollback, warning that 'weekly maintenance is the real cost' at about 6 hours [W6A4gRp6eow @ 00:02:38]. Lean Stack documents the CRM version of the same leak: bills doubling after database limits, a CRM 'on an island' forcing manual CSV exports every Friday, and freelance integrators charging 'two grand' for fragile setups [CoNZbm4aVto @ 00:00:37]. SoftSavvy adds the dialer trap, warning against picking on starting price or ignoring CRM sync, because 'if the reps hate using it, adoption dies' [uJWyOGsPXbA @ 00:12:02]. Budget maintenance hours and 24-month ownership cost, not entry-tier license fees.

Marketplace and deal-level traps hit after the first reply. Anna Stepura warns that 'scammers would be everywhere,' that fake buyers have to be screened manually instead of auto-accepted, and that a lawyer should be retained early, even with company names hidden until the NDA [oplaAtHYPlU @ 00:05:18]. Andrew Gazdecki's rule is absolute, 'don't ever do an acquisition without using escrow,' because it protects against scams and bad actors, and the platform runs social-presence checks to weed out drop-shipping scam listings while accepting only about 46% of submissions [nu3zh5FOFME @ 00:19:48]. Codie Sanchez shows the economics check that flags attractive listings: an HVAC business asking $4M on $1.28M cash flow posted 174% cash-on-cash yet ran a 12% margin, below the 15-cent floor in Sanchez's deal box [3mtS8rOAqoM @ 00:42:09]. Kenny Finance flags the mirror-image mismatch, a $150K asking price against $550K cash flow, as a red flag, and rejects whole categories, including restaurants, smoke shops, fitness, healthcare and law firms, the last because 'AI will replace' them [7znMZDlxFBU @ 00:05:36]. The gate: escrow every close, retain the lawyer before the LOI, screen every buyer or seller identity, and run margin and price-to-cash-flow sanity math before any diligence hours get spent.

callout.title: Kill Switches Before You Scale Origination
callout.body: Each gate below comes from a loss, reversal or bottleneck a practitioner hit firsthand. Clear all four before adding headcount, mailboxes or marketplace spend.
items: Do not scale BDRs or callers past 1–2 until contact data reaches roughly 85% accuracy and decision-maker connect rates move off 3% [SaaStr AI — KAz03HJ5nHg @ 00:12:09].
Never send cold acquisition email from the main domain; warm lookalike domains for 2–3 weeks and hold Microsoft mailboxes to 5 sends per day [Avi — cS2OjyHbq8U @ 00:18:14].
No acquisition closes without escrow, domestic or international, because it protects against scams and bad actors [acquiredotcom — nu3zh5FOFME @ 00:19:48].
Reject any target below the 15% margin floor before spending NDA or diligence time, even when headline cash-on-cash shows 174% [Codie Sanchez — 3mtS8rOAqoM @ 00:42:09].

chapters.pull_quote: "So the best thing you can do is be the first call when a great company comes to market. The best businesses aren't for sale." — Kenny Finance (7znMZDlxFBU @ 00:13:23).
action_checklist: Define the deal box first: under $10M revenue, blue-collar and fragmented, at least 15% margin, and no proprietary, patent-pending or biotech plays [Codie Sanchez — 3mtS8rOAqoM @ 00:14:22].

Filter BizBuySell by state, price and cash flow (Texas, about $2M price, about $500K cash flow cut 1,500 listings to 72), then use the contact form and sign the NDA [Kenny Finance — 7znMZDlxFBU @ 00:03:54].
Email sell-side brokers directly instead of browsing their duplicated listings, and work to be the first call when a great company comes to market [Kenny Finance — 7znMZDlxFBU @ 00:13:23].

Scrape off-market targets with the Apify Google Maps scraper, verify emails with MillionVerifier, qualify with a GPT agent plus Perplexity Sonar, and send through Instantly [Avi — cS2OjyHbq8U @ 00:07:10].
Run multichannel touches across email, LinkedIn, voicemail drops, letters and text; owners who ignored 3–4 emails replied after a LinkedIn message or text [Marco Palmero — x4qfCP1pVmE @ 00:11:42].
Write a short closed-deal case study and glance at it during broker calls to show skin in the game and credible associations [The Acquisition Manager — zYUvLwZ6ipc @ 00:00:35].

chapters.question_prompt: How does an SBA 7(a) loan finance a business acquisition, and what changed under SOP 50 10 8.1?
chapters.title: SBA 7(a) Acquisition Lending and the SOP 50 10 8.1 Rules
chapters.subtitle: 7(a) mechanics and pros and cons, equity injection minimums (a $1M business with about $57K down), the October 1 rule changes and technical updates, lender underwriting and the acquisition application, QoE expectations, what sellers must prepare, buying the business plus the building, and SBDC and lender training on change-of-ownership loans
chapters.executive_summary: Lenders, brokers, CPAs and SBA policy staff converge on one message: SOP 50 10 8.1 makes historical cash flow the ceiling on acquisition debt. The DSCR floor moves from 1.15x to 1.25x on historical financials. The 10% injection on initial acquisitions cannot be reduced, and full-standby seller debt can cover at most half of it, which kills the old zero-cash structure. A lender-commissioned or vendor-reviewed QoE is mandatory at a $3M business purchase price, with quotes running $5,000 to $30,000. In one worked example, a $1M deal closes with roughly $57,500 of buyer cash. In another, a target earning $185K fails a 1.25x test that requires $196.2K. Practitioners split on three points: whether a buyer QoE can be reused, which deal costs count as equity, and how the $3M trigger is measured.

key_metrics.label: Minimum Acquisition DSCR
key_metrics.value: 1.25x on historical financials (up from 1.15x, which could use projections)
key_metrics.context: Pioneer Capital Advisory reports that the floor moves to 1.25 on historical financials, and that deals over $3M must base the calculation on the QoE.

key_metrics.label: QoE Trigger on Business Purchase Price
key_metrics.metric: QoE Trigger on Business Purchase Price
key_metrics.value: $3M or more (PSA price minus appraised owner-occupied real estate)
key_metrics.context: Lion Business Advisors' example: a $4.2M price minus $1M of real estate equals $3.2M, so a QoE is required even on a $2.7M loan.

key_metrics.label: Buyer Cash on a $1M Acquisition
key_metrics.value: $57,500 buyer cash plus $57,500 seller full-standby note on a $1.15M project
key_metrics.context: Exit Ready Valuation applies the 10% injection to the whole project, then splits it evenly between a seller full-standby note and buyer cash.

key_metrics.label: Quoted QoE Engagement Cost
key_metrics.context: Price range Pioneer Capital Advisory and Midwest CPA have seen quoted for QoE engagements now that a QoE is mandatory above $3M.

sections.title: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every practitioner working the equity side repeats the same rule: the 10% injection on an initial acquisition is now a hard floor. The Money Rules states flatly that the 10% cannot be reduced, that 25% is not an SBA rule, and that seller and limited sources are capped at half of it [DyCKwhKRtK0 @ 00:02:04]. Pioneer Capital Advisory runs the same math on a $4M project: a $400K injection, of which $200K must come from the buyer [WF2-6ODNQms @ 00:36:34]. Exit Ready Valuation adds the trap most first-time buyers miss. The 10% applies to the whole project, not just the price, so a $1M business plus $150K of other uses becomes a $1.15M project and $115K down [Tt3Ae9PDn8A @ 00:00:33]. Michael S Glaspie names the casualty. The old play was 90% SBA plus a 10% seller note on full subordination, with no cash out of pocket, and it is dead. Seller standby plus non-controlling investors holding 20% or less is now limited to 50% of the injection, or '5% of the entire purchase' [WfgrSa37vaA @ 00:02:50]. All four point to the same operator move. Budget at least 5% of total project cost in your own cash, treat any standby seller note as covering no more than the other 5%, and build the stack on total project cost rather than the headline price.

Lenders and advisors agree that cash flow sets the ceiling. Ed Weeks Jr. reports that DSCR on a first-time takeover rises to 1.25x from 1.15x. It is measured on the last fiscal year or a two-year average, and lenders can no longer rely on projections [aJcoLYwi6vo @ 00:00:35]. Matthias Smith explains why: 1.15 left little margin for error and led to defaults, so the new floor is 1.25 on historical numbers only [3tkWRQX9WjI @ 00:04:43]. Jack Pastrana of Credit Bench, with about 21 years in SBA lending, frames the underwriting logic. Banks are cash flow lenders, and when cash flow will not support the debt, the business is usually overpriced [NmgNpE_W_po @ 00:34:41]. Josh KS at Lion Business Advisors shows how add-backs collapse the math. A seller claims $700K of earnings, diligence supports $550K, and debt service is $500K. The deal lands at 1.10x and fails the 1.25x test [orHTcAJcuAM @ 00:15:11]. The lesson is that the earnings figure on a listing is not the figure the bank underwrites. Only documented historical cash flow survives the credit memo, and every unsupported add-back cuts directly into the debt the buyer can carry. The 1.25x floor is now the first filter on price, not a box checked after the LOI is signed.

Structure guardrails round out the consensus. Michael S Glaspie describes a partial buyout where the seller retains equity: the buyer can own only 50% or less. Taking control requires the seller's full exit, and seller consulting is capped at 24 months [WfgrSa37vaA @ 00:04:30]. The Money Rules confirms consulting of up to two years and adds that earnouts are banned outright [DyCKwhKRtK0 @ 00:06:43]. Ray Drew of SBA Ray, who lends on $1-5M acquisitions, puts it more bluntly: 'the sba just straight up doesn't allow this you need a fixed purchase price' [9Sl18GknuZE @ 00:01:42]. SBA policy staff Dan Pashet and Emily Dachon, presenting through Coleman Report, add the valuation layer. There are four change-of-ownership types, every one needs an independent valuation, and only 7(a) Small and Express are carved out [miA6NuzVV6Y @ 00:48:20]. Taken together, the operator rule set is simple. Negotiate a fixed price with no contingent kicker. Budget for an independent valuation on every change-of-ownership deal outside Small and Express. Limit the seller's post-closing role to a consulting agreement of 24 months or less. Build the full seller exit into the LOI from day one, so the structure survives underwriting instead of collapsing in the credit memo.

sections.title: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Practitioners run the numbers from total project cost, not sticker price. Exit Ready Valuation turns a $1M business with $150K of additional uses into a $1.15M project and a $115K injection. The injection splits into $57,500 of seller full-standby note and $57,500 of buyer cash, and the SBA loan lands around $1.035M [Tt3Ae9PDn8A @ 00:00:54]. Their payment line is the reality check: 'At an example rate of 10%, that's about $13,700 a month, about $164,000 a year' [Tt3Ae9PDn8A @ 00:01:32]. The Money Rules runs the same drill for a buyer named Jordan. The $1.1M project carries $110K of equity, built from $55K of seller standby and $55K of cash. The $990K loan at prime plus 3%, or 10%, costs roughly $157K a year in payments. Earnings of $185K fail the 1.25x test because $196.2K is required [DyCKwhKRtK0 @ 00:04:32]. Matthias Smith scales it up: a $2M project means $200K down, with $100K from the buyer's own pocket. The buyer's half can be cash, a grant, or a personal loan repaid from outside the business [3tkWRQX9WjI @ 00:01:12]. Two formulas fall out of these examples. Minimum buyer cash is 10% of project cost, halved. The earnings the target must already show are annual debt service times 1.25.

Deal timelines now live or die on the QoE, and the trigger is narrower than buyers assume. Josh KS at Lion Business Advisors measures it on business purchase price. That is the PSA price minus the appraised value of owner-occupied real estate, tested before equity or seller debt. A $4.2M deal with $1M of real estate is a $3.2M business price, so a QoE is required even on a $2.7M loan. Exactly $3M counts, but a $2.8M price inside a larger project does not [orHTcAJcuAM @ 00:07:05]. Pioneer Capital Advisory spells out the required scope: proof of cash, tax reconciliation, documented adjustments and a sustainability analysis. The lender is the client [WF2-6ODNQms @ 00:29:24]. Josh adds that proof of cash covers TTM plus two fiscal years. Under PLP, the engagement must be in place when the loan number is issued, even if the report finishes later. Chris Barrett, CPA, walks through the September technical update. Buyers may now commission the QoE, though sellers still cannot. The report qualifies through either a provider reliance letter or a review by a lender-vetted provider [Ru9e1wYKGHc @ 00:00:43]. Barrett's concern is the first path: reliance letters raise provider liability, cost and scope, which feeds straight into the price of the engagement [Ru9e1wYKGHc @ 00:01:30].

Injection sourcing is the next checkpoint. Ray Drew calls verification one of the top two or three sticking points. Funds must be seasoned for two full bank statement cycles, and gifts and account transfers draw extra scrutiny. A borrowed injection, such as a HELOC, needs an outside repayment source like a spouse's W-2 income [9Sl18GknuZE @ 00:04:31]. Pioneer Capital Advisory confirms that personal loans or HELOCs work if repaid from outside the business's cash flow. Investor money inside the 10% can take tax distributions only, while funds above 10% can take profit distributions [WF2-6ODNQms @ 00:42:35]. Matthias Smith then layers on two changes to the math. Real estate amortization now blends the real estate share at 25 years and the remainder at 10. That replaces the old rule, under which 51% real estate earned a full 25-year term [3tkWRQX9WjI @ 00:07:44]. Total SBA debt plus any amortizing seller note is also capped at valuation, so a $3.5M price on a $3M valuation forces $500K of extra equity [3tkWRQX9WjI @ 00:12:10]. For expansion acquisitions, a four-digit NAICS match unlocks a deal with no down payment, but working capital cannot be financed alongside it. Smith's fix for a $300K working capital need is to negotiate it into the purchase price, rather than give up the zero-down structure and inject 10%.

callout.title: Edges Lenders and Advisors Actually Use on 8.1 Deals
callout.body: These tactics come from lenders and advisors who close SBA acquisitions. Each one either widens the lender pool or removes a common underwriting objection before it reaches the credit memo.
items: Target DSCR above the 1.25x floor rather than at it. Matthias Smith says the extra coverage brings in more lenders and a better rate. [Matthias Smith — 3tkWRQX9WjI @ 00:05:53]

Close an industry-experience gap with a one- or two-paragraph addendum to the resume that explains how your skills carry over and why you want this business. Jack Pastrana coaches borrowers to write exactly this. [Tresle Inc — NmgNpE_W_po @ 00:12:26]
If a license such as HVAC is tied to the seller, have an employee qualify for it, and bind that employee to the business with equity or an employment agreement. [SBA Ray — 9Sl18GknuZE @ 00:02:48]
Research market multiples before signing the LOI, so the third-party valuation does not come in under price and force a retrade with the seller. [Matthias Smith — 3tkWRQX9WjI @ 00:14:43]

sop_steps.title: Size the Deal to Your Own Cash
sop_steps.action: Compute 10% of total project cost and fund at least half of it personally.
sop_steps.detail: Apply the 10% to the full project, including the $150K of non-price uses in Exit Ready's $1.15M example [Exit Ready Valuation — Tt3Ae9PDn8A @ 00:00:33]. Size the deal to your own capital, because investors inside the injection must be long-term holders [Matthias Smith — 3tkWRQX9WjI @ 00:02:07].

sop_steps.title: Stress-Test Historical DSCR
sop_steps.action: Divide documented historical earnings by annual debt service and confirm the result clears 1.25x.
sop_steps.detail: Jordan's deal shows $185K of earnings against $196.2K required [The Money Rules — DyCKwhKRtK0 @ 00:04:32]. Haircut claimed add-backs the way Lion's example falls from $700K claimed to $550K supported, which ends at 1.10x [Lion Business Advisors — orHTcAJcuAM @ 00:15:11].

sop_steps.title: Engage the QoE and Valuation Early
sop_steps.action: If the business purchase price is $3M or more, lock in a QoE provider the lender accepts before the loan number is issued.
sop_steps.detail: Under PLP, the QoE must be engaged by the time the loan number is issued [Lion Business Advisors — orHTcAJcuAM @ 00:10:13]. A buyer-commissioned report qualifies through a reliance letter or a review by a lender-vetted provider [Chris Barrett, CPA — Ru9e1wYKGHc @ 00:00:43].

sop_steps.title: Submit a Clean Prequal Package
sop_steps.action: Send the application, 3 years of tax returns, a resume and 2 months of bank statements, then deliver the LOI.
sop_steps.detail: Credit Bench gives a same-day, non-binding prequal on that package [Tresle Inc — NmgNpE_W_po @ 00:13:30]. Approval takes about 2 weeks, with closing roughly 20 days later, for 30-35 days total, or 35-45 days when commercial real estate is involved [Tresle Inc — NmgNpE_W_po @ 00:14:20].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is over who owns the quality of earnings report and whether a buyer can reuse one. Pioneer Capital Advisory's team told acquisition buyers flatly that the lender has to be the client, no assignment or reliance letter is possible, and a second QoE is likely [WF2-6ODNQms @ 00:25:49]. Josh KS of Lion Business Advisors reads the September technical update differently: a seller-commissioned QoE still cannot satisfy the rule, but a buyer QoE can be used after an approved vendor reviews it, and the lender keeps both reports on file [orHTcAJcuAM @ 00:09:28]. Brad Hedock at Commercial Lending X lists the buyer-ordered QoE among the 13 key changes and calls it positive overall, while flagging that nuances remain [Rsg9fKAzdAo @ 00:03:47]. Chris Barrett, the Midwest CPA, confirms buyers may now commission the report through either a provider reliance letter or a review by a lender-vetted provider, then warns that reliance letters raise the provider's liability, cost, and scope [Ru9e1wYKGHc @ 00:01:30]. The operator read: if you commission early diligence yourself, budget for the review path rather than assuming the reliance-letter path will be cheap, and confirm early with your lender which route its approved vendors will actually accept.

Practitioners also split on which dollars count toward the buyer's half of the injection. Pioneer Capital Advisory teaches that deal costs the buyer already paid count toward their share, so diligence spending does double duty as equity [WF2-6ODNQms @ 00:55:43]. Brad Hedock calls the opposite ruling the most negative change in the September technical update: education, advisory, and agent fees no longer count as equity [Rsg9fKAzdAo @ 00:11:30]. Dan Pashet and Emily Dachon of the SBA's Office of Financial Assistance, presenting for Coleman Report, confirm that education and advisory prepaids are excluded from the injection [miA6NuzVV6Y @ 00:25:25]. The Money Rules threads the needle by stating that valuation and QoE report costs do count toward equity, which keeps third-party diligence inside the ledger while coaching and buy-side advisory fees fall outside it [DyCKwhKRtK0 @ 00:06:01]. The working playbook is to separate invoices by category before the lender writes the credit memo: valuation and QoE receipts go into the injection column, while program tuition, coaching retainers, and broker or agent fees get treated as sunk cost. A buyer who leaned on paid coaching or advisory retainers to fill their half under the older reading now has to replace that money with seasoned cash, a grant, or a personal loan repaid from outside the business cash flow.

Even the trigger date for the new rules is argued three ways. Josh KS ties it to applications received by SBA on or after October 1, stressing that September 30 filings stay on SOP 8 and that LOI or listing dates decide nothing [orHTcAJcuAM @ 00:01:38]. Michael S Glaspie frames it as applications started after October 1, 2026 [WfgrSa37vaA @ 00:00:30], while The Money Rules keys it to the date SBA issues the loan number [DyCKwhKRtK0 @ 00:00:21]. For any deal straddling the cutover, the defensive move is to underwrite to the stricter 8.1 math so a slipped submission date cannot blow up the structure. On the financing mix itself, Ray Drew explicitly runs a different playbook from the buyers chasing minimum cash: SBA does not require seller notes, but many lenders do, and beyond the full-standby half of the injection those notes are negotiable tools used to offset a weakness such as customer concentration, with examples like a 10-year note, a 1–2 year standby, or a balloon at year 5 [9Sl18GknuZE @ 00:06:36]. That makes the note's terms a negotiation chip to trade against the price, not just a way to cut the buyer's cash at the closing table.

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most common deal-killer practitioners describe is earnings that collapse under scrutiny. Josh KS walks through a buyer claiming $700,000 of earnings when only $550,000 is supported; against $500,000 of debt service that is 1.10x, a fail under the 1.25x floor [orHTcAJcuAM @ 00:15:11]. The Money Rules runs the same autopsy on a buyer named Jordan: a $1.1M project, $110,000 of equity split between a $55,000 seller standby note and $55,000 of cash, and a $990,000 loan at prime plus 3%, roughly $157,000 a year in payments. Earnings of $185,000 fall short of the $196,200 the 1.25x test demands [DyCKwhKRtK0 @ 00:04:32]. Matthias Smith explains why SBA raised the bar: the old 1.15 floor left little margin for error and led to defaults, so the new floor runs on historical numbers only, and Smith pushes buyers to clear 1.25 with room to spare [3tkWRQX9WjI @ 00:04:43]. Exit Ready Valuation puts the seller-side version of the trap bluntly: messy books can kill the loan [Tt3Ae9PDn8A @ 00:02:29]. The economics check is mechanical: take historical earnings, strip every add-back you cannot document, divide by annual debt service, and either walk away or retrade the price whenever the result lands below 1.25x.

The second trap is paying a price the appraisal will not support. Matthias Smith's example: a $3.5M price against a $3M valuation leaves a $500,000 gap that must be covered with equity, because the SBA loan plus any amortizing seller note cannot exceed the valuation; Smith's fix is to research multiples before the LOI so a retrade never becomes necessary [3tkWRQX9WjI @ 00:12:10]. Pioneer Capital Advisory frames the same cap as total debt, SBA plus any non-standby seller note, limited to valuation [WF2-6ODNQms @ 00:49:57]. Ray Drew's sequence when the number comes in low is to renegotiate with the seller first and treat overpaying as a last resort, justified only occasionally for a strategic deal [9Sl18GknuZE @ 00:01:11]. Jack Pastrana of Credit Bench by First Home Bank explains why the gap usually exists in the first place: banks are cash flow lenders, and weak cash flow usually means the business is overpriced [NmgNpE_W_po @ 00:34:41]. The economics check is to run the lender's lens before signing anything: if the debt the business can carry at 1.25x is less than the asking price minus the 10% injection, the price is wrong, not the financing. Bring that math to the seller early, while there is still room to negotiate.

The third trap hits after closing. Ray Drew calls inadequate working capital the number one reason for an early default, tells buyers to project the cash-flow deficit during the transition, and warns that SBA will not fund working capital that is not substantiated [9Sl18GknuZE @ 00:07:05]. Matthias Smith flags a sharper version on expansion acquisitions: with 100% financing, working capital cannot be financed at all, so a buyer needing $300,000 of working capital is forced back into 10% equity unless that need is negotiated into the purchase price [3tkWRQX9WjI @ 00:10:40]. SBA University adds the liquidity side: lenders want to see money left after the injection, not a buyer emptying their bank account to close [92Nd2yD33As @ 00:05:12]. Michael S Glaspie lists the operational warnings that follow a thin closing: poor bookkeeping, interest-only early payments, payment fluctuation, and the risk that the lender calls the loan [WfgrSa37vaA @ 00:08:57]. The economics check is to model the first year with the full principal-and-interest payment, a transition dip in cash flow, and the cash reserve left after injection; if that reserve cannot carry several weak months, the deal is undercapitalized before day one. Drew also warns that stingy lenders who refuse to fund real needs hurt both sides of the table.

callout.body: Each check below comes from a deal pattern these practitioners watched fail or nearly fail. Clear all four before committing serious time or diligence money to a target.

chapters.question_prompt: How do seller notes, standby rules, earnouts, and personal guarantees fill the gap between bank debt and the purchase price?
chapters.title: Seller Financing, Earnouts, and Bridging the Down Payment
chapters.subtitle: Seller notes alongside SBA loans, full-standby rule changes and the new 5% minimum, whether a seller note can cover the down payment, pairing 7(a) with seller finance, why sellers agree to carry paper, structuring and documenting earnouts vs. seller financing, all-cash vs. structured deals, SBA personal guarantees, and what to do when the bank declines after the LOI
chapters.executive_summary: SBA lenders, brokers, and deal attorneys agree that the seller note is the most-used bridge between buyer cash and the purchase price. It keeps the seller's skin in the game, keeps the old owner answering the phone, and lowers the bank's exposure. The street baseline is a 90% SBA loan, 5% buyer cash, and a 5% seller note. Under the latest rule swing, that note only counts toward equity if it sits on full standby for the life of the loan and covers no more than half the required injection. Operators bridge the 10-year wait by grossing up the price by 5%, offering interest-only where the bank allows, or splitting large notes in two. Earnouts divide the room. Roland Frasier prefers them over any note, while Jason Paul Rogers says formal earnouts will not work with SBA and substitutes a consulting agreement.

key_metrics.label: Most Common SBA Capital Stack
key_metrics.value: 90% SBA loan / 5% buyer cash / 5% seller note
key_metrics.context: Keira Hamilton calls the 5/5 split the most common structure. She sees a full 10% seller note covering the injection mostly for insiders or deep industry operators.

key_metrics.label: Seller Note Cap Toward Equity Injection
key_metrics.metric: Seller Note Cap Toward Equity Injection
key_metrics.value: No more than 50% of the required injection, on full standby for the life of the loan
key_metrics.context: Allan Peterson, an SBA lender who closed over $70 million in acquisition financing last year, describes the rule that replaced the old 2-year standby structure.

key_metrics.label: Combined Debt Service Coverage Floor
key_metrics.value: 1.25x across SBA note plus seller note payments
key_metrics.context: Josh Kim says a non-equity seller note can be structured freely only if the combined SBA and seller payments still leave 1.25x debt service coverage.

key_metrics.label: Earnout Affordability Ceiling
key_metrics.value: About 50% of available profit after debt service
key_metrics.context: Roland Frasier models a $4 million profit business with roughly $2 million going to SBA debt service. He caps earnout payouts near half of what remains.

sections.title: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every SBA operator treats the seller note as a standard layer of the capital stack, not an exotic add-on. Keira Hamilton [7RAyVC1b9Pg @ 00:00:16] lays out the canonical stack on a $1 million project: $900,000 SBA, $50,000 buyer cash, and a $50,000 seller note. She says SBA lenders love the structure because it proves the seller believes in the business and in your ability to pay them back. Josh Kim bought three businesses before turning 21 on SBA 7A money. He says almost every SBA deal he touches carries seller financing, because the bank does not want the seller throwing in the keys and walking away mid-transition [W3nhTnkKZcU @ 00:01:26]. The SBA University instructor frames it from the buyer's chair. The nightmare is a retired owner on the beach who will not return your call, and owing them money keeps their phone on [s5o1MBGuspY @ 00:01:29]. Loan To Launch banker Daniel supplies the lender math. A seller note can shrink the SBA loan amount, improve deal cash flow, and signal belief in the business, all of which reads as lower risk from the banker's desk [OSZgayF9jHw @ 00:02:26]. The shared baseline: a seller willing to carry paper is a seller vouching for the cash flow.

Practitioners agree the pitch to the seller is not charity. It is a better investment than cash sitting in a bank. Josh Kim pitches it on tax and yield. An installment sale spreads the capital gains hit across multiple years, and a seller who takes $150,000 in cash would earn far less parking it in a savings account or CD [W3nhTnkKZcU @ 00:01:50]. David C Barnett pushes sellers to swap the business-owner hat for an investor hat. Seller notes get written at four to ten percent interest, while the best US high-interest savings rate Barnett found sat a little over half a percent. Note payments can also cover a retiree's monthly expenses, so the seller never has to dip into market accounts [PO1M-_wq-m4 @ 00:11:02]. A partnership-first buyer on Beau Eckstein's channel has run deals at 60 to 100 percent seller financing. That buyer says owners who ran a company for 10, 20, or 30 years genuinely do not need a lump sum and often prefer payouts over time to save on capital gains tax [1-sviMTVjUs @ 00:02:03]. Barnett also flags the cost of refusing. Sellers who will not carry paper sit on the market longer, and their ultimate selling price typically declines as the motivations behind the sale drag on the business [PO1M-_wq-m4 @ 00:03:26].

The third point of agreement: structure gets negotiated with the lender in the room, not bolted on at the end. Escamilla Law Office breaks a $10 million headline into three pieces: $7 million cash at close, a $1 million note the buyer owes, and a $2 million earnout that may never become payable. The firm insists deferred consideration is part of the price rather than a detail to sort out later. It also wants the purchase agreement, seller note, guarantee, security documents, and senior loan built to fit together [ZGklOUqHKYg @ 00:01:36]. Josh Kim says to talk to your lender first, then put seller financing terms in the LOI instead of waiting for due diligence. He warns that most deals die from bad structure rather than bad businesses [W3nhTnkKZcU @ 00:08:10]. Evan DiLeonardi of Itero is blunt that nobody can say up front whether a bank will want a 5, 10, 15, or 20 percent note. His advice is to get a structure greenlit by the lender before you walk it to the seller [zBzv99U7MyE @ 00:04:40]. The SBA University instructor closes the loop. The lender holds ultimate approval authority over how the seller note looks and sounds, so hash out the terms at the beginning, not at the closing table [s5o1MBGuspY @ 00:04:56].

sections.title: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The equity-counting seller note runs on hard rules. Josh Kim separates two animals. A note counted toward the equity injection must sit on full standby for the life of the loan. A note layered on top of a full 10% buyer injection can be structured however you want, as long as three conditions hold: the bank stays in first position, the seller subordinates, and combined SBA plus seller payments still clear 1.25x debt service coverage [W3nhTnkKZcU @ 00:04:29]. Allan Peterson is the SBA lender on JackQuisitions who closed over $70 million in acquisition financing last year. Peterson adds the cap: the standby note cannot account for more than 50% of the required injection. That ends the old play of two years on standby followed by three years of principal-and-interest payments with no balloon [I6M8wAaqm5s @ 00:22:18]. Owner Actions spells out the floor. Buyer cash of 5% is now the minimum, reachable only with a 5% seller note on full standby across a 10-year term. Sellers who never blinked at 24 months now treat 10 years as a sticking point [lfjqb1es1E4 @ 00:00:16]. Peterson also stresses that the 10% is measured against total project cost, not just the purchase price. Total project cost includes bank-provided working capital and the line of credit Peterson always builds in [I6M8wAaqm5s @ 00:24:02].

The street tactics for selling a decade-long standby note are specific. Evan DiLeonardi's own first deal closed at 90/5/5, back when a 2-year standby still counted toward the down payment. DiLeonardi recommends stacking the note on top of the price. If you want to offer $1 million, offer $1.05 million and ask for the extra $50,000 on full standby. Alternatively, offer $1,025,000 and split the difference as a sweetener [zBzv99U7MyE @ 00:02:17]. DiLeonardi adds that some banks allow interest-only payments during the 10-year stint, so the seller still collects interest while principal waits, though that sits at the bank's discretion. Allan Peterson has watched buyers in the pipeline request a 5% note for the life of the loan, cite secondary market data showing it would be abnormal to hold the loan to maturity, and then bump the offer by 5% [I6M8wAaqm5s @ 00:23:27]. Peterson's language tip: always say 'for the life of the loan,' never '10 years.' Then instill confidence that you will pay down early or refinance into conventional business banking once you hold three years of business tax returns as owner [I6M8wAaqm5s @ 00:30:56]. Host Jack used the same play with a hyper-growth plan projecting a four-to-six-year payoff, and that seller got paid off significantly quicker [I6M8wAaqm5s @ 00:34:39].

For notes outside the injection and for contingent money, the mechanics get creative. The SBA University instructor splits large notes. A $500,000 note on a $1 million deal becomes two $250,000 notes. The first is greenlit for payments from month one, so it becomes eligible for an SBA refinance after 24 months, at which point payments start on the second [s5o1MBGuspY @ 00:06:43]. Keira Hamilton flags forgivable, performance-based note language: all or part of the note is forgiven if the buyer misses revenue, EBITDA, or customer retention targets within a set period [7RAyVC1b9Pg @ 00:03:03]. Roland Frasier sizes earnout payouts with a simple Excel model. Take a business clearing $4 million with roughly $2 million going to SBA debt service. Paying the seller $600,000 a year for 10 years eats 30% of what is left. Paying $1 million a year hits 50% and leaves little room to wiggle if things go down [onN8dTJIXAM @ 00:06:31]. Jason Paul Rogers skips the formal earnout and writes a sidebar consulting agreement instead, such as an extra $100,000 if a key client does over $1 million in sales during the first six months post close. Rogers says a formal earnout will not work inside an SBA deal, and the legal fees swamp a seven-figure transaction [7w05y7xLcNI @ 00:03:30].

callout.title: How Operators Get Sellers to Sign the Paper
callout.body: These four negotiation moves come from lenders, brokers, and dealmakers who structure seller notes and earnouts on live deals.
items: Never call it a 10-year note. Call it 'for the life of the loan,' then sell your plan to pay down early or refinance to conventional once you have three years of returns as owner [JackQuisitions — I6M8wAaqm5s @ 00:30:56].

Present one structure only, the one most favorable to you. Keep five or six ranked fallback earnout and financing positions in your pocket instead of offering an A/B/C menu [Roland Frasier — onN8dTJIXAM @ 00:08:01].

Steer sellers away from demanding payoff in 24 or 36 months. That quick repayment squeezes the buyer's cash flow and actually makes the seller's note riskier [David C Barnett Small Business and Deal Making SMB — PO1M-_wq-m4 @ 00:08:25].

When a banker pushes back, ask point-blank whether it is an SBA rule or that bank's own overlay. Well-meaning lenders often mistake their policy for SBA policy [JackQuisitions — I6M8wAaqm5s @ 00:45:19].

sop_steps.title: Pre-qualify before you hunt
sop_steps.action: Send the lender a personal financial statement and a management resume to get a bank letter of support.
sop_steps.detail: Peterson produces a buyer pre-qualification letter within 24 hours. It needs only a personal financial statement (SBA Form 413 or any template, ballpark figures accepted) plus a resume. That letter becomes your hunting license with brokers and sellers [JackQuisitions — I6M8wAaqm5s @ 00:36:56].

sop_steps.title: Get the note size greenlit by the lender
sop_steps.action: Before pitching the seller, ask the lender what note percentage and standby terms they will accept on this specific deal.
sop_steps.detail: Some banks accept a 5% note on 10-year standby. Riskier deals with customer concentration may need a 10, 15, or 20 percent note, so get a structure at least initially greenlit before the seller sees it [Evan DiLeonardi | Acquisitions — zBzv99U7MyE @ 00:04:40].

sop_steps.title: Write seller financing into the LOI
sop_steps.action: Put the seller note amount, standby terms, and repayment terms in the letter of intent rather than waiting for due diligence.
sop_steps.detail: Kim says to tell the seller on the front end that you expect seller financing. Frame it around the seller's benefits: tax reasons, a guaranteed return, a faster close, and a bank that wants them to keep a piece of the risk [Josh Kim — W3nhTnkKZcU @ 00:08:10].

sop_steps.title: Document the note like a lender would
sop_steps.action: Draft principal, rate, accrual, schedule, balloon, default and cure terms, guarantee, collateral, setoff rights, and subordination language.
sop_steps.detail: The note needs principal, interest start, payment schedule, balloon, default and cure provisions, guarantee, perfected collateral, and setoff limits [Escamilla Law Office — ZGklOUqHKYg @ 00:11:35]. Bank counsel will check it for subordination and standby language before closing [Josh Kim — W3nhTnkKZcU @ 00:08:23].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is how long an equity-counting seller note must sit dark, and the answer depends on which rule window a practitioner closed under. ProjectionHub celebrated the change that cut full standby from the life of the SBA loan to only 24 months, modeling a $1,000,000 purchase with $50,000 of seller note where the first installment moved from July 2033 to July 2025 [8Gok1YA-HS8 @ 00:00:42]. Keira Hamilton taught the looser version as partial standby, where at most the buyer pays interest only for the first two years, while noting a lender can still demand a 5-year full standby [7RAyVC1b9Pg @ 00:02:02]. Owner Actions reports the reversal from the deal desk: 5% down is now the floor, the 5% note goes on full standby for the full 10-year term, and in their experience sellers did not bat an eye at 24 months but treated 10 years as a big sticking point [lfjqb1es1E4 @ 00:00:52]. Allan Peterson, the SBA lender on JackQuisitions, calls it a return to normalcy driven by higher default rates and a view that the rollback helped sellers more than buyers [I6M8wAaqm5s @ 00:32:42]. Any partial-standby playbook is only as current as the SOP it was learned under.

Roland Frasier ranks contingent pay above fixed debt every time: between seller financing and an earnout, the earnout wins because you might not have to pay it, and on a roughly $12 million trucking deal where the owner wanted half in cash, Roland would push the other half into an earnout first and seller financing second [onN8dTJIXAM @ 00:02:44]. Escamilla Law Office refuses to lump the two together: a seller note is credit risk on money the buyer already owes, an earnout is performance risk on money that may never come due, and a vague earnout does not kill the valuation fight, it moves it from before closing to after closing [ZGklOUqHKYg @ 00:05:29]. Jason Paul Rogers says a formal earnout will not work inside an SBA deal and costs too much in legal fees on a seven-figure purchase, so the playbook is a preset price plus a sidebar consulting agreement that pays the seller for hitting retention or sales metrics, such as an extra $100,000 for keeping a key client above $1 million in sales over six months [7w05y7xLcNI @ 00:04:21]. acquiredotcom slots earnouts into high-growth businesses with uncertain short-term performance, but warns they demand trust and breed disputes over performance metrics [3Cgn92T6L1Y @ 00:02:24].

The second fault line is how to buy the seller's patience. Evan DiLeonardi prices it in: offer $1.05 million instead of $1 million and ask for the extra $50,000 on full 10-year standby, or split the difference at $1,025,000, but only where the buyer has leverage, because on competitive deals a rival will offer a structure without a decade-long wait [zBzv99U7MyE @ 00:02:17]. Allan Peterson has watched buyers request a 5% note for the life of the loan, point to secondary-market data suggesting the loan is rarely held to maturity, and raise the offer by 5% to land at 5% down [I6M8wAaqm5s @ 00:23:27]. The other split is whether the seller stays in the cap table at all. Beau Eckstein's channel pitched partial change of ownership with the seller dropping from 100% to 19% with no personal guarantee, or keeping 1% so an HVAC buyer can run on the seller's license [1-sviMTVjUs @ 00:05:09]. Under the newer SOP, Allan says any retained seller equity forces a stock sale and a 24-month seller guarantee, so the preferred route is a third-party licensed qualifier holding up to 19% with no guarantee, a route Jack backs as a self-described do-not-work-with-the-seller buyer [I6M8wAaqm5s @ 00:14:01].

sections.heading: Section 4: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive surprises come from the senior lender rewriting the seller deal after the handshake. Escamilla Law Office has seen deals where the commercial terms assumed the seller would be refinanced out at a set point, then the senior lender required the seller debt to stay in place much longer, turning a 2-year credit into a long-term loan and leaving a year-2 or year-3 balloon unpayable if the bank will not permit it [ZGklOUqHKYg @ 00:15:25]. SBA University warns that even after closing the lender has ultimate authority on when seller-note payments start and stop, and if cash flow cannot carry both loans the bank blocks the payments or the refinance, which is why full disclosure has to happen at the start rather than at the closing table or two years in [s5o1MBGuspY @ 00:07:27]. Josh Kim puts it bluntly: most deals do not fall apart because the business is bad, they fall apart because the financing or the deal was not structured correctly to begin with [W3nhTnkKZcU @ 00:07:38]. Evan DiLeonardi's fix is procedural: reach the lender ahead of time, find out how big a note they want, and walk into the seller conversation with a structure the bank has at least initially greenlit [zBzv99U7MyE @ 00:04:40].

Seller-side behavior blows up deals and notes from the other direction. David C Barnett sees sellers demand repayment in 24 or 36 months, and that quick schedule makes the note riskier because the big payments push the business into a cash squeeze where one bad stretch means missed payments [PO1M-_wq-m4 @ 00:08:25]. Barnett has also watched many sellers walk back to the table refusing a note because a financial advisor wants the money under management, countering that few places let a seller earn a 5% yield on a business they know completely [PO1M-_wq-m4 @ 00:12:45]. Escamilla Law Office flags the paper risk: a buyer often forms a fresh LLC with little history and few assets beyond the acquired company, so a seller owed $1 million has to look past the signature to guarantees, perfected collateral, priority against the bank, and any buyer right to set off indemnification claims against note payments [ZGklOUqHKYg @ 00:13:20]. The upside of underwriting like a lender shows up in Barnett's bar deal, a business banks rarely finance: the seller-financer required weekly liquor-system reports and monthly financials, and a few months after closing called the buyer to report someone was stealing [PO1M-_wq-m4 @ 00:13:34].

The buyer's own balance sheet is the last trap, and the economics checks are specific. Jon Stoddard has seen buyers sign a personal guarantee without doing their homework, watch the business tank, and then face the SBA coming for their house and savings, which is rare but catastrophic, so the push is for a limited guarantee, sunset clauses, or performance triggers [104miMfvJRg @ 00:01:35]. Roland Frasier sizes earnout and seller-note payouts against profit left after debt service: on $4 million of profit with roughly $2 million going to the SBA loan, a $600,000 annual payout is 30% of the remainder, and a $1 million payout at 50% leaves little room for wiggle if things go down [onN8dTJIXAM @ 00:07:13]. callout.body: Every item below is a pitfall practitioners hit or watched kill deals; do not move to signatures until each one is answered on paper.
items: Do not lock seller-financing terms until the lender confirms the combined structure meets debt service coverage and SBA eligibility requirements [Josh Kim — W3nhTnkKZcU @ 00:07:15].

Stress-test the seller note against a 10% revenue decline and confirm the buyer can still pay both the bank and the seller [David C Barnett Small Business and Deal Making SMB — PO1M-_wq-m4 @ 00:07:24].

Require an earnout process covering when the buyer delivers the calculation, what records come with it, how long the seller reviews it, and how disputes are resolved [Escamilla Law Office — ZGklOUqHKYg @ 00:10:27].

chapters.question_prompt: What goes into a letter of intent, and how should it be drafted before due diligence begins?
chapters.title: The Letter of Intent: Anatomy and Drafting
chapters.subtitle: Whether LOIs are necessary, binding vs. non-binding terms, the LOI's components and anatomy, terms to settle before diligence, structuring a winning small-business LOI, lawyer guidance on LOIs, the LOI's place among the M&A milestones, Acquire.com's LOI builder, and what an LOI does in a buy-sell process
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners from law firms, investment banks and acquisition marketplaces treat the LOI as a short, mostly non-binding letter that locks price, structure, payment form, working capital, timing and closing conditions before anyone pays for diligence, with exclusivity and confidentiality carrying the binding weight. The street numbers are concrete: exclusivity of 60 to 90 days, purchase agreements of 40 to 70 pages waiting downstream, 80/10/10 payment structures, seller notes at 6 to 10%, a $5M working capital target that swings price $1M either way, targeted escrows of $500K to $1M, and a 72-hour expiration. A buyer who skipped the LOI lost three weeks and an $8,000 environmental report. Disagreements center on 60 versus 90 day closing dates, setting the working capital target in the LOI versus deferring it to the QoE, and whether an LOI is needed at all.

key_metrics.label: Standard Exclusivity Window
key_metrics.value: 60 or 90 days
key_metrics.context: Brett Cenkus describes exclusivity as the seller agreeing not to talk to other parties or keep shopping the deal, commonly for 60 or 90 days, on $0.5M to $20M deals.

key_metrics.label: Downstream Purchase Agreement Length
key_metrics.value: 40 to 70 pages
key_metrics.context: SMB Law Group sizes the purchase agreement that follows the LOI at 40 to 70 pages, the reason to settle business terms in a short letter first.

key_metrics.label: Working Capital True-Up Swing
key_metrics.value: $1M up or down on a $5M target
key_metrics.context: Mike Rosendahl shows that delivering $6M against a $5M target pays the seller $1M more, while delivering $4M cuts $1M from the price after close.

key_metrics.label: Cost of Skipping the LOI
key_metrics.value: 3 weeks plus an $8,000 environmental report
key_metrics.context: A buyer negotiated price verbally for three weeks and paid for an environmental report, then lost the deal to a higher offer with no LOI and no exclusivity.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: The cheapest insurance in a deal is a signed LOI. The Letters of Intent episode opens with a buyer who spent three weeks negotiating price verbally and paid for an $8,000 environmental report, only to watch the seller take a higher offer because nothing was signed and nothing was exclusive; the verdict was that an LOI would have cost them an afternoon [VuuLz-8NiYg @ 00:00:14]. Oberman Law Firm, which handles roughly 100-plus transactions a year, frames the LOI as the framework set before anyone spends money on diligence, and warns that skipping it misaligns expectations and can burn thousands of dollars in legal fees [6uqSoqOVnsg @ 00:01:17]. Eric Pacifici and Sam Rosati of SMB Law Group make the same economic argument: the LOI locks exclusivity before the buyer commits QoE spend, it sits upstream of a purchase agreement that runs 40 to 70 pages, and it separates a serious buyer from the roughly 600 inbound inquiries a broker fields on a listing [OIcTvUbSEgM @ 00:04:29]. Mike Rosendahl of PCE Investment Bankers puts the purpose plainly: let the parties confirm very early that there is basic agreement on key terms and no deal-breaker issues before either side devotes substantial time and resources to diligence and definitive documents [n_gxsr8QgBM @ 00:00:38].

On what actually binds, the practitioners converge hard. Brett Cenkus, who works deals between $0.5M and $20M, says exclusivity and confidentiality are usually the only binding terms, with exclusivity meaning the seller will not talk to other parties or keep shopping the deal for commonly 60 or 90 days [aNioqOmfOe4 @ 00:02:47]. Lockaby PLLC names confidentiality and exclusivity as the binding pair, then rounds out the letter with conditions precedent, a non-compete, a conduct-of-business covenant, limits on public announcements, governing law, dispute resolution and a merger clause [NCbzskaBTdQ @ 00:10:25]. Mike Rosendahl adds governing law to the binding list and leaves price, structure, contingencies, diligence and working capital explicitly non-binding [n_gxsr8QgBM @ 00:01:14]. The Letters of Intent episode calls non-binding the market standard, yet pushes breakup fees, governing law and dispute resolution into the binding bucket, and warns that re-trading the economics after signing can be bad faith and potentially actionable [VuuLz-8NiYg @ 00:13:17]. The operator read is that the non-binding label is not a license to walk back the numbers. The binding clauses carry the legal teeth, but reopening agreed business terms once the other side has turned away bidders invites exactly the bad-faith accusation these practitioners describe.

The term list is remarkably stable across channels. The Letters of Intent episode scopes an LOI at about 10 to 15 deal points and names the core set: price, deposit, diligence period, closing date, exclusivity, financing contingency, what is being sold, key economics, closing conditions, confidentiality, and the binding or non-binding designation [VuuLz-8NiYg @ 00:08:49]. Cenkus covers price, form of payment as cash or seller note, assets versus stock versus merger, employees and closing conditions, in a document of a few pages and up to about 10 [aNioqOmfOe4 @ 00:01:39]. PRIME exits demands clear structure and price, a defined adjusted EBITDA with add-backs, payment terms and a no-shop with commitment on both sides, warns that vague pricing signals you are not fully committed, and tells drafters not to over-legalize the letter [32xGWYMqfWk @ 00:00:57]. On length, nobody rewards bulk: Keira Hamilton says a 15-page LOI on a $1M HVAC business likely will not be read [JulvxMkY4VY @ 00:00:43]. The consensus build is short, priced precisely, and explicit about structure, payment form, timing and the conditions that must clear before close, with the heavy legal drafting saved for the purchase agreement that follows.

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Exclusivity length is where the numbers get specific. Keira Hamilton ties it to lender speed: SBA loans take about 60 days, so ask for roughly 90 days of exclusivity, not 30 and not 180 [JulvxMkY4VY @ 00:05:21]. Ellie on the SMB PE episode says most deals close in 60 to 90 days, calls asking for 120 a bad bad move, notes that only 30 to 45 days are needed to reach a purchase agreement, and adds that deals almost never die because exclusivity runs out; the episode settles on 60 days plus automatic extensions [PF2SOneLrJ0 @ 00:08:28]. Sam Rosati of SMB Law Group pegs SBA deals at about 90 days and expects a buyer who writes 60 to come back for an extension, so the exclusivity clause should carry extension cover; Eric Pacifici writes 60 days every time and would rather lose a rare deal later than lose every deal up front with a long projected closing date [OIcTvUbSEgM @ 00:18:58]. Escamilla Law Office treats exclusivity as a meaningful commercial concession and ties its duration to financing and diligence readiness, using defined deadlines and extensions the buyer has to earn rather than an open-ended hold on the seller [juS-FdGX2o0 @ 00:08:31]. The working rule is a short headline window with pre-negotiated extension mechanics behind it.

Price mechanics start with how the dollars move. SMB Law Group structures deals 80/10/10 or 90% cash, so an $8M deal puts $7.2M on the table at close, keeps the SBA debt amount out of the letter, and prices the seller note at typical 6 to 10% rates with monthly payments favoring the seller [OIcTvUbSEgM @ 00:36:34]. Pacifici and Rosati want the note modeled through standby, interest-only and balloon periods, flag a 50% note with a 12-month balloon as a trap, and tell buyers to foreshadow the subordination agreement because the note will have to subordinate to the lender. Escamilla contrasts two $5M offers, all cash versus $4M at close plus a $500K seller note plus a $500K earnout over two years, the second loading credit and performance risk onto the seller [juS-FdGX2o0 @ 00:02:35]. The acquire.com founder demos a $1.3M offer with $700K upfront, $500K seller financing over 12 months at zero interest, and a $100K holdback for 12 months conditioned on zero outstanding litigation [MYKKpeF0xMM @ 00:01:07]. Ellie hammers the logic behind every one of these splits: you cannot pay your full purchase price at closing, you need to hold back something [PF2SOneLrJ0 @ 00:44:55].

Lockaby PLLC calls working capital the biggest deal-killer, and the practitioners attach hard numbers to it [NCbzskaBTdQ @ 00:05:34]. Rosendahl defines it as receivables plus inventory plus prepaid expenses, less accounts payable and accrued liabilities at close, with the seller keeping the cash; on a $5M target, delivering $6M pays the seller $1M more and delivering $4M cuts $1M from the price, trued up after close [n_gxsr8QgBM @ 00:04:31]. Ellie defers the target to the QoE, for example $1.5M, and uses escrow for the 60 to 90 day true-up and indemnification, replacing the fading 5 to 10% norm with targeted amounts such as $1M for ERC risk and $500K for sales tax [PF2SOneLrJ0 @ 00:31:43]. The same episode moved definitions into an exhibit and cut comments by about 80%, sets a 72-hour expiration, and adds fee-shifting on exclusivity breach. On asset scope, SMB Law Group buys all assets owned or used by the business minus the seller's stated exclusions, a stance that won a Rhode Island Chancery fight over a seller-owned Amazon account carrying 4,500 five-star reviews, a 4.7 rating and about $2M of value [OIcTvUbSEgM @ 00:23:54].
