callout.title: Drafting moves the deal lawyers actually use
callout.body: Small structural choices in the LOI change how fast it gets signed, how the seller reads the buyer, and how much leverage survives into the purchase agreement.
items: Form a buyer entity for a couple hundred dollars, sign the NDAs and the LOI through it, then assign to a NewCo at close, and check the Section 14 cross-references when you do [SMB Law Group LLP — OIcTvUbSEgM @ 00:17:14]

Drop generic placeholder praise: the firm stripped it from its template after a broker received 4 identical LOIs, and Sam Rosati parks any love letter in an exhibit because business terms decide [SMB Law Group LLP — OIcTvUbSEgM @ 00:13:41]
Put the due-diligence condition in the lead-in language and move definitions to an exhibit, which cut comments by about 80% [Dennis Unrein / SMB PE LLC — PF2SOneLrJ0 @ 00:38:52]

Specify exactly when the deposit goes hard and demand proof of funds, because a $100K deposit refundable on diligence can tie the seller up with a non-buyer [Letters of Intent — VuuLz-8NiYg @ 00:18:49]

sop_steps.title: Qualify the buyer and set up the signing vehicle
sop_steps.action: Form the acquisition entity and line up lender support before drafting the offer.
sop_steps.detail: Business acquisitions typically close in 45 to 60 days, so attach a bank pre-approval letter to show the buyer can actually perform [Letters of Intent — VuuLz-8NiYg @ 00:07:12]; sign the NDA and LOI through a freshly formed entity and assign it to a NewCo later [SMB Law Group LLP — OIcTvUbSEgM @ 00:17:14].

sop_steps.title: Lock price, payment split and seller note terms
sop_steps.action: Write one exact price with the cash-at-close, seller note, earnout and holdback components spelled out.
sop_steps.detail: Model the seller note through standby, interest-only and balloon periods [SMB Law Group LLP — OIcTvUbSEgM @ 00:41:01], call your bank before committing to note terms, and foreshadow that the note will be subordinated to the lender [SMB Law Group LLP — OIcTvUbSEgM @ 00:42:14].

sop_steps.title: Define working capital and targeted escrows
sop_steps.action: State the working capital definition, the target or the method for setting it, and the post-close true-up.
sop_steps.detail: Rosendahl treats the working capital target as one of the most important LOI terms [PCE Investment Bankers — n_gxsr8QgBM @ 00:03:40]; size escrow to specific risks such as $1M for ERC and $500K for sales tax rather than a flat 5 to 10% [Dennis Unrein / SMB PE LLC — PF2SOneLrJ0 @ 00:31:43].

sop_steps.title: Fix exclusivity, binding clauses and expiration, then sign
sop_steps.action: Mark exclusivity and confidentiality as binding, set the window with extensions, add a short expiry and execute.
sop_steps.detail: Commonly 60 or 90 days of exclusivity [Brett Cenkus — aNioqOmfOe4 @ 00:02:47]; add a 72-hour expiration and always sign the LOI rather than leaving it as an unsigned draft [Dennis Unrein / SMB PE LLC — PF2SOneLrJ0 @ 00:56:57].

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: Exclusivity length and the projected closing date produce the sharpest split. Inside SMB Law Group, Sam Rosati says SBA deals take about 90 days, so a buyer who writes 60 should expect to request an extension and needs extension cover written into the exclusivity clause, while Eric Pacifici answers '60 days every time,' preferring to lose a deal later in a very rare situation than lose every deal up front with too long a projected closing date [OIcTvUbSEgM @ 00:20:12]. Ellie on the SMB PE panel sides with the short clock: most deals close in 60 to 90 days, asking for 120 is a 'bad bad move,' and only 30 to 45 days are needed to reach a purchase agreement, because deals almost never die from running out of exclusivity; the panel's resolution is 60 days plus automatic extensions [PF2SOneLrJ0 @ 00:08:28]. Keira Hamilton runs different math: SBA loans take about 60 days, so ask for about 90 days of exclusivity, not 30 and not 180 [JulvxMkY4VY @ 00:05:21]. Escamilla Law Office rejects a fixed number entirely, tying duration to financing and diligence readiness through defined deadlines and earned extensions, and frames exclusivity as a meaningful commercial concession the seller is giving up in exchange for the buyer's proof of readiness [juS-FdGX2o0 @ 00:09:21].

Working capital splits the bankers from the lawyers. Mike Rosendahl of PCE Investment Bankers sets the target inside the LOI and calls it one of the most important terms to negotiate: on a $5M target, delivering $6M pays the seller $1M more and delivering $4M cuts $1M from the price, with the payment trued up or down after the close [n_gxsr8QgBM @ 00:03:40]. Ellie on the SMB PE panel defers the number to the QoE, using a $1.5M example, and flags that sellers want to sweep receivables, which a working-capital line of credit can offset [PF2SOneLrJ0 @ 00:28:28]. Lockaby PLLC calls working capital the biggest deal-killer and insists that the earlier the parties talk through how it works inside the structure of the deal, the better [NCbzskaBTdQ @ 00:05:34]. Structure is just as contested. KreischerMiller frames the baseline fight bluntly: buyers want assets, sellers want stock [Q6exObbgCgk @ 00:00:30]. Ellie prefers an asset deal unless contracts or licenses cannot be assigned, warns that sales tax and environmental liabilities still carry over, then says a buyer can move from asset to equity but not back, and in the same breath advises to always start out with an equity purchase. Buyers have to pick which opening anchor to throw.

Seller financing draws opposite reads. The Letters of Intent episode treats it as a red flag that the buyer cannot get a loan and expects the seller to demand a premium for carrying paper, accepting it mainly for related parties or law-firm pension sales [VuuLz-8NiYg @ 00:11:56]. acquiredotcom pitches the reverse to sellers: offering seller financing can increase the buyer pool and the chances of closing, demoed as $700K upfront plus $500K over 12 months at zero interest to de-risk the acquisition [MYKKpeF0xMM @ 00:01:27]. Eric Pacifici of SMB Law Group says you never actually have to have a seller note, yet still values one as proof of seller belief, added liquidity, and an indemnity offset, and warns it will have to be subordinated to the lender [OIcTvUbSEgM @ 00:40:04]. Document length is the second open fight. Transact Capital wants more detail in the LOI rather than deferring it, expecting about 10 pages, because the LOI phase is the seller's point of maximum leverage, accepting it bars talking to other buyers, and signing releases control to the buyer, who is now 100% committed but not 100% bound [Axofinu0FSU @ 00:00:56]. That leverage logic pushes sellers to win every economic point before the ink dries, not after.

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive failure is skipping the LOI. The Letters of Intent episode opens with a buyer who spent 3 weeks negotiating price verbally and paid for an $8,000 environmental report, only to watch the seller take a higher offer because there was no LOI and no exclusivity; an LOI would have cost them an afternoon [VuuLz-8NiYg @ 00:00:14]. The same episode walks through a $3M business where nobody discussed the diligence period, financing contingency, or asset versus stock sale, while the seller turned down other bids assuming an exclusivity that never existed. Oberman Law Firm, handling about 100-plus transactions a year, says skipping the LOI misaligns expectations and can burn thousands of dollars in legal fees [6uqSoqOVnsg @ 00:04:52]. SMB Law Group explains why the sequence matters: the LOI locks exclusivity before QoE spend, purchase agreements run 40 to 70 pages, and brokers field about 600 inbound inquiries, so an unlocked buyer is one of hundreds [OIcTvUbSEgM @ 00:04:29]. Eric Pacifici also warns never to sign an APA with a deposit and inspection period without help. Even with a signed letter, Letters of Intent cautions that a refundable $100K deposit can tie the seller up with a non-buyer, which is why they require proof of funds.

The number-one deal killer after signing is a quality-of-earnings miss. SMB Law Group cites $2M of EBITDA becoming $1.6M post-QoE, and pairs it with structure traps: don't list the SBA debt amount, and model the seller note across standby, interest-only, and balloon periods, because a 50% note with a 12-month balloon is a trap [OIcTvUbSEgM @ 00:33:34]. Escamilla Law Office's Texas $5M hypothetical stacks every failure at once: a 90-day exclusivity period, a $300K working-capital dispute, a seller-note mismatch, lender conflicts, a customer consent requirement, and broad indemnification [juS-FdGX2o0 @ 00:16:23]. Escamilla also warns that SBA lenders restrict seller notes through subordination and payment limits, so a note negotiated without the bank collapses. Two offers both priced at $5M carry very different risk: all cash versus $4M at close, a $500K seller note, and a $500K earnout over 2 years. Ellie on the SMB PE panel shows the forgivable-note downside in numbers: $3M of EBITDA at 5x is $15M, with $10M at close and $5M forgivable, and missing by $500K forgives $2.5M [PF2SOneLrJ0 @ 00:25:13]. The same panel says a buyer cannot pay the full purchase price at closing and must hold back something.

Post-signing people risk is where economics quietly leak. On the SMB PE panel, a plumbing seller and their son started competing after the sale, and a sale-based non-compete needs roughly $100K to $200K of consideration to stick; Dennis adds a $100,000 tenant-improvement bill from a landlord, with landlords demanding deposits and personal guarantees [PF2SOneLrJ0 @ 00:42:16]. Transition terms fail on small numbers: an $80M seller quit over $150 an hour versus $300 an hour, and the panel uses sweeteners like $200K or $400 an hour to get through the seller death spiral. SMB Law Group recounts a seller-owned Amazon account with 4,500 five-star reviews and a 4.7 rating, worth about $2M, that the buyer only won in Rhode Island Chancery because the LOI bought all assets owned or used by the business [OIcTvUbSEgM @ 00:23:54]. Bootstrapping to Billions warns that good deals don't get done with bad people and that paralysis by analysis kills momentum [BDlt56r8cRk @ 00:15:59]. KreischerMiller flags the board-level trap: boards with passive investors may insist on a fiduciary out to accept a higher unsolicited offer and avoid litigation, which punches a hole in the buyer's exclusivity [Q6exObbgCgk @ 00:03:14].

callout.body: Every item below is a pitfall a practitioner watched cost real money or kill a deal; clear all four before signing [SMB Law Group LLP — OIcTvUbSEgM @ 00:31:08].
items: Demand proof of funds before granting exclusivity against a refundable deposit, because a $100K deposit refundable on diligence can tie the seller up with a non-buyer [Letters of Intent — VuuLz-8NiYg @ 00:10:22].
Run lien and litigation searches and secure first-lien position for the lender; skipping them is 'probably malpractice' [SMB Law Group LLP — OIcTvUbSEgM @ 00:31:08].

action_checklist: Sign the LOI with binding exclusivity and confidentiality before spending on QoE or environmental reports [SMB Law Group LLP — OIcTvUbSEgM @ 00:04:29].

Write the working capital definition as receivables plus inventory plus prepaid expenses less accounts payable and accrued liabilities, trued up after close [PCE Investment Bankers - M&A | ESOP | Valuation — n_gxsr8QgBM @ 00:03:57].

chapters.question_prompt: What is a quality of earnings report, how is it read, and why do lenders and buyers rely on it?
chapters.title: Quality of Earnings and Financial Due Diligence
chapters.subtitle: QoE vs. reported EBITDA, a step-by-step QoE analysis and databook walkthrough, reading a QoE as a practitioner, how lenders read QoE reports and why banks reject seller EBITDA, QoE cost, financial due diligence fundamentals, common seller and inventory mistakes, and the diligence failures that kill deals
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners from Acquira's TreeWalk QoE desk, John Colley, Elliott Holland, CandiMentor, and lender-focused QoE shops agree that the purchase price is a multiple of EBITDA, so the QoE exists to prove which earnings are real, recurring, and transferable. Every add-back needs an invoice, payroll record, or genuine one-time event, and a cost recurring three years running gets rejected. Street mechanics start with proof of cash tied to bank statements and tax returns, run a three-column bridge from reported to normalized EBITDA, and set a debt-free, cash-free working capital peg from monthly data. Colley's Summit case shows a $2.3 million gap becoming $23 million at 10x; TreeWalk reports roughly half of QoEs come back clean and 20 to 25% kill the deal. Practitioners split on cost and scope, from $12,000 fixed-fee reports to $500,000 Big Four engagements.

key_metrics.label: QoE Outcome Split Across 50+ Deals
key_metrics.value: 45-50% clean; 20-25% deal-killers; ~20% gray-area renegotiation
key_metrics.context: The TreeWalk Consulting QoE lead's breakdown of last year's 50-plus transactions: about half came back clean, 20 to 25% surfaced major mistakes that stopped the deal, and the rest carried downward EBITDA pressure requiring earnouts, seller notes, or repricing.

key_metrics.label: Small-Business QoE Fixed-Fee Pricing Tiers
key_metrics.context: Midwest CPA's budgeting guide, with simple single-location businesses at the bottom tier and custom scopes above $10 million enterprise value, always billed as a fixed fee.

key_metrics.label: Summit Normalization Gap And Price Swing
key_metrics.metric: Summit Normalization Gap And Price Swing
key_metrics.value: $18.5M reported to $16.2M normalized; $2.3M gap = $23M at 10x
key_metrics.context: Colley's Summit Industrial Services case: a trimmed founder salary add-back, rejected recurring consulting fees, and a missed below-market related-party lease reset.
key_metrics.source: John Colley | The Investment Banking Practitioner ([zQE4R-z6Yww @ 00:03:17])

key_metrics.label: Lender Minimum Debt Service Coverage
key_metrics.value: At least 1.25x
key_metrics.context: Adjusted cash flow divided by annual debt payments is the key number lenders pull from the QoE before approving acquisition debt.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every practitioner who prices deals lands on the same arithmetic: the purchase price is a multiple of EBITDA or SDE, so the earnings figure itself is the asset being bought. Edspira frames the buyer's goal as learning how much of earnings is cash versus non-cash, recurring versus non-recurring, and the product of aggressive accounting, because valuation is often expressed as a multiple of adjusted EBITDA [itIweMi_DyU @ 00:00:28]. Elliott Holland is blunter: sellers lie about EBITDA, and a CIM showing $1 million at a 4x multiple implies $4 million of value when the real figure could be $800,000, $1.2 million, $500,000, or even zero [KJPGQ94h_GY @ 00:00:19]. Holland adds that once sellers know they are exiting at three to five times EBITDA, even the most honorable people hide things between data sets the buyer has no time to reconcile while chasing lenders and equity [KJPGQ94h_GY @ 00:01:09]. John Colley, drawing on 30 years across SG Cowen, Wasserstein, and Houlihan Lokey, calls the QoE the single most consequential document in M&A diligence because it answers whether the claimed EBITDA is real, targeting normalized maintainable EBITDA under new ownership [zQE4R-z6Yww @ 00:01:57]. Steve Roscioli lists the review scope: revenue, add-backs, expenses, accounting practices, customer concentration, working capital, and performance trends over time [RXawmeZf9sU @ 00:00:17].

The second consensus point is that no add-back survives on the seller's say-so. The QoE and Financial Modeling Practice channel says lenders walk through every add-back, and each one needs an invoice, a payroll record, or a clear one-time event; an add-back without documentation is usually thrown out [SBILxsNgW-o @ 00:00:00]. Their companion breakdown makes it concrete: a seller claiming $1.2 million of EBITDA after adding back a boat, a nephew, and a one-time lawsuit watches the lender toss anything without paper overboard, boat included, because banks lend on proof, not on says [yP7oBq_gKbw @ 00:00:23]. CandiMentor insists the label one-time is not enough: a non-recurring item may be removed only when there is a credible reason it will not come back, and repeated one-time costs reveal normal operations rather than genuine exceptions [QVDTq7Qd6-A @ 00:02:25]. John Colley converts this into five red flags: recurring items dressed up as one-time, above-market owner compensation add-backs that ignore replacement cost, missing negative adjustments such as below-market related-party rent, aggressive revenue normalization that assumes a departed customer returns, and understated run-rate costs from deferred maintenance or running lean for the sale process [zQE4R-z6Yww @ 00:03:34]. Every practitioner here treats the add-back schedule as the seller's burden to prove.

Consensus also holds that clean EBITDA can still produce a bad deal when cash, working capital, debt-like items, or customer dependency are misread. Corporate Finance Institute describes a CFO bragging about $50 million of EBITDA while diligence finds only $10 million converting to usable cash, usually from aging receivables or inventory built ahead of growth [FvywvHEpXKU @ 00:04:18]. The same team calls customer concentration the first red flag: if 40% of revenue comes from one customer, valuation has to plummet [FvywvHEpXKU @ 00:03:48]. The FE International guest on Jon Stoddard's channel contrasts two $10 million businesses: one client on a non-transferable rolling annual agreement versus 100 clients paying $100,000 on three-year, auto-extending, assignable contracts, the latter worth significantly more [Yr06Fv79PU0 @ 00:04:32]. Figuring Out with Rahul lays out the working capital safeguard: set a target from historical data, measure actual NWC at close, and cut the price dollar for dollar on any shortfall [xgCInPpZDiQ @ 00:05:05]. CandiMentor stretches net debt beyond the bank loan to leases, accrued interest, seller obligations, and unfunded commitments, asking whether the buyer will effectively fund them after closing [a5aX7QK8vKA @ 00:02:37]. Each speaker treats these checks as part of the same earnings question, not a separate exercise.

table.caption: Where QoE Practitioners Agree: Core Principles And Their Deal Consequences
rows: Adjusted EBITDA is the number that drives the purchase price
Valuation is often expressed as a multiple of the seller's adjusted EBITDA figure
A significant discrepancy lets the buyer renegotiate price or walk away entirely
Edspira ([itIweMi_DyU @ 00:01:16])
Sellers inflate claimed earnings when a sale multiple is in sight
Even honorable sellers lie about EBITDA when exiting at three to five times
A $1 million CIM EBITDA could really be $500,000 or even zero
Elliott Holland ([KJPGQ94h_GY @ 00:01:09])
Every add-back must be backed by documentary evidence before credit
An invoice, payroll record, or clear one-time event must support each add-back
Undocumented add-backs are usually thrown out by the lender reviewing the deal
QoE and Financial Modeling Practice ([SBILxsNgW-o @ 00:00:22])
The recurrence test kills disguised one-time costs in the bridge
A non-recurring cost appearing three years running is not actually non-recurring
Rejected add-backs reduce normalized EBITDA and move the purchase price directly
John Colley | The Investment Banking Practitioner ([zQE4R-z6Yww @ 00:03:51])
Owner personal spending running through the business must be stripped out
Sports tickets, vacations, home repairs, second homes, and boats show up in the books
Non-business costs are isolated so true business earnings become visible to the buyer
XPX - Exit Planning Exchange ([gRV7segOzzo @ 00:01:48])
Earnings must convert into cash, not just accounting profit on paper
Strong EBITDA can hide cash trapped in inventory or unpaid customer invoices
Lenders focus on cash conversion and repayment capacity under real pressure
CandiMentor ([QVDTq7Qd6-A @ 00:04:34])
Revenue durability and transferability determine what earnings are actually worth
One non-assignable client is far riskier than 100 clients on three-year contracts
Two businesses with identical $10 million earnings receive very different valuations
Jon Stoddard ([Yr06Fv79PU0 @ 00:05:07])

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: The TreeWalk Consulting QoE lead presenting on Acquira, whose midsize CPA firm of about 65 people ran roughly 50 to 55 transactions last year with 85% in the lower mid-market, says proof of cash is the first step on every engagement [g_fy5eeJpHE @ 00:01:29]. Mechanically, revenue net of AR movement and expenses net of AP and capex movement are tied to what actually hits and leaves the bank statements; about 85% of the time it works out because owners watch cash closely, and the businesses where it does not are red flags to run from [g_fy5eeJpHE @ 00:05:30]. The lender version is a three-way tie: bank deposits to the P&L, the P&L to the tax returns, and if the three sources disagree the lender wants to know why [SBILxsNgW-o @ 00:00:43]. Elliott Holland explains why the tie-out cannot be skipped in small companies: in 16 years they have seen cash-ish and accrual-ish books, never straight either one, so interpreting revenue recognition is a core QoE task [KJPGQ94h_GY @ 00:00:54]. Chris Barrett of Midwest CPA prices the work off that complexity: percent-completion, revenue recognition, inventory and project tracking, multiple locations, carve-outs, and overall size all add hours to the engagement [36OTOiIXSrk @ 00:00:13].

John Colley's three-column framework runs reported EBITDA, adjusted EBITDA after genuinely non-recurring items, and normalized EBITDA after normalization and pro forma adjustments [zQE4R-z6Yww @ 00:04:50]. On the Summit Industrial Services case, $18.5 million of reported EBITDA accepts a $1.8 million litigation add-back as legitimate, cuts a $900,000 founder salary add-back to $500,000 because the replacement costs $400,000, rejects $600,000 of 'one-time' consulting in its third straight year, and adds a missed $350,000 hit from a family-trust warehouse lease 30% below market, landing at $16.2 million [zQE4R-z6Yww @ 00:05:30]. At 10x, that $2.3 million gap is a $23 million price swing [zQE4R-z6Yww @ 00:03:17]. Figuring Out with Rahul runs the same math: $10 million reported normalizes to $7.5 million, a 25% drop, and at 5x the price falls from $50 million to $37.5 million [xgCInPpZDiQ @ 00:06:06]. Verified Metrics builds the bridge in a databook: management adjustments picked from a drop-down of account names, a separate diligence-adjustments block for items like IPO share listing and legal fees, and annual plus LTM columns [EzOFN-69wBU @ 00:01:24]. CandiMentor adds the bridge check that the same benefit is never counted twice [QVDTq7Qd6-A @ 00:04:34].

Working capital is where the TreeWalk lead says deals die, ranking the peg a top-two or top-three killer [g_fy5eeJpHE @ 00:16:31]. Their M&A definition is debt-free, cash-free: strip lines of credit, deferred revenue, bank indebtedness, and other debt-like items from current liabilities and remove cash from current assets. On an $8.7 million deal, closer to $10 million with earnouts, a seller's tax accountant netted the line of credit and produced roughly $300,000, while the QoE produced $2.1 million because city contracts paid in six months, $2.5 million sat in AR, and 10% retainage was withheld [g_fy5eeJpHE @ 00:18:16]. They insist monthly P&Ls and monthly adjustments matter more than any other tab, since bonus payouts, PTO, and large vendor payments around the closing date belong in net debt or the peg [g_fy5eeJpHE @ 00:29:14]. Verified Metrics shows the manual override: delete the formula and key in only the partial amount of accrued employee expenses to exclude, then read the three-month average NWC against longer averages [EzOFN-69wBU @ 00:02:41]. Lenders then test whether the peg leaves enough cash at closing and whether adjusted cash flow covers annual debt payments at least 1.25 times [yP7oBq_gKbw @ 00:01:03].

Average around 8 to 9, lowest about 3, highest seen in the mid-20s
Acquira ([g_fy5eeJpHE @ 00:15:31])

Chris Barrett, CPA ([36OTOiIXSrk @ 00:01:31])

callout.title: Moves The Pros Use To Lock The Numbers Down
callout.body: These are the small procedural habits practitioners say separate a defensible QoE from a closing-table fight.
items: After any working capital meeting, send the seller a written email with the number in bold stating exactly how much stays in the business; one seller agreed to $750,000 in a presentation, then insisted two days before closing they were only leaving $150,000 [Acquira — g_fy5eeJpHE @ 00:38:03]

Net every owner compensation add-back against the replacement hire: a $500,000 owner salary with a $350,000 replacement CEO is a $150,000 add-back, not $500,000 [John Colley | The Investment Banking Practitioner — zQE4R-z6Yww @ 00:03:51]
Leave account names in the databook exactly as they appear in the source financials; renaming them breaks the auto-populated outputs [Verified Metrics — EzOFN-69wBU @ 00:01:09]
Insist on a fixed-fee QoE engagement so quick clarifying calls with the provider never generate surprise bills mid-diligence [Chris Barrett, CPA — 36OTOiIXSrk @ 00:02:52]

sop_steps.title: Define The QoE Scope And Budget
sop_steps.action: Agree in writing what the provider means by quality of earnings before work starts, and budget by deal size and complexity.
sop_steps.detail: There is no standard definition: one buyer gets a one-hour tax accountant review, another a $150,000 three-month Big Four report, so clarify scope right after signing the LOI [Acquira — g_fy5eeJpHE @ 00:07:59]; budget $12,000 to $25,000-plus by revenue, enterprise value, and complexity [Chris Barrett, CPA — 36OTOiIXSrk @ 00:01:31].

sop_steps.title: Run Proof Of Cash And The Three-Way Tie
sop_steps.action: Reconcile bank activity to the presented financials and the financials to tax returns before touching adjustments.
sop_steps.detail: Tie revenue net of AR movement and expenses net of AP and capex movement to bank statements [Acquira — g_fy5eeJpHE @ 00:05:30]; confirm bank deposits, P&L, and tax returns tell one story or demand an explanation [QoE and Financial Modeling Practice — SBILxsNgW-o @ 00:00:43].

sop_steps.title: Build And Interrogate The EBITDA Bridge
sop_steps.action: Walk reported to adjusted to normalized EBITDA, challenging every add-back for evidence and recurrence.
sop_steps.detail: Use the three-column framework and reject any one-time cost seen three years running [John Colley | The Investment Banking Practitioner — zQE4R-z6Yww @ 00:04:50]; throw out any add-back lacking an invoice, payroll record, or truly one-time event [QoE and Financial Modeling Practice — yP7oBq_gKbw @ 00:00:23].

sop_steps.title: Set The Debt-Free, Cash-Free Working Capital Peg
sop_steps.action: Strip debt-like items and cash, set the peg from historical monthly data, and size the closing adjustment.
sop_steps.detail: Remove lines of credit, deferred revenue, bank indebtedness, and cash before calculating NWC [Acquira — g_fy5eeJpHE @ 00:18:16]; measure actual NWC at close against the target and reduce price dollar for dollar on any shortfall [Figuring Out with Rahul — xgCInPpZDiQ @ 00:05:05].

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
sections.title: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: There is no agreed product called a quality of earnings, and practitioners split hard on how much of one a buyer should pay for. Acquira's QoE lead says there is no unique and standard definition: they have watched a local tax accountant spend one hour on the books and call it a QoE, while Big Four reports they saw at Deloitte cost $150,000 and took three months [g_fy5eeJpHE @ 00:07:27] [g_fy5eeJpHE @ 00:07:44]. Chris Barrett, CPA prices the small-deal version as a fixed fee: $12,000 to $15,000 for a simple, single-location business under $2.5 million in revenue, roughly $14,000 to $23,000 up to $10 million enterprise value, and $25,000-plus on a custom scope above that [36OTOiIXSrk @ 00:01:31]. Barrett refuses to sell a light option because a skipped step can leave a buyer owning a business they regret [36OTOiIXSrk @ 00:02:23]. Jon Stoddard runs the opposite model from the sell side, building the QoE in-house with ex-PwC, KPMG and Deloitte staff, and calls one buyer's half-million-dollar Big Four QoE on a $3 million deal overkill [Yr06Fv79PU0 @ 00:00:49] [Yr06Fv79PU0 @ 00:07:23]. Steve Roscioli says QoE is more common in larger or complex deals because of the expense, while Acquira insists small deals are where buyers want it most [RXawmeZf9sU @ 00:01:13] [g_fy5eeJpHE @ 00:00:50].

The practitioners also disagree on what kind of animal a QoE is and why the numbers are wrong in the first place. Elliott Holland calls it an audit-like tool you run because sellers lie about EBITDA, and argues that when owners know they are selling at three to five times EBITDA, even the most honorable people will hide things between data sets a buyer has no time to reconcile [KJPGQ94h_GY @ 00:00:00] [KJPGQ94h_GY @ 00:01:09]. Jon Stoddard reads the same gap differently: sellers often get numbers wrong without malice, and even their accountants can be wrong, so having an accountant does not make the numbers accurate [Yr06Fv79PU0 @ 00:01:09]. Edspira lands in between, noting that seller management simply has the incentive to make the company look as good as possible, and compares the QoE to having a mechanic inspect a used car [itIweMi_DyU @ 00:01:46]. On method, Figuring Out with Rahul rejects the audit comparison outright: an audit is the referee checking that past plays followed the rules, while a QoE is the scout reading game tape to forecast future cash flow [xgCInPpZDiQ @ 00:01:22]. Holland's own close is blunt: you cannot overpay for an asset, so the QoE exists to validate the EBITDA the multiple sits on [KJPGQ94h_GY @ 00:01:43].

Even add-backs everyone agrees exist get sized differently depending on who is across the table. John Colley refuses to add back the full owner salary: if the owner takes $500,000 and a replacement CEO costs $350,000, the real add-back is $150,000, and on the Summit case a $900,000 founder add-back shrinks to $500,000 against a $400,000 replacement [zQE4R-z6Yww @ 00:03:51] [zQE4R-z6Yww @ 00:05:30]. Acquira treats post-close costs as negotiation rather than math: a buyer whose insurance rises argues a $1 million EBITDA business is really $900,000, the seller says that is not their problem, and the gap gets bridged with earnout or more forgivable seller note instead of a straight cut [g_fy5eeJpHE @ 00:26:42] [g_fy5eeJpHE @ 00:27:34]. Only flat-out errors, like a $400,000 add-back that never belonged, get pushed as a full purchase-price adjustment [g_fy5eeJpHE @ 00:26:01]. CandiMentor splits the audience: a buyer cares about sustainable earnings and future value, while a lender focuses on cash conversion, downside protection and repayment under pressure [QVDTq7Qd6-A @ 00:05:47]. QoE and Financial Modeling Practice shows what that lens means in practice: an add-back without an invoice, payroll record or clear one-time event is usually thrown out, and most lenders want debt service coverage of at least 1.25 times [SBILxsNgW-o @ 00:00:22] [SBILxsNgW-o @ 00:01:02].

Buyer hires a fixed-fee CPA: $12,000 to $15,000 small, $25,000-plus above $10 million
Sell-side broker builds it in-house; half-million Big Four QoE on $3 million deal called overkill
Chris Barrett, CPA ([36OTOiIXSrk @ 00:01:31]) vs Jon Stoddard ([Yr06Fv79PU0 @ 00:07:23])
Whether a QoE is basically an audit
Audit-like outsourced accounting tool that validates the EBITDA the multiple gets applied to
Scout reading game tape to forecast future cash flow, not a referee checking rules
Elliott Holland ([KJPGQ94h_GY @ 00:01:28]) vs Figuring Out with Rahul ([xgCInPpZDiQ @ 00:01:22])
Why the seller's EBITDA comes in wrong
Sellers lie about EBITDA; even honorable people hide things between data sets
Often not malicious; sellers and even their accountants simply get the numbers wrong
Elliott Holland ([KJPGQ94h_GY @ 00:01:09]) vs Jon Stoddard ([Yr06Fv79PU0 @ 00:01:09])
Whose lens decides which adjustments survive
Buyer prices sustainable earnings and future value creation off adjusted EBITDA
Lender throws out undocumented add-backs and wants debt service coverage of at least 1.25 times
CandiMentor ([QVDTq7Qd6-A @ 00:05:47]) vs QoE and Financial Modeling Practice ([SBILxsNgW-o @ 00:01:02])
How to close the gap after EBITDA drops
Flat-out seller error like a $400,000 bogus add-back becomes a full price cut
Gray-area costs like higher insurance get bridged with earnout or forgivable seller note
Acquira ([g_fy5eeJpHE @ 00:26:01]); Acquira ([g_fy5eeJpHE @ 00:27:34])
Buy-side versus sell-side diligence posture
Buy side acts as professional skeptic actively hunting for reasons to pay less
Seller runs the same playbook first; an existing sell-side QoE makes buyer pushback harder
Corporate Finance Institute ([FvywvHEpXKU @ 00:06:34]) vs Acquira ([g_fy5eeJpHE @ 00:43:14])
Choosing targets to reduce QoE error risk
Recurring Shopify, WooCommerce or SaaS revenue tied to third-party platforms reads cleanest
Never buy a poor-fit business just to cut error risk; let QoE experts handle complexity
Acquira ([g_fy5eeJpHE @ 00:44:42]); Acquira ([g_fy5eeJpHE @ 00:44:56])

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
sections.title: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive failures come from add-backs and revenue that collapse under the first real tie-out. Acquira's team watched an e-commerce seller book a $125,000 purchase order as revenue and receivable before invoicing; on a deal with about $425,000 of EBITDA the error ran over 20 percent, and the deal died on the spot [g_fy5eeJpHE @ 00:33:13] [g_fy5eeJpHE @ 00:33:42]. On a $3.2 million EBITDA deal in November 2025, the seller added back roughly $500,000 of family payroll that the tax accountant had already reclassified to distributions at year end, double counting it; the deal went into renegotiation with trust and months lost [g_fy5eeJpHE @ 00:34:53]. Construction is the repeat offender: the team estimates about 75 percent of work-in-progress businesses record WIP wrong, and revenue recognition is a main reason EBITDA comes back 10, 20 or 30 percent lower [g_fy5eeJpHE @ 00:03:44] [g_fy5eeJpHE @ 00:13:36]. John Colley's Summit case shows the subtler version: a $600,000 'one-time' consulting fee in its third consecutive year, plus a missed $350,000 hit from a warehouse leased from the founder's family trust at 30 percent below market, help shrink $18.5 million reported EBITDA to $16.2 million [zQE4R-z6Yww @ 00:05:50] [zQE4R-z6Yww @ 00:06:13]. CandiMentor's rule: a 'one-time' cost that shows up every year is normal operations [QVDTq7Qd6-A @ 00:06:06].

Working capital is where deals die late. Acquira ranks the net working capital peg among the top two or three deal killers and has lived it: a seller's tax accountant netted a line of credit against current assets and got roughly $300,000, while a debt-free, cash-free calculation that stripped lines of credit, deferred revenue and cash produced $2.1 million on an $8.7 million deal [g_fy5eeJpHE @ 00:17:41]. Another seller refused to leave any working capital when the buyer needed about $550,000, and the deal died; a third agreed to a $750,000 peg in a presentation, then said two days before closing they had only ever meant $150,000 [g_fy5eeJpHE @ 00:35:55] [g_fy5eeJpHE @ 00:37:01]. The fix now is a bolded follow-up email spelling out what stays in the business [g_fy5eeJpHE @ 00:37:48]. Figuring Out with Rahul describes the protection: set an NWC target from history, measure the actual figure at close, and cut the price dollar for dollar on any shortfall [xgCInPpZDiQ @ 00:05:05]. Miss the peg and the buyer funds payroll and operations out of pocket after close [g_fy5eeJpHE @ 00:20:43]. Verified Metrics adds the timing check: a company running consistently negative working capital, with a recent three-month average worse than longer-term averages, may be leaning on short-term financing to fund operations [EzOFN-69wBU @ 00:03:47] [EzOFN-69wBU @ 00:04:03].

Acquira says roughly half of its 50-plus QoEs last year came back clean, 20 to 25 percent surfaced deal-killing mistakes, and the rest needed retrades or creative repricing; a small deal averages eight or nine EBITDA adjustments, from a low of three to the mid-twenties [g_fy5eeJpHE @ 00:27:49] [g_fy5eeJpHE @ 00:15:31]. Proof of cash is the first screen: Acquira finds it ties about 85 percent of the time, and the businesses that miss are ones to run from [g_fy5eeJpHE @ 00:06:00]. The XPX panel agrees inventory always ends up on the list and funky revenue accounting always brings a cutoff problem; one sell-side software client still carried material revenue adjustments after two separate recognition studies [gRV7segOzzo @ 00:00:21] [gRV7segOzzo @ 00:01:25]. At scale the same miss is catastrophic: Corporate Finance Institute recounts HP paying $11 billion for Autonomy, missing channel stuffing and invented sales, and writing down $8.8 billion, while Microsoft's Nokia deal ended in a $7.6 billion write-off after diligence validated the past but not the market shift [FvywvHEpXKU @ 00:09:06] [FvywvHEpXKU @ 00:10:23]. Lenders have their own tripwires: QoE and Financial Modeling Practice lists unexplained deposits, shrinking margins, personal expenses in the books, and numbers that change every version as the signals that make a lender run for the woods [yP7oBq_gKbw @ 00:01:23].

callout.title: OPERATOR GATE: Clear These Four Traps Before Closing
callout.body: Each check below comes from a deal that died, repriced or nearly blew up at the closing table.
items: Run proof of cash first: tie bank deposits and disbursements to the P&L and the P&L to tax returns; businesses where cash does not match are ones to run from [Acquira — g_fy5eeJpHE @ 00:06:16].

Put the working capital peg and what it means in a bolded written email to the seller well before closing week; a verbal yes on $750,000 turned into $150,000 two days out [Acquira — g_fy5eeJpHE @ 00:37:48].

Strike every add-back that lacks an invoice, payroll record or truly one-time event; the lender tosses it overboard anyway, boat included [QoE and Financial Modeling Practice — yP7oBq_gKbw @ 00:00:23].
Reclassify any non-recurring cost that has appeared three years running as recurring before it reaches the multiple [John Colley | The Investment Banking Practitioner — zQE4R-z6Yww @ 00:03:34].

chapters.pull_quote: "The quality of earnings report isn't an accounting document. It's a pricing document. Every adjustment you accept or challenge directly moves the purchase price." — John Colley | The Investment Banking Practitioner (zQE4R-z6Yww @ 00:06:50).
action_checklist: Before signing the engagement, confirm in writing exactly what the provider's quality of earnings covers, since a one-hour tax-accountant review and a three-month $150,000 Big Four report share the same name [Acquira — g_fy5eeJpHE @ 00:07:44].

Budget the QoE as a fixed fee by size: $12,000 to $15,000 under $2.5 million revenue, about $14,000 to $23,000 up to $10 million enterprise value, and $25,000-plus above that [Chris Barrett, CPA — 36OTOiIXSrk @ 00:01:31].

Build the EBITDA bridge in three columns, reported, adjusted for genuinely non-recurring items, and normalized, then price off the third column [John Colley | The Investment Banking Practitioner — zQE4R-z6Yww @ 00:04:31].

Pull monthly P&Ls and monthly adjustments, then hunt for bonuses, PTO payouts and large vendor payments landing right after close and push them into net debt or the peg [Acquira — g_fy5eeJpHE @ 00:29:42].
Calculate working capital debt-free and cash-free by stripping lines of credit, deferred revenue, bank indebtedness and cash before agreeing to any peg [Acquira — g_fy5eeJpHE @ 00:18:16].
Run the lender's math on the surviving numbers: adjusted cash flow divided by annual debt payments must clear at least 1.25 times [QoE and Financial Modeling Practice — yP7oBq_gKbw @ 00:01:03].

chapters.question_prompt: Which EBITDA and SDE add-backs hold up, and how is net working capital defined and calculated for a deal?
chapters.title: Add-Backs, Cash Flow, and Calculating Net Working Capital
chapters.subtitle: Qualifying vs. rejected EBITDA add-backs, common SDE add-backs, the three-question add-back test, QoE adjustments, why 'EBITDA is an opinion, cash flow is a fact', defining working capital for the peg, calculating NWC, financial-diligence working capital analysis, the indirect-method sign logic, and common working-capital issues
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners from growthink, The Finance Lab, Transact Capital, A Simple Model and John Colley converge on one operating truth: adjusted EBITDA sets the price, but working capital and cash conversion decide what the buyer actually gets. growthink shows $250,000 of accepted add-backs worth about $1.5 million at six times, with the burden of proof on the seller. The Finance Lab's three-question test caps credible add-backs near 15 to 20 percent of reported EBITDA and sizes owner pay against a replacement salary. Transact Capital adjusts $1.8 million of reported working capital to $1.85 million, sets a $1.6 million twelve-month target, and books a $143,000 closing excess. Colley's bridge turns $20.7 million of EBITDA into $8.1 million of free cash flow. Fault lines run through owner-salary add-backs, debt-like liabilities, deferred revenue and lookback periods.

sections.heading: Section 1: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: Every practitioner on this beat treats adjusted EBITDA as the number that actually gets priced, so every add-back is real money. Jeff Jones of growthink frames it in dollars: at six times trailing-twelve-month EBITDA in an LOI, $250,000 of accepted add-backs equals roughly $1.5 million of enterprise value, which is why sellers fight for full credit and buyers stay skeptical [UfQ-Ho_j61s @ 00:03:52]. Elliott Holland walks the same chain from the buyer's chair: start with EBITDA as reported, review every adjustment for things the owner ran through the business that a new owner will not pay for, then land on the final adjusted EBITDA you will be paying a multiple of [XDVFloSBuko @ 00:00:18]. The Finance Lab calls the adjusted EBITDA schedule the place where deals are made and lost and where sellers are most creative, with every line an argument that a cost did not really happen, will not recur, or leaves with the owner [hIU9zSg4cQg @ 00:00:00]. The shared rule underneath: the burden of proof sits with the seller, and adjustments do not fly without clear, consistent documentation tracked over time, because buyers come in naturally skeptical and a trend backed by records is what gets everyone comfortable [UfQ-Ho_j61s @ 00:09:04].

The categories line up across shops. growthink's Antonio lists the standard accepted buckets: one-time items such as legal settlements, advisory fees tied to an initiative, plant relocation and transaction financing costs; owner discretionary spend where family expenses flow through the company for tax mitigation; owner compensation only to the extent it runs above market rate; related-party rent normalized plus or minus to market; and, on services deals, equity taken as compensation [UfQ-Ho_j61s @ 00:10:45]. Edspira sorts quality of earnings work into three groups: non-recurring or non-operational adjustments like asset impairments, disposal gains or losses, lease termination fees and severance; pro forma adjustments that push recent rent, salary or raw-material increases into historical EBITDA; and accounting adjustments that convert cash-basis books to accrual or reverse improperly capitalized expenses and misrecognized revenue [j5A0VGOV88E @ 00:00:14]. ProjectionHub's Adam runs four buckets in its free SDE calculator template: owner compensation, personal expenses such as a $10,000-a-year personal vehicle billed through the business, non-cash depreciation and amortization, and one-time costs like a $25,000 move [OiLlMiZv9ZQ @ 00:01:47]. Kirk Michie adds the direction check most owners miss: owner economics such as self-owned buildings rented below or above market and blended personal trips must be recalibrated, and a few of those adjustments push EBITDA down, not up [BHyx6-mgFe8 @ 00:00:55].

On the balance sheet side, the consensus is that deals close cash-free and debt-free with a normalized level of working capital left behind. Ross Harris of Transact Capital says that is how 90 to 95 percent of deals work: the seller keeps the cash, pays off debts two or three days before closing, and leaves the buyer a fair level of working capital, and the seller does not get to choose how much gas the car needs because a process sets it [YAk3dxgnsBU @ 00:00:31]. Kirk Michie reduces deal-math working capital to accounts receivable plus inventory minus accounts payable, including taxes payable in a pass-through LLC or S corp, and warns the peg draws lots and lots of post-purchase disputes [QqemANnN2ZM @ 00:00:43]. Morse frames the buyer's motive as refusing to buy a business with the cupboards bare, with buyer and seller negotiating a target equal to the cash and working capital needed for a month or two of operations so the buyer does not have to inject cash after closing [0V-By_uyuhM @ 00:00:20]. A Simple Model draws the line between accounting and deal definitions: cash is excluded, not every current account is included, and accrued taxes, litigation accounts, lines of credit, notes payable and current debt are common carve-outs [DbHq5BHo_XA @ 00:01:16].

sections.heading: Section 2: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Add-back vetting runs on a three-question test from The Finance Lab: was it truly non-recurring, would a new owner actually save it, and is the amount reasonable. On the first question, ask for the invoice behind any legal add-back, because one litigation settlement passes while a pattern of recurring disputes fails; on the second, a seller paying themselves $900,000 against a $350,000 replacement CEO supports a $550,000 add-back only if you will really hire at that salary and the owner was doing one person's job [hIU9zSg4cQg @ 00:00:38]. The reasonableness bar is hard: add-backs above 15 to 20 percent of reported EBITDA are a structural warning, and $1.5 million of add-backs on $5 million of EBITDA means the books need a full forensic review [hIU9zSg4cQg @ 00:00:59]. ProjectionHub runs the same math smaller: a $100,000 owner salary against a $75,000 replacement hire nets a $25,000 add-back, settled by negotiation [OiLlMiZv9ZQ @ 00:02:09]. Elliott Holland measures total adjustments as a percentage of adjusted EBITDA on a trailing-twelve-month basis, then strips out the seller's salary: two-thirds looks large, but once the $1 million salary is pulled, the remaining $300,000 is not significant against $1.8 million [XDVFloSBuko @ 00:00:36]. The Finance Lab's closing instruction is to rebuild the adjusted EBITDA schedule from scratch, treating the seller's version as a starting point, never a conclusion.

Transact Capital's working capital build is the cleanest worked example. Run the internal balance sheet: $7.5 million of current assets minus $5.7 million of current liabilities gives $1.8 million of reported working capital; zero out cash and the line of credit and definitional working capital drops to $1.3 million [YAk3dxgnsBU @ 00:04:04]. Then strip tax items and debt-like liabilities: the deferred tax asset generally always goes, credit card payables are almost always debt-like unless the card replaces the payables account, commissions payable go debt-like about 80 percent of the time, and vacation PTO is a 50-50 fight, landing adjusted working capital at $1.85 million. Run that same formula monthly; the six-month average is $1.575 million and the twelve-month average $1.607 million, and the twelve-month average is most common for stable businesses [YAk3dxgnsBU @ 00:09:42]. A Simple Model shows a balance-level carve-out: excluding receivables aged over 90 days cuts $10 million of AR to $8.3 million because the buyer should not pay for cash it may never collect [DbHq5BHo_XA @ 00:02:38]. CandiMentor's distributor case nets $18 million receivables plus $12 million inventory minus $14 million payables and $4 million accruals to a $12 million target; a $14.4 million closing balance hands the seller a potential $2.4 million adjustment [siH_wi11PX8 @ 00:04:31].

The true-up follows a fixed sequence. A Simple Model lays it out: agree a target, close with part of the price parked in a working capital escrow, give the buyer 60 to 120 days to deliver a closing statement, then give the seller roughly 30 days to object in writing with reasonable detail; signing the working capital calculation agreement releases escrow, with excess paid to the seller and shortfall released to the buyer [C-seCQXqtM4 @ 00:01:47]. MCM Capital says the items that most often drive the adjustment start with accruals, such as earned-but-unpaid bonuses when closing near year-end, and inventory, which MCM always suggests settling with a physical count at close, especially in manufacturing [almKwAlo5T4 @ 00:00:34]. John Colley then bridges adjusted earnings to cash: Summit's $20.7 million of normalized EBITDA loses $6.2 million to maintenance CapEx, $1.8 million to working capital, $2.8 million to cash taxes, $1.2 million to interest and $0.6 million to other items, leaving $8.1 million of free cash flow, a 39 percent conversion against a healthy 60 to 80 percent for industrials [ha9dRzcYak4 @ 00:06:43]. Colley's punchline: the $180 million headline at 8.7 times normalized EBITDA is really 22 times free cash flow, so debt paydown will be slow.

callout.title: How the pros protect add-back credit and the working capital number
callout.body: These are the moves practitioners use to keep add-backs from getting haircut in quality of earnings and to keep the working capital peg from turning into a post-close fight.

Build your own adjusted EBITDA schedule from scratch and use the seller's schedule only as a starting point, never a conclusion [The Finance Lab — hIU9zSg4cQg @ 00:01:19]

sections.heading: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split on add-backs is where the alarm bell should ring. The Finance Lab draws a hard line: add-backs above 15 to 20% of reported EBITDA are a structural warning signal, and a business reporting $5 million of EBITDA with $1.5 million in add-backs is telling you the financials sit so far from economic reality that nothing can be relied on without a full forensic review [hIU9zSg4cQg @ 00:00:59]. growthink's Antonio runs a far looser tolerance, saying add-backs at 30%, 40%, 50% or more of adjusted EBITDA do not mean automatic rejection, only that the buyer leans in harder and starts asking whether those numbers will hold through quality of earnings or whether the offer is wasted diligence money [UfQ-Ho_j61s @ 00:22:00]. Elliott Holland splits the difference by decomposing the ratio instead of reacting to it: adjustments running two-thirds of adjusted EBITDA look ugly until you pull out the $1 million seller salary, at which point the remaining $300,000 is not significant against $1.8 million [XDVFloSBuko @ 00:00:58]. The operator playbook that falls out of this is simple: screen the headline ratio Finance Lab-style, strip owner compensation the Holland way, then test whatever remains before deciding whether the deal deserves forensic money or a polite pass.

Owner compensation is the add-back everyone fights over, and practitioners price it in at least three different ways. ProjectionHub warns that sellers routinely add back the full salary, say $100,000, when the buyer must hire a $75,000 replacement to do the same job, so only $25,000 belongs in SDE, and even that figure is a negotiation between buyer and seller [OiLlMiZv9ZQ @ 00:02:26]. The Finance Lab runs identical math at middle-market scale, $900,000 of owner pay against a $350,000 replacement CEO for a $550,000 add-back, but attaches two conditions: the buyer must actually plan to hire at that salary, and the owner must genuinely have been doing the work of one person [hIU9zSg4cQg @ 00:00:38]. growthink goes further in multi-owner shops, carving out compensation entirely when a retiring owner will not be replaced post-close, while flagging that owner pay is not an add-back per se, only the above-market slice is [UfQ-Ho_j61s @ 00:12:11]. Edspira pushes the opposite direction, insisting pro forma adjustments also cut EBITDA when rent, salaries, or raw materials have recently risen, because historical statements are backward looking [j5A0VGOV88E @ 00:00:49]. Sellers chasing the full-salary add-back should expect buyers armed with the replacement-cost test, and buyers should expect sellers to argue redundancy.

On net working capital, the definitional fights are where practitioners openly contradict each other, and taxes are the cleanest example. Kirk Michie's deal-math formula is receivables plus inventory minus payables, explicitly including taxes payable in a pass-through LLC or S corp [QqemANnN2ZM @ 00:00:43]. Transact Capital's Ross Harris takes the opposite line: anything tax related is the seller's responsibility, is not assumed by the buyer at closing, and gets removed from the calculation [YAk3dxgnsBU @ 00:04:35]. Break Into Finance refuses both absolutes, arguing that regular current tax obligations cycling in and out can be argued as working capital, while a large unpaid income tax liability is probably a net debt item, and the outcome depends on how the negotiation goes [S31vo0Umk5M @ 00:38:12]. Deferred revenue splits the room the same way. MCM Capital frames customer prepayments as a loan from your customer, more often than not treated as debt rather than working capital, yet admits they have seen it go both ways in the final contract definitions [almKwAlo5T4 @ 00:02:08]. The operator read is blunt: each of these lines is a direct price lever on both sides of the table, and whoever writes the inclusion schedule controls the size of the closing check.

sections.heading: Firsthand Failure Modes, Traps & Economics Checks
paragraphs: The most expensive add-back failure is the last-mile retrade. growthink reports that the majority of the time, once the quality of earnings report lands with the buyer, there is pushback and an attempted haircut to add-backs or EBITDA, and that is exactly when deals blow up [UfQ-Ho_j61s @ 00:18:34]. The trap usually starts with categories sellers assume are one-time. In one growthink case, bad debts appeared on the P&L every single year, which already proved they were not non-recurring and would struggle to survive as add-backs [UfQ-Ho_j61s @ 00:33:07]. The Finance Lab applies the same logic to legal fees: one litigation settlement is legitimate, a pattern of recurring legal disputes is not, and the buyer should demand to see the invoice before crediting a dollar [hIU9zSg4cQg @ 00:00:20]. The economics are brutal in both directions. At six times trailing EBITDA, $250,000 of accepted adjustments is worth $1.5 million of enterprise value if the seller gets full credit [UfQ-Ho_j61s @ 00:03:52]. That multiplier cuts both ways: every line a buyer strikes during diligence comes off the price at six times its face value, so a seller defending a weak add-back is defending value that was never really there.

Working capital is where signed deals go to die after the handshake. Kirk Michie says nondisclosure agreements almost never trigger lawsuits, but net working capital pegs and formulas generate lots and lots of post-purchase disputes, and the letter of intent is a ceiling that only gets worse afterward [QqemANnN2ZM @ 00:03:07]. Transact Capital's Ross Harris has watched deals die over working capital when sellers did not understand the process, with closings turning contentious and deal threatening [YAk3dxgnsBU @ 00:12:43]. The post-close clock is unforgiving. A Simple Model lays out the timeline: the buyer gets 60 to 120 days to deliver a closing statement, the seller gets roughly 30 days to review it, and any disagreement must be delivered in writing with reasonable detail before that window expires, while escrowed funds stay frozen until both sides sign [C-seCQXqtM4 @ 00:02:18]. Break Into Finance flags the gaming risk built into the mechanism itself: a seller who understands cyclicality can let the peg get set off a trough month and then close in a known peak month like January to harvest a big purchase price uplift [S31vo0Umk5M @ 00:24:20]. Sellers who sleep through the review window and buyers who accept a trough-based peg both eat the loss.

The final economics check is whether the cash actually shows up. John Colley has seen companies report $20 million of EBITDA yet generate only $8 million of free cash flow, with $12 million vanishing into working capital, maintenance CapEx, and customer deposits that never materialized [ha9dRzcYak4 @ 00:00:25]. His Summit Services walkthrough turns $20.7 million of normalized EBITDA into $8.1 million of free cash flow, a 39% conversion ratio against the 60 to 80% a healthy industrial services business should post, and he calls that result poor without hedging [ha9dRzcYak4 @ 00:06:43]. Day one is its own trap. Break Into Finance walks through a target with two cash outflows in the first week, a payroll run and a supplier run, before the first customer collection lands, and advises PE buyers without a treasury function to make the vendor leave enough cash or stand up a revolver immediately [S31vo0Umk5M @ 00:57:05]. MCM Capital adds the inventory landmine: they always push for a physical inventory at close, especially for manufacturers, because gaps between the books and the warehouse that were never trued up surface right when the adjustment gets calculated [almKwAlo5T4 @ 00:00:34]. Every one of these gaps is cash somebody funds after closing.

callout.title: Four Kill Switches Before You Sign
callout.body: Each gate comes straight from a loss, dispute, or retrade the practitioners watched happen. Clear all four before the purchase agreement locks the numbers.
items: Do not agree to a net working capital peg in the letter of intent until you understand exactly what the formula means, because the LOI is a ceiling that only gets worse [Kirk Michie — QqemANnN2ZM @ 00:03:07].

Strike any add-back that fails the three-question test: truly non-recurring, actually saved by a new owner, and reasonable in size, and demand the invoice behind every legal fee [The Finance Lab — hIU9zSg4cQg @ 00:00:20].

Build the EBITDA-to-free-cash-flow bridge and, if conversion lands below 60%, find exactly where the cash is going and whether that is fixable [John Colley | The Investment Banking Practitioner — ha9dRzcYak4 @ 00:08:30].
Map day-one cash obligations against collection dates and make the vendor leave enough cash or put a revolver or overdraft in place immediately [Break Into Finance — S31vo0Umk5M @ 00:57:05].

chapters.pull_quote: EBITDA is an opinion. Cash flow is a fact. If you're pricing a deal on EBITDA, but the cash isn't there, you're buying a mirage. — John Colley | The Investment Banking Practitioner (ha9dRzcYak4 @ 00:00:01).
action_checklist: Rebuild the adjusted EBITDA schedule from scratch, using the seller's schedule as a starting point rather than a conclusion, and run every line through the three-question test [The Finance Lab — hIU9zSg4cQg @ 00:01:37].

Track add-backs monthly inside the operating model and run personal pass-through expenses on one credit card so every item is clean, tracked, and evidenced at transaction time [growthink — UfQ-Ho_j61s @ 00:14:50].

Rerun the adjusted net working capital calculation for each historical month and set the target off the 12-month average, the most common choice for stable businesses [Transact Capital — YAk3dxgnsBU @ 00:09:42].
Negotiate exclusions for receivables aged 90 days or more and obsolete inventory so the peg only pays for balances that will actually convert to cash [A Simple Model — DbHq5BHo_XA @ 00:02:07].
Take a physical inventory at close, especially in manufacturing, and reconcile book-to-warehouse differences well before the adjustment mechanism is triggered [MCM Capital — almKwAlo5T4 @ 00:00:34].

Separate maintenance CapEx from growth CapEx by asking what breaks within 12 months if all CapEx stops, and request a three-year breakdown by asset category [John Colley | The Investment Banking Practitioner — ha9dRzcYak4 @ 00:03:38].

chapters.question_prompt: How do working capital pegs and true-ups change the price paid at closing, and how are those and other key terms negotiated in the LOI?
chapters.title: Closing Price Mechanics and LOI Negotiation
chapters.subtitle: Working capital adjustments in asset sales, targets and true-up calculations, WC adjustments vs. the locked-box approach, negotiating NWC in lower-middle-market deals, how sellers capture value through the peg, buyer's cash vs. seller's cash, plus negotiating LOI terms such as exclusivity, shifting leverage, and seller-side lessons
chapters.executive_summary: Practitioners from David C Barnett to John Colley converge on one hard truth: the headline price is not the check at closing. Deals are priced cash-free/debt-free with a normal working capital peg, and every dollar delivered short of that peg comes off the seller's proceeds dollar for dollar, trued up 60 to 90 days post-close against escrow or seller notes. Street numbers: Anchor Partners' Westbrook owner lost a net $100K by pushing collections and stretching suppliers against a $900K peg; Colley's Summit case swung $900K on seasonal timing. On the LOI side, exclusivity is the seller's last real leverage, typically 30 to 120 days. The fights: whether the peg belongs in the LOI or after diligence, whether historical averages or zero is the right opening anchor, and closing-accounts true-ups versus locked box.

sections.heading: The Practitioner Consensus
paragraphs: The headline number on the LOI is not the wire that hits the seller's account. Anchor Partners puts it bluntly: deliver less working capital than the peg, 'and the price comes down by exactly that amount,' and the damage usually happens in the last 30 days before close [ob7Q-yxAsNs @ 00:01:06]. RareBrain hammers the same trap from the seller's chair: a 'cash free debt free' purchase agreement still generally requires the owner to leave a normal amount of working capital in the business, so cash splits into buyer's cash and seller's cash, and an under-capitalized company lets the owner take nothing off the table [fPwi8HVhX3Q @ 00:00:44]. Mergers & Inquisitions frames the buyer's logic: in cash-free/debt-free private deals the adjustment keeps the buyer's effective price constant while the seller's proceeds float, which incentivizes the owner to run the business normally instead of delaying bills or under-ordering inventory [oa8dUICluLM @ 00:00:28]. FinanceKid writes it straight into the LOI template, pricing the deal cash-free/debt-free with normal working capital, and notes working capital can be priced separately with lower goodwill [JSIfjvnhOco @ 00:25:22]. Every one of these operators treats the peg as a second price negotiation running alongside the multiple, not an accounting footnote to clean up later.

What goes into the peg is itself a negotiation. Brett Cenkus starts from the textbook, current assets minus current liabilities, then warns the definition is negotiated, and in practice it often collapses to receivables minus payables because cash usually does not transfer [lPy47SFZqDw @ 00:00:17]. John Colley gives the cleanest definition sheet: strip out cash, debt and tax items, keep receivables, inventory, prepaids, payables, accruals and deferred revenue, and recognize that working capital causes more post-closing disputes than any other mechanism in the deal [x_72u8PgHpc @ 00:02:55]. FinanceKid adds the edge cases: exclude related-party accounts and corporate income tax, but keep GST/HST inside the formula [8AOvKeCdAH0 @ 00:06:20]. David C Barnett takes the same logic down to Main Street, where sellers keep cash and receivables, inventory transfers, and the seller retains payables, credit cards and the personally guaranteed loan, so the buyer walks away with $2,500 of $2,800 in assets and no liabilities. Barnett's core warning is that the reported balance sheet reflects the owner's whims, desires and fears, and 'what's missing here is normalization' [gFJZwK-3sq0 @ 00:14:36]. The shared baseline: agree the line items before anyone argues about the number, because the number follows the definition.

On the LOI itself, the consensus is that exclusivity is the one real chip the seller hands over, and it transfers leverage the moment the document is signed. A Simple Model shows the power curve flipping at execution because the LOI lets the buyer secure an exclusivity period that bars talks with other groups [mADDz83tbN0 @ 00:00:14]. Jeff Brooker at McGuireWoods works the sell side on that premise, holding the buyer's feet to the fire on every term that matters because once exclusivity is granted the seller has lost leverage, and Greg Hawver agrees seller power peaks before signing; only exclusivity, confidentiality and expenses are binding, and punting an issue usually favors the buyer [OzPzqbUSgPw @ 00:02:51]. PCE Investment Bankers lists the non-binding economics, price, structure, earnout or seller note, contingencies, diligence and working capital, against binding exclusivity, confidentiality and governing law [YJMOV57uFMk @ 00:01:40]. MySaasForSale reduces it to one line for small software sellers: exclusivity is the one thing a seller gives up at this stage, so its length matters, with 30 days common and an end date in writing [OOlka50xFck @ 00:01:41]. The operating rule across all four: negotiate hard before signing, because afterward the seller is bargaining from inside a locked room.

sections.heading: Exact Street Mechanics, Tools & Numbers
paragraphs: Setting the peg is arithmetic on monthly data, not a glance at year-end. Anchor Partners builds net working capital as receivables plus inventory minus payables minus accruals and pegs it at the trailing-12-month average; on Westbrook that ran $1.6M plus $150K minus $700K minus $150K for a $900K peg [ob7Q-yxAsNs @ 00:00:48]. John Colley's rule is 'use trailing 12 months, never a single month' [x_72u8PgHpc @ 00:07:31]. FinanceKid goes deeper: pull 24 to 36 months of monthly statements and track net working capital as a percentage of TTM revenue, which typically lands at 5 to 6% and can run up to 15 to 20% [8AOvKeCdAH0 @ 00:28:44]. For a declining business FinanceKid weights the last 6 to 12 months; in the worked example the ratio sat at 17.6% against 5.8%, and the target landed at 10 to 11%. For a flat business, unexplained low months get excluded, moving the range to 14 to 16% versus 12 to 14%, and one sample month computes as $900K minus $159K for $740K against a $701K average [8AOvKeCdAH0 @ 00:32:15]. Normalizations show up in 2 to 3 of every 10 deals, so the monthly build is where the real money is argued.

The true-up is a two-step cash event: an estimate at close, then a recalculation 60 to 90 days later. Brett Cenkus runs the surplus case: a $5M price, a $500K target and a $600K seller estimate means the buyer pays $100K extra at closing, then recalculates post-close with every incentive to push the figure down; GAAP is not perfect science, so 'there's a lot of litigation around that' [ydfu0lpiDjc @ 00:03:34]. FinanceKid shows the deficit side: a $100K shortfall comes back out of a $200K escrow holdback, or gets cut from the vendor take-back note or earn-out [8AOvKeCdAH0 @ 00:08:56]. ProjectionHub flags the closing-week drift buyers forget: payroll due two days after close, a $40,000 customer check landing the morning of closing, an undisclosed $2,000 payable the seller must reimburse, and both sides escrowing money, $50,000 each in their example, with a lawyer and CPA defining the cutoff [BvJfOb1y6x8 @ 00:04:05]. RareBrain's nasty-surprise case is $1M of inventory found half obsolete at the post-close count, producing a $500K shortfall, a seller paid $500K less, and a buyer claim against a $1M escrow [fPwi8HVhX3Q @ 00:01:58]. Escrow, holdback or note offset is the enforcement tool in every version.

On Main Street deals, David C Barnett shows how normalization rewrites the price. His sample balance sheet carries $2,000 of inventory, $500 of payables and a $300 credit card; normalized, inventory drops to $1,500 for old stock and ordering inefficiency, payables rise to $750 because bills were being paid early, and the credit card falls to $100 because the owner ran charges for airline points [gFJZwK-3sq0 @ 00:15:48]. Barnett then adds a $750 inventory and receivables line of credit, supportable because the inventory is fungible, leaving normalized working capital of $200, so a $2,000 price becomes $1,800 and the buyer lines up the credit line [gFJZwK-3sq0 @ 00:18:45]. Mergers & Inquisitions runs the leveraged-buyout version: a 12x multiple on $50 of EBITDA gives a 600 headline, a 50 deficit against a 100 target cuts enterprise value to 550 plus 50 of working capital funding, so the buyer's effective price stays 600, while a surplus pushes EV to 650 and seller equity from 500 to 600 [oa8dUICluLM @ 00:02:03]. John Colley draws the contrast that sets negotiating priorities: an EBITDA dollar moves through the multiple, $1 times 10 equals $10, while working capital moves dollar for dollar [x_72u8PgHpc @ 00:06:53].

callout.title: Where the Money Moves Before and After Signing
callout.body: Four levers practitioners pull to shift closing dollars without touching the headline multiple, starting from the rule that every dollar less of working capital is a dollar in the seller's pocket [Brett Cenkus — lPy47SFZqDw @ 00:02:52].
items: Open the peg at zero: Brett Cenkus argues a profitable business needs zero working capital, answers PE diligence teams with 'who cares what it's been historically,' and falls back to forward-looking need, or historical only if historical is low [Brett Cenkus — lPy47SFZqDw @ 00:03:08].

Shrink the peg a year out: at $33K per day of billing, collecting one week faster takes $230K off the peg, so shorten the cash cycle a year before the LOI and track working capital monthly, because you cannot negotiate a number you only see once a year [Anchor Partners — ob7Q-yxAsNs @ 00:02:49].

Trade, never concede: a lower price buys more paid at closing or shorter support, an earn-out buys a higher total plus read-only access to the numbers, longer exclusivity buys a faster diligence list or an escrow deposit, and longer support buys paid hours [MySaasForSale — OOlka50xFck @ 00:03:06].

Manufacture competition before signing: a seller with one real bidder flew to the buyer-universe cities listed in the CIM, let calls go to voicemail, called back from hotel phones, and answered 'some last minute work nothing big'; the buyer matched area codes, raised the price and rushed the LOI [A Simple Model — mADDz83tbN0 @ 00:01:11].

sop_steps.title: Build the monthly working capital history
sop_steps.action: Pull 24 to 36 months of monthly statements and chart NWC as a percentage of TTM revenue.
sop_steps.detail: FinanceKid benchmarks NWC at 5 to 6% of TTM revenue and up to 15 to 20%, weights the last 6 to 12 months for declining businesses, and excludes unexplained low months for flat ones [FinanceKid — 8AOvKeCdAH0 @ 00:25:15].

sop_steps.title: Normalize and strip distortions
sop_steps.action: Remove seasonal peaks, one-time receivables, accelerated collections and owner quirks.
sop_steps.detail: Colley excluded August and September, a $400K insurance receivable and $600K of accelerated collections to land $8.3M against the seller's $9.2M [John Colley | The Investment Banking Practitioner — x_72u8PgHpc @ 00:06:16]; Barnett normalizes inventory, early-paid payables and points-driven card balances [David C Barnett Small Business and Deal Making SMB — gFJZwK-3sq0 @ 00:15:48].

sop_steps.title: Paper the structure into the LOI
sop_steps.action: Front-load share vs. asset structure, payment forms, exclusivity end date and personal sticking points.
sop_steps.detail: The Built to Sell guest's attorney had them settle title, comp, earn-outs and legal-fee reimbursement in the LOI because parties a thousand feet apart blow up at the finish line [Built to Sell — 3FGfilDTCro @ 00:00:13]; an LOI that just says 'acquisition' for a C corp can hide millions between asset and stock deals [McGuireWoods LLP — OzPzqbUSgPw @ 00:12:20].

sop_steps.title: Run the closing estimate and true-up
sop_steps.action: Set the cutoff, fund escrow, close on an estimate and reconcile at 60 to 90 days.
sop_steps.detail: ProjectionHub has a lawyer and CPA define the cutoff and both sides escrow money, $50,000 each in their example [ProjectionHub — BvJfOb1y6x8 @ 00:07:22]; Colley insists the purchase agreement carry dispute procedures for the 60-to-90-day final figure [John Colley | The Investment Banking Practitioner — x_72u8PgHpc @ 00:05:00].

sections.heading: Section 3: Where Practitioners Disagree & Alternative Playbooks
paragraphs: The sharpest split is over when the peg gets locked. Anchor Partners defines NWC as receivables plus inventory minus payables and accruals. They set the peg at the trailing-twelve-month average and negotiate it inside the LOI itself, while the seller still holds leverage [ob7Q-yxAsNs @ 00:00:48]. FinanceKid runs the opposite play on lower-middle-market sell-side deals. There is no peg in the LOI, only a condition that the target is 'to be negotiated during due diligence.' The one exception is volatile working capital, where the number gets pinned before the seller grants 90-day exclusivity [8AOvKeCdAH0 @ 00:16:54]. Brett Cenkus describes the US default as sitting between the two. Price is fixed at the LOI, the LOI binds only on exclusivity and confidentiality, and the target is set during the 30, 60 or 90 days of diligence that follow [ydfu0lpiDjc @ 00:02:07]. The McGuireWoods team prices the cost of waiting from the seller's chair. Punting an issue usually favors the buyer, because sometimes a buyer just wants to get the exclusivity and live to fight another day [OzPzqbUSgPw @ 00:03:27]. The operator choice is a straight trade-off. Lock a number while seller leverage peaks, or let monthly diligence data produce a figure both sides can defend when the true-up arrives.

The second fight is over the starting anchor for the target. Brett Cenkus attacks the private equity habit of presenting historical working capital as 'the number.' His answer is 'who cares what it's been historically,' because every dollar less of working capital is a dollar in the seller's pocket [lPy47SFZqDw @ 00:01:46]. His opening position is that a profitable business needs zero working capital. His fallbacks are a forward-looking need, or history only when history is low. He concedes that denying working capital to a business that genuinely needs it is 'swimming upstream' [lPy47SFZqDw @ 00:03:08]. John Colley takes the buyer-protective line: use trailing 12 months, never a single month. He then strips out seasonal peaks, one-time receivables and accelerated collections before the average counts [x_72u8PgHpc @ 00:07:31]. FinanceKid builds the target from 24 to 36 months of monthly statements and tracks NWC as a percentage of trailing revenue. He reports that real normalizations show up in only 2 to 3 of every 10 deals [8AOvKeCdAH0 @ 00:25:15]. The gap shapes the whole negotiation. Cenkus argues from what the business needs going forward, while Colley and FinanceKid argue from measured monthly history. A seller facing a history-based buyer should arrive with a forward-looking case already built, or concede the average early.

Closing mechanics and paperwork depth also split practitioners. Brett Cenkus works the $2 to $20 million emerging middle market. He rarely uses the European locked box but recommends it for complex or low-trust deals. Price is fixed on today's balance sheet, the seller avoids riding the trade, disputes shrink and permitted leakage is allowed. The cost is heavier upfront diligence [ydfu0lpiDjc @ 00:06:37]. FinanceKid offers two alternatives to a single fixed peg. High-growth businesses get a minimum target, and seasonal or commodity businesses get a collar, for example $4 to $6 million [8AOvKeCdAH0 @ 00:46:57]. On LOI length the camps diverge hard. FinanceKid says 1 to 3 page LOIs cause deal failure. His LOIs run 6 to 9 pages covering payment forms, covenants, vendor take-back terms and the working capital target [JSIfjvnhOco @ 00:02:18]. MySaasForSale went the other way and compressed the InvoicePing deal to one page, which was signed the next day. Its terms were €88,000 at closing through a jointly chosen escrow, and two weeks of email support capped at 10 hours a week. It also set 30-day auto-ending exclusivity, 21-day diligence and a two-year non-compete limited to invoice reminder tools [OOlka50xFck @ 00:04:11]. Both formats pin hard numbers on the terms that later get fought over.
